abstract: Accurate saccades require interaction between brainstem circuitry and the cerebeJJum. A model of this interaction is described, based on Kawato's principle of feedback-error-Iearning. In the model a part of the brainstem (the superior colliculus) acts as a simple feedback controJJer with no knowledge of initial eye position, and provides an error signal for the cerebeJJum to correct for eye-muscle nonIinearities. This teaches the cerebeJJum, modelled as a CMAC, to adjust appropriately the gain on the brainstem burst-generator's internal feedback loop and so alter the size of burst sent to the motoneurons. With direction-only errors the system rapidly learns to make accurate horizontal eye movements from any starting position, and adapts realistically to subsequent simulated eye-muscle weakening or displacement of the saccadic target.

paragraphs: The paper models how the brainstem and cerebellum cooperate to make accurate saccades, the rapid eye movements that shift gaze. It uses feedback-error learning: a feedback controller supplies an error signal that teaches another component how to improve movement control. Here, the superior colliculus serves as a simple controller without knowledge of the eye’s initial position.

The cerebellum is represented by a CMAC learning model. It learns to compensate for nonlinear eye-muscle behavior by adjusting the gain of an internal feedback loop in the brainstem’s burst generator. This changes the size of the burst delivered to motoneurons, linking the learned correction to the command that moves the eye.

Using errors that indicate direction alone, the system rapidly learns accurate horizontal movements from any starting position. It also adapts realistically when the simulations weaken eye muscles or shift the target. These findings show how a relatively limited teaching signal can support adaptive accuracy through an interaction between feedback circuitry and a learned adjustment mechanism.
summary.tldr: A brainstem–cerebellum model learns accurate horizontal eye movements from direction-only errors and adapts to simulated muscle and target changes.

title: A Neural Net Model for Adaptive Control of Saccadic Accuracy by Primate Cerebellum and Brainstem

abstract: Learning of continuous valued functions using neural network en(cid:173) sembles (committees) can give improved accuracy, reliable estima(cid:173) tion of the generalization error, and active learning. The ambiguity is defined as the variation of the output of ensemble members aver(cid:173) aged over unlabeled data, so it quantifies the disagreement among the networks. It is discussed how to use the ambiguity in combina(cid:173) tion with cross-validation to give a reliable estimate of the ensemble generalization error, and how this type of ensemble cross-validation can sometimes improve performance. It is shown how to estimate the optimal weights of the ensemble members using unlabeled data. By a generalization of query by committee, it is finally shown how the ambiguity can be used to select new training data to be labeled in an active learning scheme.

paragraphs: The paper examines committees of neural networks for learning functions with continuous-valued outputs. It connects three uses of such ensembles: improving prediction accuracy, estimating error on new examples, and choosing additional training data. The common quantity is ambiguity, defined as the variation among network outputs averaged over unlabeled inputs.

Ambiguity measures how much the members disagree without requiring correct answers for those inputs. The authors explain how to combine it with cross-validation to obtain a reliable estimate of ensemble generalization error. They also discuss cases where this ensemble form of cross-validation improves performance, and show how unlabeled data can help estimate optimal weights for combining the members.

The same disagreement measure supports active learning through an extension of query by committee. It helps select new examples whose labels should be acquired. Thus, unlabeled inputs contribute both to understanding the current ensemble and to deciding how to improve it. The paper's central connection is that variation among predictors can inform evaluation, combination, and future data collection within one framework.
summary.tldr: Disagreement among neural networks helps estimate ensemble error, choose combination weights, and select new examples for labeling.

title: Neural Network Ensembles, Cross Validation, and Active Learning

abstract: We present a graph-based method for rapid, accurate search through prototypes for transformation-invariant pattern classifica(cid:173) tion. Our method has in theory the same recognition accuracy as other recent methods based on ''tangent distance" [Simard et al., 1994], since it uses the same categorization rule. Nevertheless ours is significantly faster during classification because far fewer tan(cid:173) gent distances need be computed. Crucial to the success of our system are 1) a novel graph architecture in which transformation constraints and geometric relationships among prototypes are en(cid:173) coded during learning, and 2) an improved graph search criterion, used during classification. These architectural insights are applica(cid:173) ble to a wide range of problem domains. Here we demonstrate that on a handwriting recognition task, a basic implementation of our system requires less than half the computation of the Euclidean sorting method.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the cost of searching stored prototypes when classification must tolerate transformations of an input pattern. It builds on tangent-distance methods, retaining their categorization rule while changing how candidate prototypes are searched. The central aim is to reduce the number of tangent-distance calculations needed to reach a classification decision.

The method organizes prototypes in a graph that records transformation constraints and geometric relationships during learning. At classification time, an improved graph search criterion uses that structure to guide the search. This makes the organization of the stored examples an important part of the computational method, because it helps determine which comparisons need to be performed.

The authors state that the method has the same theoretical recognition accuracy as the tangent-distance approaches using the same rule. On a handwriting recognition task, a basic implementation requires less than half the computation of Euclidean sorting. The reported benefit is therefore faster classification through fewer distance evaluations while preserving the underlying decision rule.
summary.tldr: A graph-guided prototype search reduces tangent-distance computations while preserving the underlying transformation-invariant classification rule.

title: A Rapid Graph-based Method for Arbitrary Transformation-Invariant Pattern Classification

abstract: We present an algorithm that samples the hypothesis space of ker(cid:173) nel classifiers. Given a uniform prior over normalised weight vectors and a likelihood based on a model of label noise leads to a piece(cid:173) wise constant posterior that can be sampled by the kernel Gibbs sampler (KGS). The KGS is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method that chooses a random direction in parameter space and samples from the resulting piecewise constant density along the line chosen. The KGS can be used as an analytical tool for the exploration of Bayesian transduction, Bayes point machines, active learning, and evidence-based model selection on small data sets that are contam(cid:173) inated with label noise. For a simple toy example we demonstrate experimentally how a Bayes point machine based on the KGS out(cid:173) performs an SVM that is incapable of taking into account label noise.

paragraphs: The Kernel Gibbs Sampler explores the hypothesis space of kernel classifiers through Bayesian sampling. The setup assumes a uniform prior over normalized weight vectors and a likelihood based on label noise. Together, these choices produce a posterior density that is constant within separate regions of parameter space.

The algorithm exploits that structure with Markov chain Monte Carlo. It chooses a random direction in parameter space and samples from the piecewise constant density along the resulting line. Repeating this operation provides a way to explore the posterior over classifiers, making the label-noise model part of the inference procedure.

The authors present the sampler as an analytical tool for small datasets with noisy labels, with possible uses in Bayesian transduction, Bayes point machines, active learning, and evidence-based model selection. In a simple toy experiment, a Bayes point machine using the sampler outperforms an SVM that cannot account for label noise. That comparison illustrates the usefulness of explicitly representing noisy labels in the particular example studied.
summary.tldr: The Kernel Gibbs Sampler samples noisy-label classifier posteriors through random-direction updates and supports Bayesian analysis of small datasets.

title: The Kernel Gibbs Sampler

abstract: It is well known that under noisy conditions we can hear speech much more clearly when we read the speaker's lips. This sug(cid:173) gests the utility of audio-visual information for the task of speech enhancement. We propose a method to exploit audio-visual cues to enable speech separation under non-stationary noise and with a single microphone. We revise and extend HMM-based speech enhancement techniques, in which signal and noise models are fac(cid:173) tori ally combined, to incorporate visual lip information and em(cid:173) ploy novel signal HMMs in which the dynamics of narrow-band and wide band components are factorial. We avoid the combina(cid:173) torial explosion in the factorial model by using a simple approxi(cid:173) mate inference technique to quickly estimate the clean signals in a mixture. We present a preliminary evaluation of this approach using a small-vocabulary audio-visual database, showing promising improvements in machine intelligibility for speech enhanced using audio and visual information.

paragraphs: This paper uses visible lip movements to help separate speech from noise recorded by a single microphone. The motivation is that visual speech cues can make noisy speech easier to understand. The proposed method targets non-stationary noise, where the interference changes over time and must be handled alongside the speech signal.

The authors extend speech enhancement methods based on hidden Markov models by incorporating lip information into a factorial combination of signal and noise models. They also introduce signal models with separate dynamics for narrow-band and wide-band components. This represents multiple evolving aspects of the recording, but combining them creates a potentially expensive inference problem.

A simple approximate inference method avoids the combinatorial growth of the factorial model and quickly estimates clean signals from the mixture. A preliminary evaluation on a small-vocabulary audiovisual database finds promising improvements in machine intelligibility. The evidence therefore supports the usefulness of combining sound and lip information in that evaluation, with the preliminary and limited-vocabulary setting remaining part of the claim.
summary.tldr: An audiovisual hidden Markov model uses lip movements to improve preliminary single-microphone speech separation results under changing noise.

title: Audio-Visual Sound Separation Via Hidden Markov Models

abstract: We develop a systems theoretical treatment of a behavioural system that interacts with its environment in a closed loop situation such that its mo- tor actions inﬂuence its sensor inputs. The simplest form of a feedback is a reﬂex. Reﬂexes occur always “too late”; i.e., only after a (unpleas- ant, painful, dangerous) reﬂex-eliciting sensor event has occurred. This deﬁnes an objective problem which can be solved if another sensor input exists which can predict the primary reﬂex and can generate an earlier reaction. In contrast to previous approaches, our linear learning algo- rithm allows for an analytical proof that this system learns to apply feed- forward control with the result that slow feedback loops are replaced by their equivalent feed-forward controller creating a forward model. In other words, learning turns the reactive system into a pro-active system. By means of a robot implementation we demonstrate the applicability of the theoretical results which can be used in a variety of different areas in physics and engineering.

paragraphs: A reflex reacts after its triggering sensory event has already occurred. This paper asks how a system can learn to act earlier when another sensory input predicts that event. It studies this question in a closed loop, where motor actions change the environment and thereby influence the sensory inputs the system subsequently receives.

The authors develop a linear learning algorithm and a systems-theoretic analysis of its behavior. Their analytical result shows that the studied system learns feed-forward control, replacing a slow feedback loop with an equivalent anticipatory controller. The availability of a predictive sensory input is central: it provides the information needed to generate an earlier response.

This creates a forward model of the reflex and turns the system's behavior from reactive to proactive. A robot implementation demonstrates the applicability of the theoretical results. The work connects learning and control by showing how a predictive cue can support earlier action within a system whose own movements influence what it senses.
summary.tldr: A linear learning rule lets a closed-loop system use predictive sensory cues to replace delayed reflex feedback with anticipatory control.

title: Learning a Forward Model of a Reflex

abstract: We report and compare the performance of different learning algorithms based on data from cortical recordings. The task is to predict the orienta- tion of visual stimuli from the activity of a population of simultaneously recorded neurons. We compare several ways of improving the coding of the input (i.e., the spike data) as well as of the output (i.e., the orienta- tion), and report the results obtained using different kernel algorithms.
originalAbstract: We report and compare the performance of different learning algorithms based on data from cortical recordings. The task is to predict the orienta- tion of visual stimuli from the activity of a population of simultaneously recorded neurons. We compare several ways of improving the coding of the input (i.e., the spike data) as well as of the output (i.e., the orienta- tion), and report the results obtained using different kernel algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether the activity of a recorded neural population can predict the orientation of a visual stimulus. The input consists of spike data from cortical neurons recorded simultaneously. The learning task connects a population's observed activity to a property of the stimulus associated with that activity.

The comparison addresses both sides of the prediction problem. The authors examine different ways to encode the spike data supplied to the learner and different ways to encode the orientation being predicted. This distinguishes the choice of learning algorithm from the choices used to represent its inputs and outputs, making representation an explicit part of the study.

Several kernel algorithms are evaluated using these cortical recordings, and the paper reports their prediction results. Its contribution is a comparative examination of neural decoding in which the algorithm and the coding of the task are considered together. The study therefore asks not only how a learner handles recorded spikes, but also how the form of the prediction problem affects that learning.
summary.tldr: The paper compares kernel algorithms and input/output encodings for predicting visual orientation from simultaneously recorded neural spikes.

title: Prediction on Spike Data Using Kernel Algorithms

abstract: Many techniques for complex speech processing such as denoising and deconvolution, time/frequency warping, multiple speaker separation, and multiple microphone analysis operate on sequences of short-time power spectra (spectrograms), a representation which is often well-suited to these tasks. However, a signiﬁcant problem with algorithms that manipu- late spectrograms is that the output spectrogram does not include a phase component, which is needed to create a time-domain signal that has good perceptual quality. Here we describe a generative model of time-domain speech signals and their spectrograms, and show how an efﬁcient opti- mizer can be used to ﬁnd the maximum a posteriori speech signal, given the spectrogram. In contrast to techniques that alternate between esti- mating the phase and a spectrally-consistent signal, our technique di- rectly infers the speech signal, thus jointly optimizing the phase and a spectrally-consistent signal. We compare our technique with a standard method using signal-to-noise ratios, but we also provide audio ﬁles on the web for the purpose of demonstrating the improvement in perceptual quality that our technique offers.

paragraphs: Many speech-processing methods work with sequences of short-time power spectra. After such a representation is modified, it lacks the phase information needed to reconstruct a time-domain signal with good perceptual quality. This paper focuses on recovering a speech waveform from that phaseless spectrogram.

The authors introduce a generative model connecting speech waveforms with their spectrograms. An efficient optimizer finds the maximum a posteriori waveform given the spectrogram. Instead of alternating between separate phase estimates and spectrally consistent signals, the method infers the waveform directly. This makes phase and spectral consistency parts of a joint optimization.

The paper compares the approach with a standard method using signal-to-noise ratios and supplies audio demonstrations of improved perceptual quality. The stated benefit concerns the reconstructed speech as something listeners hear, alongside its numerical evaluation. The contribution is a probabilistic reconstruction formulation that works directly on the desired signal while accounting jointly for information that phaseless spectral processing leaves unresolved.
summary.tldr: A generative model reconstructs speech directly from phaseless spectrograms by jointly optimizing the waveform and its implied phase.

title: Probabilistic Inference of Speech Signals from Phaseless Spectrograms

abstract: We propose a new interpretation of spiking neurons as Bayesian integrators accumulating evidence over time about events in the external world or the body, and communicating to other neurons their certainties about these events. In this model, spikes signal the occurrence of new information, i.e. what cannot be predicted from the past activity. As a result, firing statistics are close to Poisson, albeit providing a deterministic representation of probabilities. We proceed to develop a theory of Bayesian inference in spiking neural networks, recurrent interactions implementing a variant of belief propagation.

paragraphs: This paper proposes interpreting spiking neurons as units that accumulate evidence about events in the world or the body. A neuron maintains a degree of certainty as information arrives over time and communicates that certainty to other neurons. Bayesian inference provides the framework for describing how evidence changes these internal beliefs.

In the proposed model, spikes communicate information that could not be predicted from previous activity. This makes the timing of a spike meaningful in relation to what has already been conveyed. The resulting firing statistics are close to Poisson, even though the probabilities have a deterministic representation. Thus, apparently irregular spike activity can arise within a structured account of probabilistic computation.

The authors extend this interpretation from individual neurons to interacting spiking networks. Recurrent connections implement a variant of belief propagation, allowing evidence to influence beliefs through exchanges between neurons. The contribution is a proposed computational theory linking evidence accumulation, spike generation, and network interactions within a common probabilistic interpretation.
summary.tldr: The paper models spikes as new information in Bayesian evidence accumulation and recurrent neural interactions as a form of belief propagation.

title: Bayesian inference in spiking neurons

abstract: We study the problem of online prediction of a noisy labeling of a graph with the perceptron. We address both label noise and concept noise. Graph learning is framed as an instance of prediction on a finite set. To treat label noise we show that the hinge loss bounds derived by Gentile [1] for online perceptron learning can be transformed to relative mistake bounds with an optimal leading constant when applied to prediction on a finite set. These bounds depend crucially on the norm of the learned concept. Often the norm of a concept can vary dramatically with only small perturbations in a labeling. We analyze a simple transformation that stabilizes the norm under perturbations. We derive an upper bound that depends only on natural properties of the graph the graph diameter and the cut size of a partitioning of the graph which are only indirectly dependent on the size of the graph. The impossibility of such bounds for the graph geodesic nearest neighbors algorithm will be demonstrated.

paragraphs: The paper studies online prediction of graph labels with a perceptron when the labeling is noisy. It addresses both label noise and concept noise by framing graph learning as prediction over a finite set. Within that formulation, existing hinge-loss bounds can be converted into relative mistake bounds with an optimal leading constant.

A crucial issue is that these bounds depend on the norm of the learned concept. Small changes in a labeling can sometimes produce large changes in that norm, making the bound sensitive to perturbations. The authors analyze a simple transformation that stabilizes the norm, addressing this sensitivity within the theoretical treatment.

They derive an upper bound depending on graph diameter and the cut size of a graph partition, with graph size entering only indirectly through those properties. This connects prediction guarantees to structural features of the graph and its labeling. The paper also demonstrates that bounds of this kind are impossible for the graph geodesic nearest-neighbor algorithm, distinguishing the perceptron analysis from that alternative.
summary.tldr: A stabilized perceptron analysis bounds noisy graph-prediction mistakes using graph diameter and partition cut size.

title: Prediction on a Graph with a Perceptron

abstract: Everyday social interactions are heavily influenced by our snap judgments about others goals. Even young infants can infer the goals of intentional agents from observing how they interact with objects and other agents in their environment: e.g., that one agent is helping or hindering anothers attempt to get up a hill or open a box. We propose a model for how people can infer these social goals from actions, based on inverse planning in multiagent Markov decision problems (MDPs). The model infers the goal most likely to be driving an agents behavior by assuming the agent acts approximately rationally given environmental constraints and its model of other agents present. We also present behavioral evidence in support of this model over a simpler, perceptual cue-based alternative.

We propose a model for how people can infer these social goals from actions, based on inverse planning in multiagent Markov decision problems (MDPs). paragraphs: People often judge another agent's social goal from a short sequence of actions, such as whether it helps or obstructs someone trying to reach an objective. This paper develops a computational explanation for that judgment. The problem is to infer an underlying intention from observed behavior in an environment containing other agents.

The model uses inverse planning in multiagent Markov decision problems. It reasons backward from an action to the goal that would make the action plausible. Its key assumption is that an agent acts approximately rationally, taking account of environmental constraints and its own model of the other agents present. Social interpretation therefore depends on what an action accomplishes in context.

The authors present behavioral evidence favoring this account over a simpler alternative based on perceptual cues. That evidence supports the idea that social-goal judgments involve reasoning about purposeful action. The model provides a way to connect an observed interaction with a likely intention through assumptions about planning and other agents.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian inverse-planning model explains helping and hindering judgments by inferring goals under an assumption of approximately rational action.

title: Help or Hinder: Bayesian Models of Social Goal Inference

abstract: For over half a century, psychologists have been struck by how poor people are at expressing their internal sensations, impressions, and evaluations via rating scales. When individuals make judgments, they are incapable of using an absolute rating scale, and instead rely on reference points from recent experience. This relativity of judgment limits the usefulness of responses provided by individuals to surveys, questionnaires, and evaluation forms. Fortunately, the cognitive processes that transform internal states to responses are not simply noisy, but rather are influenced by recent experience in a lawful manner. We explore techniques to remove sequential dependencies, and thereby decontaminate a series of ratings to obtain more meaningful human judgments. In our formulation, decontamination is fundamentally a problem of inferring latent states (internal sensations) which, because of the relativity of judgment, have temporal dependencies. We propose a decontamination solution using a conditional random field with constraints motivated by psychological theories of relative judgment. Our exploration of decontamination models is supported by two experiments we conducted to obtain ground-truth rating data on a simple length estimation task. Our decontamination techniques yield an over 20% reduction in the error of human judgments.

paragraphs: Human ratings can depend on recent experience rather than a stable, absolute scale. This paper treats those sequential effects as systematic influences that can be modeled, instead of merely unpredictable noise. Its goal is to recover more meaningful judgments from a sequence whose individual ratings have been shaped by earlier experiences.

The authors formulate this correction as inference over latent internal states, such as sensations that are not directly observed. Relative judgment introduces temporal dependencies into that inference problem. Their proposed solution uses a conditional random field with constraints motivated by psychological theories, connecting the computational model to an account of how people produce ratings.

Two experiments on a simple length-estimation task supply ground-truth rating data for examining the models. The decontamination techniques reduce human judgment error by more than 20% in the reported work. This supports the possibility of correcting systematic sequential influences in that setting; surveys and questionnaires provide the broader motivation, while the stated experimental evidence comes from length estimation.
summary.tldr: A psychologically constrained conditional random field corrects sequential effects in ratings, reducing judgment error by over 20% in length-estimation experiments.

title: Improving Human Judgments by Decontaminating Sequential Dependencies

abstract: We discuss new methods for the recovery of signals with block-sparse structure, based on l1-minimization. Our emphasis is on the efficiently computable error bounds for the recovery routines. We optimize these bounds with respect to the method parameters to construct the estimators with improved statistical properties. We justify the proposed approach with an oracle inequality which links the properties of the recovery algorithms and the best estimation performance.
originalAbstract: We discuss new methods for the recovery of signals with block-sparse structure, based on l1-minimization. Our emphasis is on the efficiently computable error bounds for the recovery routines. We optimize these bounds with respect to the method parameters to construct the estimators with improved statistical properties. We justify the proposed approach with an oracle inequality which links the properties of the recovery algorithms and the best estimation performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering signals with block-sparse structure, where sparsity is organized in blocks. The proposed recovery methods are based on l1 minimization. Their distinguishing focus is not only producing an estimate, but also obtaining error bounds that can be computed efficiently for the recovery routines.

The authors use those bounds to choose method parameters. Specifically, they optimize the bounds with respect to the parameters, constructing estimators with improved statistical properties. This makes the error analysis an active ingredient in designing the estimator: a computable assessment of recovery accuracy guides how the procedure is configured.

The theoretical justification takes the form of an oracle inequality connecting properties of the recovery algorithms with the best estimation performance. Such a comparison gives a way to assess the proposed procedures relative to a benchmark for estimation quality. The contribution is the combination of block-structured recovery, efficiently evaluated error guarantees, and parameter selection driven by those guarantees, rather than treating accuracy analysis as a separate step after the method has been chosen.
summary.tldr: Computable error bounds guide parameter selection for l1-based block-sparse signal recovery, supported by an oracle inequality.

title: On the accuracy of l1-filtering of signals with block-sparse structure

abstract: This paper studies privacy preserving M-estimators using perturbed histograms. The proposed approach allows the release of a wide class of M-estimators with both differential privacy and statistical utility without knowing a priori the particular inference procedure. The performance of the proposed method is demonstrated through a careful study of the convergence rates. A practical algorithm is given and applied on a real world data set containing both continuous and categorical variables.

The proposed approach allows the release of a wide class of M-estimators with both differential privacy and statistical utility without knowing a priori the particular inference procedure. A practical algorithm is given and applied on a real world data set containing both continuous and categorical variables.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to release statistical estimates while providing differential privacy. Its focus is a broad family of procedures called M-estimators. A central challenge is to preserve useful statistical information without requiring the data-release process to know in advance exactly which inference procedure will later be used.

The proposed approach uses perturbed histograms as the basis for releasing estimates. By working through this shared representation, the method supports a wide class of M-estimators while combining a privacy guarantee with statistical utility. The ability to avoid choosing the particular inference procedure beforehand is a defining feature of the approach.

The authors analyze convergence rates to characterize the method’s statistical performance as the amount of data grows. They also provide a practical algorithm and apply it to a real dataset containing both continuous and categorical variables. Together, the analysis and application connect the general release strategy to an implementable procedure, showing how privacy-preserving estimation can accommodate mixed kinds of data.
summary.tldr: Perturbed histograms support differentially private release of a wide class of M-estimators without choosing the inference procedure in advance.

title: Differentially Private M-Estimators

abstract: We theoretically analyze and compare the following five popular multiclass classification methods: One vs. All, All Pairs, Tree-based classifiers, Error Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) with randomly generated code matrices, and Multiclass SVM. In the first four methods, the classification is based on a reduction to binary classification. We consider the case where the binary classifier comes from a class of VC dimension $d$, and in particular from the class of halfspaces over $\reals^d$. We analyze both the estimation error and the approximation error of these methods. Our analysis reveals interesting conclusions of practical relevance, regarding the success of the different approaches under various conditions. Our proof technique employs tools from VC theory to analyze the \emph{approximation error} of hypothesis classes. This is in sharp contrast to most, if not all, previous uses of VC theory, which only deal with estimation error.

The first four build multiclass decisions from binary classifiers. The analysis considers binary hypothesis classes with VC dimension d, including halfspaces in d-dimensional real space.

Estimation error concerns learning from a limited sample, while approximation error concerns what a chosen hypothesis class can represent. Studying both allows the authors to examine how the construction of a multiclass classifier affects its possibilities as well as its demands on data.

summary.tldr: A theoretical comparison of five multiclass methods examines both estimation and approximation error, using VC theory in an unusual role.

title: Multiclass Learning Approaches: A Theoretical Comparison with Implications

abstract: Links between probabilistic and non-probabilistic learning algorithms can arise by performing small-variance asymptotics, i.e., letting the variance of particular distributions in a graphical model go to zero. For instance, in the context of clustering, such an approach yields precise connections between the k-means and EM algorithms. In this paper, we explore small-variance asymptotics for exponential family Dirichlet process (DP) and hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP) mixture models. Utilizing connections between exponential family distributions and Bregman divergences, we derive novel clustering algorithms from the asymptotic limit of the DP and HDP mixtures that feature the scalability of existing hard clustering methods as well as the flexibility of Bayesian nonparametric models. We focus on special cases of our analysis for discrete-data problems, including topic modeling, and we demonstrate the utility of our results by applying variants of our algorithms to problems arising in vision and document analysis.

title: Small-Variance Asymptotics for Exponential Family Dirichlet Process Mixture Models

abstract: This paper presents four major results towards solving decentralized partially observable Markov decision problems (DecPOMDPs) culminating in an algorithm that outperforms all existing algorithms on all but one standard infinite-horizon benchmark problems. (1) We give an integer program that solves collaborative Bayesian games (CBGs). The program is notable because its linear relaxation is very often integral. (2) We show that a DecPOMDP with bounded belief can be converted to a POMDP (albeit with actions exponential in the number of beliefs). These actions correspond to strategies of a CBG. (3) We present a method to transform any DecPOMDP into a DecPOMDP with bounded beliefs (the number of beliefs is a free parameter) using optimal (not lossless) belief compression. (4) We show that the combination of these results opens the door for new classes of DecPOMDP algorithms based on previous POMDP algorithms. We choose one such algorithm, point-based valued iteration, and modify it to produce the first tractable value iteration method for DecPOMDPs which outperforms existing algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper develops a route to solving decentralized partially observable decision problems by connecting them to tools for ordinary POMDPs. It first introduces an integer program for collaborative Bayesian games. Its linear relaxation is often integral, making that relaxation useful in many instances without claiming this property always holds.

The authors then show that a DecPOMDP with a bounded number of beliefs can be converted into a POMDP. The converted actions represent strategies in a collaborative Bayesian game, although their number grows exponentially with the number of beliefs. A further method transforms any DecPOMDP into one with bounded beliefs through optimal compression, with the number of retained beliefs chosen as a free parameter.

That compression is explicitly not lossless. Combining the results nevertheless enables adaptation of POMDP algorithms, and the authors develop a tractable point-based value-iteration method for DecPOMDPs. It outperforms existing algorithms on all but one standard infinite-horizon benchmark problem. The achievement is a practical algorithm built from the connections among game solving, belief compression, and centralized planning.
summary.tldr: Optimal but lossy belief compression enables tractable DecPOMDP value iteration with strong results on standard infinite-horizon benchmarks.

title: Point Based Value Iteration with Optimal Belief Compression for Dec-POMDPs

abstract: Finite-State Transducers (FST) are a standard tool for modeling paired input-output sequences and are used in numerous applications, ranging from computational biology to natural language processing. Recently Balle et al. presented a spectral algorithm for learning FST from samples of aligned input-output sequences. In this paper we address the more realistic, yet challenging setting where the alignments are unknown to the learning algorithm. We frame FST learning as finding a low rank Hankel matrix satisfying constraints derived from observable statistics. Under this formulation, we provide identifiability results for FST distributions. Then, following previous work on rank minimization, we propose a regularized convex relaxation of this objective which is based on minimizing a nuclear norm penalty subject to linear constraints and can be solved efficiently.

paragraphs: Finite-state transducers model relationships between paired input and output sequences. Learning them is more difficult when the correspondence between positions in the two sequences is unknown. This paper addresses that setting, extending beyond an earlier spectral learning approach that required aligned input-output samples.

The authors reformulate learning as finding a low-rank Hankel matrix that satisfies constraints obtained from observable statistics. This expresses the hidden sequence model through a structured matrix and restrictions that can be derived without supplied alignments. Within this formulation, they establish identifiability results for transducer distributions, addressing when the observable information can distinguish the underlying distribution.

To obtain an efficiently solvable objective, the paper proposes a regularized convex relaxation of rank minimization. It uses a nuclear-norm penalty together with linear constraints. This gives the matrix formulation a computational route rather than leaving it as a difficult rank-search problem. The contribution combines distribution-identification theory with an efficient relaxed optimization approach for learning paired-sequence models when their alignments are not available.
summary.tldr: Unaligned transducer learning is formulated as constrained low-rank matrix estimation, with identifiability results and an efficiently solvable convex relaxation.

title: Unsupervised Spectral Learning of Finite State Transducers

abstract: We consider the problem of online optimization, where a learner chooses a decision from a given decision set and suffers some loss associated with the decision and the state of the environment. The learner's objective is to minimize its cumulative regret against the best fixed decision in hindsight. Over the past few decades numerous variants have been considered, with many algorithms designed to achieve sub-linear regret in the worst case. However, this level of robustness comes at a cost. Proposed algorithms are often over-conservative, failing to adapt to the actual complexity of the loss sequence which is often far from the worst case. In this paper we introduce a general algorithm that, provided with a safe learning algorithm and an opportunistic benchmark, can effectively combine good worst-case guarantees with much improved performance on easy data. We derive general theoretical bounds on the regret of the proposed algorithm and discuss its implementation in a wide range of applications, notably in the problem of learning with shifting experts (a recent COLT open problem). Finally, we provide numerical simulations in the setting of prediction with expert advice with comparisons to the state of the art.

paragraphs: In online optimization, a learner repeatedly makes decisions and incurs losses as the environment unfolds. Its performance is often measured by regret: accumulated loss compared with the best single decision chosen after seeing the whole sequence. Algorithms designed for difficult worst cases can be overly cautious when the actual sequence is easier.

This paper introduces a general method that combines a safe learning algorithm with an opportunistic benchmark. The goal is to preserve useful worst-case guarantees while taking advantage of favorable data. The construction is explicitly based on having these two ingredients, rather than claiming that every existing online algorithm automatically adapts well to easier sequences.

The authors derive general regret bounds and discuss implementations across several applications, including learning with shifting experts. They also present numerical simulations for prediction with expert advice and compare against existing leading methods. The contribution is a framework for reconciling robustness with adaptability, supported by theoretical guarantees and empirical comparisons in the stated prediction setting.
summary.tldr: A general online-optimization method combines a safe algorithm with an opportunistic benchmark to exploit easy data while retaining worst-case guarantees.

title: Exploiting easy data in online optimization

abstract: Deriving from the gradient vector of a generative model of local features, Fisher vector coding (FVC) has been identified as an effective coding method for image classification. Most, if not all, FVC implementations employ the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to characterize the generation process of local features. This choice has shown to be sufficient for traditional low dimensional local features, e.g., SIFT; and typically, good performance can be achieved with only a few hundred Gaussian distributions. However, the same number of Gaussians is insufficient to model the feature space spanned by higher dimensional local features, which have become popular recently. In order to improve the modeling capacity for high dimensional features, it turns out to be inefficient and computationally impractical to simply increase the number of Gaussians. In this paper, we propose a model in which each local feature is drawn from a Gaussian distribution whose mean vector is sampled from a subspace. With certain approximation, this model can be converted to a sparse coding procedure and the learning/inference problems can be readily solved by standard sparse coding methods. By calculating the gradient vector of the proposed model, we derive a new fisher vector encoding strategy, termed Sparse Coding based Fisher Vector Coding (SCFVC). Moreover, we adopt the recently developed Deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) descriptor as a high dimensional local feature and implement image classification with the proposed SCFVC. Our experimental evaluations demonstrate that our method not only significantly outperforms the traditional GMM based Fisher vector encoding but also achieves the state-of-the-art performance in generic object recognition, indoor scene, and fine-grained image classification problems.

The approach addresses the modeling challenge by changing how feature variation is represented, with evidence of benefits across the tested classification settings.
summary.tldr: A sparse coding generative model produces Fisher vectors better suited to high-dimensional local image features.

title: Encoding High Dimensional Local Features by Sparse Coding Based Fisher Vectors

abstract: The class of shuffle ideals is a fundamental sub-family of regular languages. The shuffle ideal generated by a string set $U$ is the collection of all strings containing some string $u \in U$ as a (not necessarily contiguous) subsequence. In spite of its apparent simplicity, the problem of learning a shuffle ideal from given data is known to be computationally intractable. In this paper, we study the PAC learnability of shuffle ideals and present positive results on this learning problem under element-wise independent and identical distributions and Markovian distributions in the statistical query model. A constrained generalization to learning shuffle ideals under product distributions is also provided. In the empirical direction, we propose a heuristic algorithm for learning shuffle ideals from given labeled strings under general unrestricted distributions. Experiments demonstrate the advantage for both efficiency and accuracy of our algorithm.

paragraphs: A shuffle ideal consists of strings that contain at least one generating string as a subsequence. The required symbols must appear in order, but other symbols may occur between them. Although this describes a simple-looking family of regular languages, learning such a language from data is computationally intractable in general.

The paper investigates whether restrictions on how strings are distributed make learning feasible. It establishes positive PAC-learning results in the statistical query model for element-wise independent and identical distributions and for Markovian distributions. It also gives a constrained extension to product distributions. These results tie learnability to particular distributional structure rather than removing the general difficulty.

For unrestricted distributions, the authors take an empirical route and propose a heuristic for learning from labeled strings. Experiments demonstrate advantages in both efficiency and accuracy. The theoretical and empirical contributions serve different purposes: the former identify settings with learning guarantees, while the latter provides an experimentally supported method for broader data. Together they clarify where provable learning is available and how the problem can be approached outside those settings.
summary.tldr: Shuffle ideals become provably learnable under specified distribution restrictions, while a heuristic performs well experimentally on unrestricted data.

title: Learning Shuffle Ideals Under Restricted Distributions

abstract: Models for collecting and aggregating categorical data on crowdsourcing platforms typically fall into two broad categories: those assuming agents honest and consistent but with heterogeneous error rates, and those assuming agents strategic and seek to maximize their expected reward. The former often leads to tractable aggregation of elicited data, while the latter usually focuses on optimal elicitation and does not consider aggregation. In this paper, we develop a Bayesian model, wherein agents have differing quality of information, but also respond to incentives. Our model generalizes both categories and enables the joint exploration of optimal elicitation and aggregation. This model enables our exploration, both analytically and experimentally, of optimal aggregation of categorical data and optimal multiple-choice interface design.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced categorical responses depend both on what contributors know and on how they respond to incentives. Existing modeling approaches often emphasize one side: either honest contributors with differing error rates or strategic contributors seeking rewards. This paper develops a Bayesian model that includes differences in information quality alongside incentive-sensitive behavior.

That joint treatment connects two decisions that are often studied separately. Elicitation concerns how to obtain responses, while aggregation concerns how to combine the responses into a useful result. Because the model includes both contributor knowledge and strategic choices, it allows those decisions to be examined within the same probabilistic framework.

The authors use analytical and experimental work to investigate optimal aggregation and the design of multiple-choice interfaces. The contribution is a model that generalizes both earlier categories and supports reasoning about collection and combination together. Its significance is that interface design and aggregation can be evaluated with a shared account of the people producing the data, rather than relying on separate behavioral assumptions.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian crowdsourcing model combines unequal information quality with strategic behavior to study response collection and aggregation jointly.

title: Eliciting Categorical Data for Optimal Aggregation

abstract: It has recently been shown that supervised learning linear classifiers with two of the most popular losses, the logistic and square loss, is equivalent to optimizing an equivalent loss over sufficient statistics about the class: Rademacher observations (rados). It has also been shown that learning over rados brings solutions to two prominent problems for which the state of the art of learning from examples can be comparatively inferior and in fact less convenient: protecting and learning from private examples, learning from distributed datasets without entity resolution. Bis repetita placent: the two proofs of equivalence are different and rely on specific properties of the corresponding losses, so whether these can be unified and generalized inevitably comes to mind. This is our first contribution: we show how they can be fit into the same theory for the equivalence between example and rado losses. As a second contribution, we show that the generalization unveils a surprising new connection to regularized learning, and in particular a sufficient condition under which regularizing the loss over examples is equivalent to regularizing the rados (i.e. the data) in the equivalent rado loss, in such a way that an efficient algorithm for one regularized rado loss may be as efficient when changing the regularizer. This is our third contribution: we give a formal boosting algorithm for the regularized exponential rado-loss which boost with any of the ridge, lasso, \slope, l_\infty, or elastic nets, using the same master routine for all. Because the regularized exponential rado-loss is the equivalent of the regularized logistic loss over examples we obtain the first efficient proxy to the minimisation of the regularized logistic loss over examples using such a wide spectrum of regularizers. Experiments with a readily available code display that regularization significantly improves rado-based learning and compares favourably with example-based learning.

paragraphs: Rademacher observations, or rados, are class-related sufficient statistics that can support learning linear classifiers. Earlier work established separate equivalences between learning from examples and learning from rados for logistic and square losses. This paper develops a common theory that unifies and generalizes those previously separate results.

The theory also exposes a connection to regularization. Under a sufficient condition, regularizing the example-based loss is equivalent to modifying the rados used in the corresponding rado loss. This moves the regularization effect into the transformed data and suggests that an efficient learning routine may remain efficient when the regularizer changes.

Because this rado loss corresponds to regularized logistic loss over examples, the algorithm supplies an efficient proxy across that range of penalties. Experiments show that regularization substantially improves rado-based learning and compares favorably with example-based learning, supporting the practical value of the theoretical connection.
summary.tldr: A unified theory connects example and rado losses, enabling one boosting routine to handle a broad range of regularizers.

title: On Regularizing Rademacher Observation Losses

abstract: We developed task-optimized deep neural networks (DNNs) that achieved state-of-the-art performance in different evaluation scenarios for automatic music tagging. These DNNs were subsequently used to probe the neural representations of music. Representational similarity analysis revealed the existence of a representational gradient across the superior temporal gyrus (STG). Anterior STG was shown to be more sensitive to low-level stimulus features encoded in shallow DNN layers whereas posterior STG was shown to be more sensitive to high-level stimulus features encoded in deep DNN layers.

Anterior STG was shown to be more sensitive to low-level stimulus features encoded in shallow DNN layers whereas posterior STG was shown to be more sensitive to high-level stimulus features encoded in deep DNN layers.

paragraphs: The researchers developed deep neural networks for automatic music tagging and then used their learned representations to investigate how the brain represents music. The networks achieved state-of-the-art tagging performance across different evaluation scenarios. Their role in the neuroscience analysis was to provide representations at different depths that could be compared with neural representations.

The comparison used representational similarity analysis. Rather than treating music representation as a single undifferentiated quantity, the study related brain responses to features encoded at shallow and deep network layers. This provided a way to examine whether different parts of the superior temporal gyrus were associated with different levels of musical stimulus information.

The reported result was a gradient across that brain region. Anterior superior temporal gyrus was more sensitive to low-level features represented in shallow layers, whereas posterior superior temporal gyrus was more sensitive to high-level features represented in deeper layers. These findings connect network representation depth with differences across brain locations; they establish a representational relationship rather than identifying the brain with the trained network.
summary.tldr: Music-tagging networks reveal a gradient linking anterior and posterior superior temporal gyrus to lower- and higher-level musical features, respectively.

title: Brains on Beats

abstract: A novel variational autoencoder is developed to model images, as well as associated labels or captions. The Deep Generative Deconvolutional Network (DGDN) is used as a decoder of the latent image features, and a deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is used as an image encoder; the CNN is used to approximate a distribution for the latent DGDN features/code. The latent code is also linked to generative models for labels (Bayesian support vector machine) or captions (recurrent neural network). When predicting a label/caption for a new image at test, averaging is performed across the distribution of latent codes; this is computationally efficient as a consequence of the learned CNN-based encoder. Since the framework is capable of modeling the image in the presence/absence of associated labels/captions, a new semi-supervised setting is manifested for CNN learning with images; the framework even allows unsupervised CNN learning, based on images alone.

Since the framework is capable of modeling the image in the presence/absence of associated labels/captions, a new semi-supervised setting is manifested for CNN learning with images; the framework even allows unsupervised CNN learning, based on images alone.

A convolutional neural network encodes an image into an approximate distribution over latent features. A Deep Generative Deconvolutional Network decodes those features as part of the image model.

The same latent code connects to a Bayesian support vector machine for labels or a recurrent neural network for captions. When predicting for a new image, the model averages over the distribution of latent codes. The learned image encoder makes this averaging computationally efficient, allowing predictions to account for multiple possible latent representations.

Because the framework models images whether or not they have annotations, it supports semi-supervised CNN learning from a mixture of annotated and unannotated images. It also permits unsupervised learning from images alone. The central contribution is a shared generative framework linking image representation, label prediction, and caption generation, with annotation availability determining which learning signals can be used rather than whether an image can enter the model.
summary.tldr: A variational autoencoder links images to labels or captions through latent-code distributions and supports learning with partial or no annotations.

title: Variational Autoencoder for Deep Learning of Images, Labels and Captions

abstract: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional multi-response linear models with structured parameters. By exploiting the noise correlations among different responses, we propose an alternating estimation (AltEst) procedure to estimate the model parameters based on the generalized Dantzig selector (GDS). Under suitable sample size and resampling assumptions, we show that the error of the estimates generated by AltEst, with high probability, converges linearly to certain minimum achievable level, which can be tersely expressed by a few geometric measures, such as Gaussian width of sets related to the parameter structure. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-asymptotic statistical guarantee for such AltEst-type algorithm applied to estimation with general structures.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear models that predict several responses at once while using many parameters with an underlying structure. Its central observation is that noise across the responses can be correlated. Those relationships provide information that an estimation procedure can exploit when learning the model parameters.

The proposed alternating estimation procedure, AltEst, builds on the generalized Dantzig selector. The theoretical question is how the estimation error changes as the procedure progresses. Under suitable sample-size and resampling assumptions, the authors show that the error decreases at a linear rate with high probability until it reaches a particular achievable floor. Linear convergence here describes repeated proportional reduction toward that floor, rather than an assurance that error disappears.

The error floor is expressed through geometric quantities associated with the parameter structure, including Gaussian width. This connects statistical accuracy to the shape of the structured estimation problem. The authors identify their result as the first finite-sample statistical guarantee for an alternating procedure of this kind accommodating general structures.
summary.tldr: AltEst exploits correlated response noise and, under stated sampling assumptions, converges geometrically toward a structure-dependent estimation error floor.

title: Alternating Estimation for Structured High-Dimensional Multi-Response Models

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new technique named \textit{Stochastic Path-Integrated Differential EstimatoR} (SPIDER), which can be used to track many deterministic quantities of interests with significantly reduced computational cost. Combining SPIDER with the method of normalized gradient descent, we propose SPIDER-SFO that solve non-convex stochastic optimization problems using stochastic gradients only. We provide a few error-bound results on its convergence rates. Specially, we prove that the SPIDER-SFO algorithm achieves a gradient computation cost of $\mathcal{O}\left( \min( n^{1/2} \epsilon^{-2}, \epsilon^{-3} ) \right)$ to find an $\epsilon$-approximate first-order stationary point. In addition, we prove that SPIDER-SFO nearly matches the algorithmic lower bound for finding stationary point under the gradient Lipschitz assumption in the finite-sum setting. Our SPIDER technique can be further applied to find an $(\epsilon, \mathcal{O}(\ep^{0.5}))$-approximate second-order stationary point at a gradient computation cost of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \min( n^{1/2} \epsilon^{-2}+\epsilon^{-2.5}, \epsilon^{-3} ) \right)$.

paragraphs: SPIDER is a stochastic estimation technique designed to track deterministic quantities with substantially reduced computation. Its analysis focuses on how many gradient computations are needed to reach approximate stationary points.

For first-order stationarity, the algorithm has a gradient cost of order min(sqrt(n)/epsilon², 1/epsilon³). Here n is the finite-sum size and epsilon specifies the desired accuracy. First-order stationarity means the gradient is small; it does not by itself establish that the point is a global optimum. Under a Lipschitz-gradient assumption in the finite-sum setting, the bound nearly matches an algorithmic lower bound.

The authors also extend SPIDER to approximate second-order stationarity and give a corresponding gradient-computation bound. This broadens the technique beyond controlling gradient size alone. The central finding is a near-optimal efficiency result for finding first-order stationary points under the stated assumptions, alongside an extension to a stronger stationarity criterion.
summary.tldr: SPIDER reduces stochastic gradient computation and nearly matches a lower bound for finite-sum first-order stationarity under a Lipschitz-gradient assumption.

title: SPIDER: Near-Optimal Non-Convex Optimization via Stochastic Path-Integrated Differential Estimator

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GAN) are a powerful subclass of generative models. Despite a very rich research activity leading to numerous interesting GAN algorithms, it is still very hard to assess which algorithm(s) perform better than others. We conduct a neutral, multi-faceted large-scale empirical study on state-of-the art models and evaluation measures. We find that most models can reach similar scores with enough hyperparameter optimization and random restarts. This suggests that improvements can arise from a higher computational budget and tuning more than fundamental algorithmic changes. To overcome some limitations of the current metrics, we also propose several data sets on which precision and recall can be computed. Our experimental results suggest that future GAN research should be based on more systematic and objective evaluation procedures. Finally, we did not find evidence that any of the tested algorithms consistently outperforms the non-saturating GAN introduced in \cite{goodfellow2014generative}.

paragraphs: When many generative adversarial network algorithms report strong results, it can be difficult to tell whether their differences reflect better methods or better experimental circumstances. This paper addresses that comparison problem through a large empirical study of leading GAN models and the measures used to evaluate them.

The central finding is that most tested models can achieve similar scores when given enough hyperparameter tuning and random restarts. This suggests that some apparent progress may come from spending more computation on finding successful configurations. It does not establish that all GAN algorithms are equivalent; it shows why tuning effort matters when interpreting the evaluated results.

The authors also introduce datasets on which precision and recall can be computed, addressing some limitations of existing evaluation measures. Across their study, they find no evidence that a tested algorithm consistently outperforms the non-saturating GAN. Together, these findings motivate more systematic evaluation: a compelling comparison needs to account for how models are tuned and what the chosen measures actually reveal.
summary.tldr: A large GAN comparison finds that tuning and restarts often close performance gaps, motivating more systematic evaluation of algorithmic progress.

title: Are GANs Created Equal? A Large-Scale Study

abstract: We describe a new software framework for fast training of generalized linear models. The framework, named Snap Machine Learning (Snap ML), combines recent advances in machine learning systems and algorithms in a nested manner to reflect the hierarchical architecture of modern computing systems. We prove theoretically that such a hierarchical system can accelerate training in distributed environments where intra-node communication is cheaper than inter-node communication. Additionally, we provide a review of the implementation of Snap ML in terms of GPU acceleration, pipelining, communication patterns and software architecture, highlighting aspects that were critical for achieving high performance. We evaluate the performance of Snap ML in both single-node and multi-node environments, quantifying the benefit of the hierarchical scheme and the data streaming functionality, and comparing with other widely-used machine learning software frameworks. Finally, we present a logistic regression benchmark on the Criteo Terabyte Click Logs dataset and show that Snap ML achieves the same test loss an order of magnitude faster than any of the previously reported results, including those obtained using TensorFlow and scikit-learn.

paragraphs: Snap ML is a software framework for accelerating generalized linear model training. Its central design nests learning algorithms and systems techniques to reflect the hierarchy of modern computing hardware. This matters in distributed training because communication within one machine can be cheaper than communication between machines.

The authors prove that a hierarchical arrangement can accelerate training under that communication-cost condition. They also describe implementation choices involving GPU acceleration, pipelining, communication patterns, and software architecture. Evaluations in single-node and multi-node environments measure the benefits of both the hierarchical scheme and data streaming, connecting the theoretical motivation to the behavior of the implemented framework.

A logistic regression benchmark on the Criteo Terabyte Click Logs dataset reaches the same test loss an order of magnitude faster than previously reported results, including TensorFlow and scikit-learn results. That comparison ties the reported speed advantage to a shared predictive-loss target. The paper therefore contributes both a hardware-aware training framework and evidence that coordinating algorithmic and systems design can substantially reduce training time in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Snap ML aligns training with hardware hierarchy and reports an order-of-magnitude speedup at equal test loss on a large logistic regression benchmark.

title: Snap ML: A Hierarchical Framework for Machine Learning

abstract: Data exhibited with multiple modalities are ubiquitous in real-world clustering tasks. Most existing methods, however, pose a strong assumption that the pairing information for modalities is available for all instances. In this paper, we consider a more challenging task where each instance is represented in only one modality, which we call mixed-modal data. Without any extra pairing supervision across modalities, it is difficult to find a universal semantic space for all of them. To tackle this problem, we present an adversarial learning framework for clustering with mixed-modal data. Instead of transforming all the samples into a joint modality-independent space, our framework learns the mappings across individual modal spaces by virtue of cycle-consistency. Through these mappings, we could easily unify all the samples into a single modal space and perform the clustering. Evaluations on several real-world mixed-modal datasets could demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework.

paragraphs: Clustering data from multiple modalities becomes harder when there are no paired observations linking those modalities. This paper considers a setting in which each instance appears in only one modality. Methods that expect every instance to have corresponding representations across modalities cannot directly rely on that information here.

DM2C uses adversarial learning to build mappings between the individual modality spaces. Cycle-consistency provides the organizing constraint for these mappings: moving between modalities and back should preserve consistency. The framework therefore learns relationships among existing modality spaces instead of requiring all samples to be transformed directly into a new modality-independent space.

Once those mappings are available, the samples can be brought into one modality space and clustered together. This makes cross-modal translation the means of assembling a shared representation for clustering without extra pairing supervision. Evaluations on several real-world mixed-modal datasets report superior performance for the proposed framework, supporting the usefulness of this strategy in the tested unpaired setting.
summary.tldr: DM2C clusters unpaired mixed-modal data by learning cycle-consistent mappings that bring samples into a single modality space.

title: DM2C: Deep Mixed-Modal Clustering

abstract: We propose a deep video prediction model conditioned on a single image and an action class. To generate future frames, we first detect keypoints of a moving object and predict future motion as a sequence of keypoints. The input image is then translated following the predicted keypoints sequence to compose future frames. Detecting the keypoints is central to our algorithm, and our method is trained to detect the keypoints of arbitrary objects in an unsupervised manner. Moreover, the detected keypoints of the original videos are used as pseudo-labels to learn the motion of objects. Experimental results show that our method is successfully applied to various datasets without the cost of labeling keypoints in videos. The detected keypoints are similar to human-annotated labels, and prediction results are more realistic compared to the previous methods.

paragraphs: Predicting a video from one image requires a model to determine both how an object moves and how future frames should look. This paper conditions prediction on the starting image and an action class. It organizes generation around a sequence of keypoints, providing an intermediate representation of the object's future motion.

The model first detects keypoints on the moving object and predicts how those points evolve. It then translates the input image according to the predicted keypoint sequence to construct future frames. Keypoint detection is learned without human keypoint annotations, and detections from the original training videos serve as pseudo-labels for learning object motion.

Experiments show successful application across multiple datasets without paying the cost of labeling video keypoints. The learned points resemble human annotations, and the generated predictions are reported to look more realistic than those from previous methods. The result supports using automatically learned spatial landmarks to connect motion prediction and image generation, with an explicit action class guiding the future behavior.
summary.tldr: Automatically learned keypoints guide action-conditioned video prediction from a single image without requiring human keypoint labels.

title: Unsupervised Keypoint Learning for Guiding Class-Conditional Video Prediction

abstract: Sparse coding is typically solved by iterative optimization techniques, such as the Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (ISTA). Unfolding and learning weights of ISTA using neural networks is a practical way to accelerate estimation. In this paper, we study the selection of adapted step sizes for ISTA. We show that a simple step size strategy can improve the convergence rate of ISTA by leveraging the sparsity of the iterates. However, it is impractical in most large-scale applications. Therefore, we propose a network architecture where only the step sizes of ISTA are learned. We demonstrate that for a large class of unfolded algorithms, if the algorithm converges to the solution of the Lasso, its last layers correspond to ISTA with learned step sizes. Experiments show that our method is competitive with state-of-the-art networks when the solutions are sparse enough.

We show that a simple step size strategy can improve the convergence rate of ISTA by leveraging the sparsity of the iterates. However, it is impractical in most large-scale applications. Therefore, we propose a network architecture where only the step sizes of ISTA are learned. paragraphs: Sparse coding is commonly solved through repeated optimization updates, including the Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm, or ISTA. Unfolded networks turn those updates into neural network layers and learn parameters to accelerate estimation. This paper investigates how much can be gained by learning only the step sizes used by ISTA.

The authors first show that a simple step-size strategy can improve ISTA’s convergence rate by using the sparsity of intermediate iterates. Because that strategy is impractical for most large-scale applications, they propose a network that learns the step sizes instead. This concentrates learning on the update size while retaining the underlying ISTA structure.

The paper also establishes a conditional structural result: for a broad class of unfolded algorithms, convergence to the Lasso solution implies that the final layers take the form of ISTA with learned step sizes. Experiments show competitive performance against state-of-the-art networks when the target solutions are sufficiently sparse. That qualification is central to the reported empirical effectiveness of the simpler architecture.
summary.tldr: Learning only ISTA step sizes yields a theoretically motivated unfolded network that is competitive when solutions are sufficiently sparse.

title: Learning step sizes for unfolded sparse coding

abstract: An agent who interacts with a wide population of other agents needs to be aware that there may be variations in their understanding of the world. Furthermore, the machinery which they use to perceive may be inherently different, as is the case between humans and machines. In this work, we present both an image reference game between a speaker and a population of listeners where reasoning about the concepts other agents can comprehend is necessary and a model formulation with this capability. We focus on reasoning about the conceptual understanding of others, as well as adapting to novel gameplay partners and dealing with differences in perceptual machinery. Our experiments on three benchmark image/attribute datasets suggest that our learner indeed encodes information directly pertaining to the understanding of other agents, and that leveraging this information is crucial for maximizing gameplay performance.

paragraphs: An agent communicating with many partners needs to account for differences in what those partners understand. Even when agents encounter the same world, their concepts and perceptual systems may differ. This paper studies that problem through an image reference game involving a speaker and a population of listeners.

The game requires reasoning about which concepts other agents can comprehend. The authors introduce a model formulated to perform this reasoning, with attention to adapting to unfamiliar partners and handling differences in perception. The modeling target is the listener's conceptual understanding, making the identity and capabilities of the communication partner relevant to gameplay.

Experiments on three image-and-attribute benchmark datasets suggest that the learner represents information directly related to other agents' understanding. They also indicate that using this information is crucial for maximizing performance in the game. The findings support modeling communication partners' conceptual knowledge as a useful part of interactive behavior, with the evidence specifically grounded in the tested reference-game setting.
summary.tldr: An image reference-game model learns about partners' conceptual understanding to improve communication across differing perceptual capabilities.

title: Modeling Conceptual Understanding in Image Reference Games

abstract: We propose MDP-GapE, a new trajectory-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search algorithm for planning in a Markov Decision Process in which transitions have a finite support. We prove an upper bound on the number of sampled trajectories needed for MDP-GapE to identify a near-optimal action with high probability. This problem-dependent result is expressed in terms of the sub-optimality gaps of the state-action pairs that are visited during exploration. Our experiments reveal that MDP-GapE is also effective in practice, in contrast with other algorithms with sample complexity guarantees in the fixed-confidence setting, that are mostly theoretical.
