We prove an upper bound on the number of sampled trajectories needed for MDP-GapE to identify a near-optimal action with high probability. This problem-dependent result is expressed in terms of the sub-optimality gaps of the state-action pairs that are visited during exploration. Our experiments reveal that MDP-GapE is also effective in practice, in contrast with other algorithms with sample complexity guarantees in the fixed-confidence setting, that are mostly theoretical.

paragraphs: Planning in a Markov decision process can use simulated trajectories to compare candidate actions. The practical question is how many trajectories are needed before choosing an action that is sufficiently close to optimal. This paper introduces MDP-GapE, a trajectory-based Monte Carlo tree search algorithm for that purpose, in a setting where transition distributions have finite support.

The authors prove an upper bound on the number of trajectories required to identify a near-optimal action with high probability. The bound depends on the suboptimality gaps of state-action pairs visited during exploration. These gaps describe how far choices fall short of optimality, so the guarantee reflects features of the particular planning problem rather than only broad problem dimensions.

Experiments show that MDP-GapE is effective in practice as well as carrying a sample-complexity guarantee. The abstract contrasts this with other fixed-confidence algorithms whose contributions are mostly theoretical. The significance is the combination of a problem-dependent guarantee and demonstrated practical behavior: the method connects reliable action selection to the distinctions encountered during its own exploration, under the stated finite-support assumption.
summary.tldr: MDP-GapE combines practical tree-search planning with a high-probability sample bound that depends on explored state-action suboptimality gaps.

title: Planning in Markov Decision Processes with Gap-Dependent Sample Complexity

abstract: While neural conversation models have shown great potentials towards generating informative and engaging responses via introducing external knowledge, learning such a model often requires knowledge-grounded dialogues that are difficult to obtain. To overcome the data challenge and reduce the cost of building a knowledge-grounded dialogue system, we explore the problem under a zero-resource setting by assuming no context-knowledge-response triples are needed for training. To this end, we propose representing the knowledge that bridges a context and a response and the way that the knowledge is expressed as latent variables, and devise a variational approach that can effectively estimate a generation model from independent dialogue corpora and knowledge corpora. Evaluation results on three benchmarks of knowledge-grounded dialogue generation indicate that our model can achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods that rely on knowledge-grounded dialogues for training, and exhibits a good generalization ability over different datasets.

paragraphs: Knowledge-grounded dialogue models aim to produce informative responses using external knowledge, but training usually requires examples pairing a conversation context, relevant knowledge, and a response. Such triples are difficult to obtain. This paper studies a zero-resource setting in which no aligned context-knowledge-response triples are needed for training.

The proposed model treats both the knowledge connecting a context to a response and the way that knowledge is expressed as latent variables. A variational learning approach estimates the generation model from independent dialogue and knowledge corpora. This allows the training procedure to use the two sources without requiring them to be supplied as explicitly matched examples.

Evaluation on three knowledge-grounded dialogue benchmarks shows performance comparable to leading methods trained with knowledge-grounded dialogues. The model also demonstrates good generalization across different datasets. These results suggest that modeling the hidden connection between conversation and knowledge can reduce the need for expensive aligned training data. Here, zero-resource refers specifically to the absence of the paired triples; the method still learns from dialogue and knowledge corpora.
summary.tldr: A latent-variable dialogue model learns from separate dialogue and knowledge corpora, achieving comparable benchmark performance without aligned training triples.

title: Zero-Resource Knowledge-Grounded Dialogue Generation

abstract: Solving optimization problems with unknown parameters often requires learning a predictive model to predict the values of the unknown parameters and then solving the problem using these values. Recent work has shown that including the optimization problem as a layer in the model training pipeline results in predictions of the unobserved parameters that lead to higher decision quality. Unfortunately, this process comes at a large computational cost because the optimization problem must be solved and differentiated through in each training iteration; furthermore, it may also sometimes fail to improve solution quality due to non-smoothness issues that arise when training through a complex optimization layer. To address these shortcomings, we learn a low-dimensional surrogate model of a large optimization problem by representing the feasible space in terms of meta-variables, each of which is a linear combination of the original variables. By training a low-dimensional surrogate model end-to-end, and jointly with the predictive model, we achieve: i) a large reduction in training and inference time; and ii) improved performance by focusing attention on the more important variables in the optimization and learning in a smoother space. Empirically, we demonstrate these improvements on a non-convex adversary modeling task, a submodular recommendation task and a convex portfolio optimization task.

paragraphs: Many decisions require first predicting unknown quantities and then solving an optimization problem using those predictions. Training the predictor through the optimization problem can improve the resulting decisions, but it requires repeatedly solving and differentiating through a potentially expensive computation. Non-smooth behavior can also prevent this training process from improving decision quality.

This paper learns a smaller surrogate for the optimization problem alongside the predictor. It represents the feasible space using meta-variables, each formed as a linear combination of the original variables. Training both components together makes the compact representation responsive to the decisions the system needs to make, rather than treating dimensionality reduction as a separate preliminary step.

The authors report reduced training and inference time together with better performance. They attribute these benefits to concentrating on important optimization variables and learning in a smoother space. Experiments demonstrate improvements in non-convex adversary modeling, submodular recommendation, and convex portfolio optimization. These findings support learning the optimization representation itself as a way to make decision-focused prediction both more efficient and more effective.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning a compact optimization surrogate and a predictor improves decision quality while reducing computation in the reported tasks.

title: Automatically Learning Compact Quality-aware Surrogates for Optimization Problems

abstract: A deep visual tracker is typically based on either object detection or template matching while each of them is only suitable for a particular group of scenes. It is straightforward to consider fusing them together to pursue more reliable tracking. However, this is not wise as they follow different tracking principles. Unlike previous fusion-based methods, we propose a novel ensemble framework, named DTNet, with an online decision mechanism for visual tracking based on hierarchical reinforcement learning. The decision mechanism substantiates an intelligent switching strategy where the detection and the template trackers have to compete with each other to conduct tracking within different scenes that they are adept in. Besides, we present a novel detection tracker which avoids the common issue of incorrect proposal. Extensive results show that our DTNet achieves state-of-the-art tracking performance as well as good balance between accuracy and efficiency. The project website is available at https://vsislab.github.io/DTNet/.

paragraphs: Visual trackers commonly use either object detection or template matching, and each approach suits different kinds of scenes. Combining them is appealing, but their different operating principles make straightforward fusion problematic. This paper introduces DTNet, an ensemble that decides online which tracking approach should take responsibility in the current scene.

Its decision mechanism uses hierarchical reinforcement learning to develop a switching strategy. Detection and template trackers compete to perform tracking where each is most capable, making selection between methods part of the tracking process. The paper also introduces a detection tracker designed to avoid the common problem of incorrect proposals.

The reported experiments show state-of-the-art tracking performance together with a good balance between accuracy and efficiency. These findings support an ensemble design in which the central learned behavior is choosing the appropriate tracker as conditions change. The contribution combines that decision mechanism with the new detection component, addressing both the coordination of different tracking approaches and a specific failure source within detection-based tracking.
summary.tldr: DTNet uses hierarchical reinforcement learning to switch between detection and template trackers according to the scene.

title: Online Decision Based Visual Tracking via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning robotic grasps from visual observations is a promising yet challenging task. Recent research shows its great potential by preparing and learning from large-scale synthetic datasets. For the popular, 6 degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) grasp setting of parallel-jaw gripper, most of existing methods take the strategy of heuristically sampling grasp candidates and then evaluating them using learned scoring functions. This strategy is limited in terms of the conflict between sampling efficiency and coverage of optimal grasps. To this end, we propose in this work a novel, end-to-end \emph{Grasp Proposal Network (GPNet)}, to predict a diverse set of 6-DOF grasps for an unseen object observed from a single and unknown camera view. GPNet builds on a key design of grasp proposal module that defines \emph{anchors of grasp centers} at discrete but regular 3D grid corners, which is flexible to support either more precise or more diverse grasp predictions. To test GPNet, we contribute a synthetic dataset of 6-DOF object grasps; evaluation is conducted using rule-based criteria, simulation test, and real test. Comparative results show the advantage of our methods over existing ones. Notably, GPNet gains better simulation results via the specified coverage, which helps achieve a ready translation in real test. Our code and dataset are available on \url{https://github.com/CZ-Wu/GPNet}.

paragraphs: A robot choosing how to grasp an object must consider both the gripper's position and its orientation. Many approaches first sample possible grasps using heuristics and then score them with a learned model. This creates a tension: sampling fewer candidates saves effort, but may overlook useful ways to grasp the object.

GPNet learns to propose a diverse collection of six-degree-of-freedom grasps directly from a single view of an unseen object, without knowing the camera view in advance. Its proposal module places grasp-center anchors at regularly spaced corners of a three-dimensional grid. This structure can support predictions that emphasize greater precision or greater diversity.

The authors introduce a synthetic grasp dataset and evaluate their method using rule-based criteria, simulation, and physical tests. They report advantages over existing methods and connect improved simulation results to the specified grasp coverage, which helps transfer to real testing. The stated contribution is thus both a learned proposal mechanism and evidence that its coverage of candidate grasps has practical value beyond scoring isolated predictions.
summary.tldr: GPNet uses structured three-dimensional anchors to predict diverse robotic grasps directly from a single unknown camera view.

title: Grasp Proposal Networks: An End-to-End Solution for Visual Learning of Robotic Grasps

abstract: We introduce a new category of generative autoencoders called automodulators. These networks can faithfully reproduce individual real-world input images like regular autoencoders, but also generate a fused sample from an arbitrary combination of several such images, allowing instantaneous "style-mixing" and other new applications. An automodulator decouples the data flow of decoder operations from statistical properties thereof and uses the latent vector to modulate the former by the latter, with a principled approach for mutual disentanglement of decoder layers. Prior work has explored similar decoder architecture with GANs, but their focus has been on random sampling. A corresponding autoencoder could operate on real input images. For the first time, we show how to train such a general-purpose model with sharp outputs in high resolution, using novel training techniques, demonstrated on four image data sets. Besides style-mixing, we show state-of-the-art results in autoencoder comparison, and visual image quality nearly indistinguishable from state-of-the-art GANs. We expect the automodulator variants to become a useful building block for image applications and other data domains.

paragraphs: Automodulators are generative autoencoders designed both to reconstruct real input images and to combine several inputs into a new image. The combination enables immediate style mixing from arbitrary collections of input images. This brings image fusion into a model that can also reproduce particular observed images.

The decoder separates the flow of data through its operations from the statistical properties used to modulate those operations. A latent vector controls this modulation, and the method includes a principled approach to disentangling decoder layers from one another. Related decoder designs had been explored with generative adversarial networks focused on random sampling; the autoencoder setting connects the mechanism directly to real inputs.

The authors introduce training techniques that produce sharp, high-resolution outputs and demonstrate them on four image datasets. They report state-of-the-art results in autoencoder comparisons and visual quality close to leading GANs. These findings support the model's combination of reconstruction and generation capabilities. Its proposed usefulness in other image applications and data domains is presented as an expectation, while the stated demonstrations concern image datasets and style mixing.
summary.tldr: Automodulators reconstruct real images and mix their styles through latent-controlled decoder modulation, producing sharp high-resolution outputs.

title: Deep Automodulators

abstract: We study MinMax solution methods for a general class of optimization problems related to (and including) optimal transport. Theoretically, the focus is on fitting a large class of problems into a single MinMax framework and generalizing regularization techniques known from classical optimal transport. We show that regularization techniques justify the utilization of neural networks to solve such problems by proving approximation theorems and illustrating fundamental issues if no regularization is used. We further study the relation to the literature on generative adversarial nets, and analyze which algorithmic techniques used therein are particularly suitable to the class of problems studied in this paper. Several numerical experiments showcase the generality of the setting and highlight which theoretical insights are most beneficial in practice.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems that can be expressed through competing minimization and maximization steps. Optimal transport is one member of the class, but the aim is broader: to place a range of related problems in a shared MinMax framework. This makes it possible to investigate common mathematical and computational tools across them.

A central focus is regularization. The authors extend techniques from classical optimal transport and prove approximation results that justify solving the regularized problems with neural networks. They also illustrate fundamental problems that arise without regularization. Regularization therefore plays a role in establishing why neural-network approximations are appropriate for the optimization problems under study.

The paper connects this framework to generative adversarial networks and examines which algorithmic techniques from that literature suit the studied problems. Numerical experiments demonstrate the breadth of the framework and investigate which theoretical insights are most helpful in practice. The overall contribution joins formulation, approximation theory, and numerical methods, showing how a common MinMax viewpoint can guide neural-network solutions across optimal transport and related settings.
summary.tldr: A shared MinMax framework uses regularization and approximation theory to support neural-network solutions for optimal transport and related problems.

title: MinMax Methods for Optimal Transport and Beyond: Regularization, Approximation and Numerics

abstract: Popular Maximum Entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning approaches require the computation of expected state visitation frequencies for the optimal policy under an estimate of the reward function. This usually requires intermediate value estimation in the inner loop of the algorithm, slowing down convergence considerably. In this work, we introduce a novel class of algorithms that only needs to solve the MDP underlying the demonstrated behavior once to recover the expert policy. This is possible through a formulation that exploits a probabilistic behavior assumption for the demonstrations within the structure of Q-learning. We propose Inverse Action-value Iteration which is able to fully recover an underlying reward of an external agent in closed-form analytically. We further provide an accompanying class of sampling-based variants which do not depend on a model of the environment. We show how to extend this class of algorithms to continuous state-spaces via function approximation and how to estimate a corresponding action-value function, leading to a policy as close as possible to the policy of the external agent, while optionally satisfying a list of predefined hard constraints. We evaluate the resulting algorithms called Inverse Action-value Iteration, Inverse Q-learning and Deep Inverse Q-learning on the Objectworld benchmark, showing a speedup of up to several orders of magnitude compared to (Deep) Max-Entropy algorithms. We further apply Deep Constrained Inverse Q-learning on the task of learning autonomous lane-changes in the open-source simulator SUMO achieving competent driving after training on data corresponding to 30 minutes of demonstrations.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning works backward from demonstrated behavior to a reward that can explain it. This paper introduces algorithms that need to solve the decision process underlying the demonstrations only once to recover the expert policy.

The approach places a probabilistic assumption about demonstrated behavior inside a Q-learning formulation. Inverse Action-value Iteration analytically recovers an underlying reward in closed form. Related sampling-based versions avoid requiring an environment model. Function approximation extends the approach to continuous states, while an optional constrained version seeks a policy close to the demonstrator’s behavior that also satisfies predefined hard constraints.

On Objectworld, the authors report speedups reaching several orders of magnitude over the compared maximum-entropy methods. They also apply Deep Constrained Inverse Q-learning to autonomous lane changes in the SUMO simulator. Training on demonstrations corresponding to 30 minutes produces competent driving in that setting. These results illustrate both the computational benefit and the possibility of incorporating explicit behavioral requirements.
summary.tldr: A Q-learning formulation recovers rewards from demonstrations more efficiently and can learn imitation policies subject to predefined hard constraints.

title: Deep Inverse Q-learning with Constraints

abstract: We present a deep learning algorithm for the numerical solution of parametric families of high-dimensional linear Kolmogorov partial differential equations (PDEs). Our method is based on reformulating the numerical approximation of a whole family of Kolmogorov PDEs as a single statistical learning problem using the Feynman-Kac formula. Successful numerical experiments are presented, which empirically confirm the functionality and efficiency of our proposed algorithm in the case of heat equations and Black-Scholes option pricing models parametrized by affine-linear coefficient functions. We show that a single deep neural network trained on simulated data is capable of learning the solution functions of an entire family of PDEs on a full space-time region. Most notably, our numerical observations and theoretical results also demonstrate that the proposed method does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, distinguishing it from almost all standard numerical methods for PDEs.

paragraphs: This paper uses a single neural network to approximate solutions across a parameterized family of high-dimensional linear Kolmogorov equations. The objective includes variation across equation parameters as well as space and time. Learning the family together provides a common representation of solutions throughout a full space-time region.

The method uses the Feynman-Kac formula to reformulate numerical approximation of the whole equation family as one statistical learning problem. Training uses simulated data. This reformulation makes it possible to apply deep learning to a collection of related differential equations through a shared prediction task.

The authors report successful experiments on heat equations and Black-Scholes option pricing models parameterized by affine-linear coefficient functions. These experiments support the algorithm’s functionality and efficiency and demonstrate learning an entire family with one network. The paper also presents numerical observations and theoretical results showing that the proposed method avoids the curse of dimensionality in its studied setting. That claim concerns this approach to the specified equation families, rather than arbitrary differential equations.
summary.tldr: A Feynman-Kac learning formulation lets one neural network approximate entire families of high-dimensional Kolmogorov equation solutions.

title: Numerically Solving Parametric Families of High-Dimensional Kolmogorov Partial Differential Equations via Deep Learning

abstract: In the robust submodular partitioning problem, we aim to allocate a set of items into $m$ blocks, so that the evaluation of the minimum block according to a submodular function is maximized. Robust submodular partitioning promotes the diversity of every block in the partition. It has many applications in machine learning, e.g., partitioning data for distributed training so that the gradients computed on every block are consistent. We study an extension of the robust submodular partition problem with additional constraints (e.g., cardinality, multiple matroids, and/or knapsack) on every block. For example, when partitioning data for distributed training, we can add a constraint that the number of samples of each class is the same in each partition block, ensuring data balance. We present two classes of algorithms, i.e., Min-Block Greedy based algorithms (with an $\Omega(1/m)$ bound), and Round-Robin Greedy based algorithms (with a constant bound) and show that under various constraints, they still have good approximation guarantees. Interestingly, while normally the latter runs in only weakly polynomial time, we show that using the two together yields strongly polynomial running time while preserving the approximation guarantee. Lastly, we apply the algorithms on a real-world machine learning data partitioning problem showing good results.

paragraphs: Robust submodular partitioning divides items into blocks while maximizing the score of the weakest block. This objective encourages diversity throughout the partition, rather than allowing a few strong blocks to compensate for poor ones. The paper extends the problem by imposing additional requirements on every block, including size, matroid, and knapsack constraints.

Such constraints make the formulation useful for data allocation. For distributed training, the objective can encourage informative blocks, while extra rules can require equal numbers of examples from each class. The authors develop two algorithm families: Min-Block Greedy methods with an approximation bound of order 1/m, and Round-Robin Greedy methods with a constant approximation bound, where m is the number of blocks.

The guarantees continue to hold under various studied constraints. Although Round-Robin Greedy normally has only weakly polynomial running time, combining the two families produces a strongly polynomial algorithm while preserving the approximation guarantee. An application to a real-world machine-learning partitioning problem also gives good results. The main contribution is a way to combine balanced block quality, allocation requirements, and provable computational guarantees.
summary.tldr: Greedy algorithms partition items into diverse, constrained blocks with approximation guarantees, and their combination improves the running-time guarantee.

title: Constrained Robust Submodular Partitioning

abstract: Dental forensic identification targets to identify persons with dental traces.The task is vital for the investigation of criminal scenes and mass disasters because of the resistance of dental structures and the wide-existence of dental imaging. However, no widely accepted automated solution is available for this labour-costly task. In this work, we pioneer to study deep learning for dental forensic identification based on panoramic radiographs. We construct a comprehensive benchmark with various dental variations that can adequately reflect the difficulties of the task. By considering the task's unique challenges, we propose FoID, a deep learning method featured by: (\textit{i}) clinical-inspired attention localization, (\textit{ii}) domain-specific augmentations that enable instance discriminative learning, and (\textit{iii}) transformer-based self-attention mechanism that dynamically reasons the relative importance of attentions. We show that FoID can outperform traditional approaches by at least \textbf{22.98\%} in terms of Rank-1 accuracy, and outperform strong CNN baselines by at least \textbf{10.50\%} in terms of mean Average Precision (mAP). Moreover, extensive ablation studies verify the effectiveness of each building blocks of FoID. Our work can be a first step towards the automated system for forensic identification among large-scale multi-site databases. Also, the proposed techniques, \textit{e.g.}, self-attention mechanism, can also be meaningful for other identification tasks, \textit{e.g.}, pedestrian re-identification.Related data and codes can be found at \href{https://github.com/liangyuandg/FoID}{https://github.com/liangyuandg/FoID}.

paragraphs: Dental identification can help establish identity in criminal investigations and mass disasters because dental structures resist damage and dental images are widely available. The task remains labor-intensive. This paper investigates deep learning for identification from panoramic radiographs and builds a benchmark containing dental variations intended to capture the task's distinctive difficulties.

The proposed method, FoID, combines three components. Clinically inspired attention localization guides what the model examines. Dental-specific data augmentation supports learning features that distinguish individuals. Transformer self-attention then reasons dynamically about the relative importance of the attended information. Together, these components adapt the identification model to dental imagery.

The authors report improvements of at least 22.98% in Rank-1 accuracy over traditional approaches and at least 10.50% in mean Average Precision over strong CNN baselines. Ablation studies support each component's effectiveness. The work is presented as a first step toward automated identification across large, multisite databases; the possible value of its techniques for other identification tasks remains a proposed broader application.
summary.tldr: FoID combines dental-specific learning and attention mechanisms to improve forensic identification from panoramic radiographs.

title: Exploring Forensic Dental Identification with Deep Learning

abstract: We provide a probabilistic interpretation of attention and show that the standard dot-product attention in transformers is a special case of Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) inference. The proposed approach suggests the use of Expectation Maximization algorithms for on-line adaptation of key and value model parameters. This approach is useful for cases in which external agents, e.g., annotators, provide inference-time information about the correct values of some tokens, e.g., the semantic category of some pixels, and we need for this new information to propagate to other tokens in a principled manner. We illustrate the approach on an interactive semantic segmentation task in which annotators and models collaborate online to improve annotation efficiency. Using standard benchmarks, we observe that key adaptation boosts model performance ($\sim10\%$ mIoU) in the low feedback regime and value propagation improves model responsiveness in the high feedback regime. A PyTorch layer implementation of our probabilistic attention model is available here: https://github.com/apple/ml-probabilistic-attention.

paragraphs: Interactive segmentation allows an annotator to provide information about some pixels while a model predicts labels for the rest. A central challenge is deciding how that feedback should influence other pixels during inference. This paper develops a probabilistic account of attention that gives such updates an explicit inference-based interpretation.

The authors show that ordinary dot-product attention is a special case of maximum a posteriori inference. Their formulation suggests expectation-maximization procedures for adapting the parameters associated with attention keys and values online. This makes it possible to incorporate externally supplied token information and propagate it through the model within the proposed probabilistic framework.

On standard interactive segmentation benchmarks, adapting keys improves performance by approximately 10% mIoU in the low-feedback setting, as reported in the abstract. With more feedback, value propagation improves how responsively the model incorporates annotations. The results distinguish two useful forms of adaptation at different feedback levels and demonstrate how reinterpreting attention can lead to a practical mechanism for collaboration between annotators and models.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic interpretation of attention enables online adaptation that helps segmentation models incorporate annotator feedback.

title: Probabilistic Attention for Interactive Segmentation

abstract: We study fast algorithms for statistical regression problems under the strong contamination model, where the goal is to approximately optimize a generalized linear model (GLM) given adversarially corrupted samples. Prior works in this line of research were based on the \emph{robust gradient descent} framework of \cite{PrasadSBR20}, a first-order method using biased gradient queries, or the \emph{Sever} framework of \cite{DiakonikolasKK019}, an iterative outlier-removal method calling a stationary point finder. We present nearly-linear time algorithms for robust regression problems with improved runtime or estimation guarantees compared to the state-of-the-art. For the general case of smooth GLMs (e.g.\ logistic regression), we show that the robust gradient descent framework of \cite{PrasadSBR20} can be \emph{accelerated}, and show our algorithm extends to optimizing the Moreau envelopes of Lipschitz GLMs (e.g.\ support vector machines), answering several open questions in the literature. For the well-studied case of robust linear regression, we present an alternative approach obtaining improved estimation rates over prior nearly-linear time algorithms. Interestingly, our algorithm starts with an identifiability proof introduced in the context of the sum-of-squares algorithm of \cite{BakshiP21}, which achieved optimal error rates while requiring large polynomial runtime and sample complexity. We reinterpret their proof within the Sever framework and obtain a dramatically faster and more sample-efficient algorithm under fewer distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression when an adversary can corrupt samples under the strong contamination model. The objective is to approximately optimize a generalized linear model despite those corruptions. The authors develop algorithms with nearly linear running time that improve either computation or estimation guarantees relative to earlier methods.

For smooth generalized linear models, including logistic regression, they show how to accelerate robust gradient descent, a framework that works with biased gradient estimates. They also extend the algorithm to optimizing Moreau envelopes of Lipschitz generalized linear models, including support vector machines. This broadens the optimization settings covered by the accelerated approach.

They reinterpret an identifiability proof previously used in a computationally expensive sum-of-squares method within the Sever framework, which iteratively removes outliers. The resulting algorithm is substantially faster and more sample-efficient under fewer distributional assumptions. The paper thus shows how a proof developed for one algorithmic approach can inform a more efficient robust procedure.
summary.tldr: New nearly linear-time robust regression algorithms accelerate generalized-model optimization and improve linear-regression estimation guarantees.

title: Robust Regression Revisited: Acceleration and Improved Estimation Rates

abstract: Sharing forecasts of network timeseries data, such as cellular or electricity load patterns, can improve independent control applications ranging from traffic scheduling to power generation. Typically, forecasts are designed without knowledge of a downstream controller's task objective, and thus simply optimize for mean prediction error. However, such task-agnostic representations are often too large to stream over a communication network and do not emphasize salient temporal features for cooperative control. This paper presents a solution to learn succinct, highly-compressed forecasts that are co-designed with a modular controller's task objective. Our simulations with real cellular, Internet-of-Things (IoT), and electricity load data show we can improve a model predictive controller's performance by at least 25% while transmitting 80% less data than the competing method. Further, we present theoretical compression results for a networked variant of the classical linear quadratic regulator (LQR) control problem.

paragraphs: Controllers can make better decisions when they receive forecasts of network activity, such as cellular traffic or electricity demand. Yet a forecast optimized only for average prediction error may overlook the temporal information that matters most to a particular control task. It may also require too much data to transmit efficiently over a communication network.

This paper learns compressed forecasts together with the objective of a modular downstream controller. The central idea is to make the transmitted representation useful for the decisions it will support. Compression and forecast design are therefore considered in relation to control performance, rather than judged solely by how closely a forecast reproduces the original time series.

Simulations using real cellular, Internet-of-Things, and electricity load data show at least a 25% improvement in model predictive controller performance while transmitting 80% less data than the competing method. These are results for the reported simulations. The paper also derives theoretical compression results for a networked linear quadratic regulator problem, giving a mathematical counterpart to its task-aware forecast design.
summary.tldr: Designing compressed forecasts around a controller's objective improves simulated control performance while substantially reducing transmitted data.

title: Data Sharing and Compression for Cooperative Networked Control

abstract: Many applications of generative models rely on the marginalization of their high-dimensional output probability distributions. Normalization functions that yield sparse probability distributions can make exact marginalization more computationally tractable. However, sparse normalization functions usually require alternative loss functions for training since the log-likelihood is undefined for sparse probability distributions. Furthermore, many sparse normalization functions often collapse the multimodality of distributions. In this work, we present ev-softmax, a sparse normalization function that preserves the multimodality of probability distributions. We derive its properties, including its gradient in closed-form, and introduce a continuous family of approximations to ev-softmax that have full support and can be trained with probabilistic loss functions such as negative log-likelihood and Kullback-Leibler divergence. We evaluate our method on a variety of generative models, including variational autoencoders and auto-regressive architectures. Our method outperforms existing dense and sparse normalization techniques in distributional accuracy. We demonstrate that ev-softmax successfully reduces the dimensionality of probability distributions while maintaining multimodality.

paragraphs: Generative models often need to sum probabilities over many possible outputs. Sparse distributions can make these exact sums more manageable by assigning zero probability to many possibilities. However, zeros create problems for likelihood-based training, and existing sparse normalization methods can remove distinct peaks that represent different plausible outcomes.

The paper introduces ev-softmax, a normalization function designed to produce sparse distributions while preserving multiple modes. The authors derive its mathematical properties and a closed-form gradient. They also construct a continuous family of approximations that retain positive probability throughout the output space, allowing training with negative log-likelihood and Kullback-Leibler divergence.

This separates the desire for a compact distribution from the need for a trainable probabilistic objective. Evaluations include variational autoencoders and autoregressive models, where the method achieves better distributional accuracy than the dense and sparse alternatives considered. The reported findings show that reducing the effective size of an output distribution need not collapse its multiple plausible outcomes into a single dominant mode.
summary.tldr: Ev-softmax creates sparse distributions that preserve multiple modes, with full-support approximations enabling standard probabilistic training.

title: Evidential Softmax for Sparse Multimodal Distributions in Deep Generative Models

abstract: Active inference is a unifying theory for perception and action resting upon the idea that the brain maintains an internal model of the world by minimizing free energy. From a behavioral perspective, active inference agents can be seen as self-evidencing beings that act to fulfill their optimistic predictions, namely preferred outcomes or goals. In contrast, reinforcement learning requires human-designed rewards to accomplish any desired outcome. Although active inference could provide a more natural self-supervised objective for control, its applicability has been limited because of the shortcomings in scaling the approach to complex environments. In this work, we propose a contrastive objective for active inference that strongly reduces the computational burden in learning the agent's generative model and planning future actions. Our method performs notably better than likelihood-based active inference in image-based tasks, while also being computationally cheaper and easier to train. We compare to reinforcement learning agents that have access to human-designed reward functions, showing that our approach closely matches their performance. Finally, we also show that contrastive methods perform significantly better in the case of distractors in the environment and that our method is able to generalize goals to variations in the background.

paragraphs: Active inference describes agents that maintain an internal model of the world and act toward preferred outcomes. In this view, goals take the form of optimistic predictions the agent tries to fulfill. The paper investigates how to make this approach practical in complex environments, where learning the internal model and planning actions can be computationally demanding.

The proposed change is a contrastive objective for active inference. It substantially reduces the computational burden associated with both model learning and planning. This matters because the appeal of a self-supervised control objective depends on whether agents can actually learn and use it efficiently when observations are complex, including images.

In image-based tasks, the method performs substantially better than likelihood-based active inference while being cheaper to compute and easier to train. It also closely matches reinforcement learning agents that receive human-designed rewards. Further experiments show stronger performance for contrastive methods when distractors are present, and demonstrate that the proposed agent can carry goals across background variations. These findings support its usefulness for visual control without establishing that it replaces reward-based learning in every setting.
summary.tldr: A contrastive objective makes active inference cheaper and more effective on visual control tasks, with improved handling of distractors and background changes.

title: Contrastive Active Inference

abstract: Sampling from a complex distribution $\pi$ and approximating its intractable normalizing constant $\mathrm{Z}$ are challenging problems. In this paper, a novel family of importance samplers (IS) and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers is derived. Given an invertible map $\mathrm{T}$, these schemes combine (with weights) elements from the forward and backward Orbits through points sampled from a proposal distribution $\rho$. The map $\mathrm{T}$ does not leave the target $\pi$ invariant, hence the name NEO, standing for Non-Equilibrium Orbits. NEO-IS provides unbiased estimators of the normalizing constant and self-normalized IS estimators of expectations under $\pi$ while NEO-MCMC combines multiple NEO-IS estimates of the normalizing constant and an iterated sampling-importance resampling mechanism to sample from $\pi$. For $\mathrm{T}$ chosen as a discrete-time integrator of a conformal Hamiltonian system, NEO-IS achieves state-of-the art performance on difficult benchmarks and NEO-MCMC is able to explore highly multimodal targets. Additionally, we provide detailed theoretical results for both methods. In particular, we show that NEO-MCMC is uniformly geometrically ergodic and establish explicit mixing time estimates under mild conditions.

paragraphs: Sampling from a complicated probability distribution and estimating its normalizing constant can both be difficult. Starting from proposal samples, the methods combine weighted points obtained by applying that transformation forward and backward.

summary.tldr: NEO uses weighted forward and backward trajectories of an invertible transformation to estimate normalizing constants and sample complex distributions.

title: NEO: Non Equilibrium Sampling on the Orbits of a Deterministic Transform

abstract: Query embedding (QE)---which aims to embed entities and first-order logical (FOL) queries in low-dimensional spaces---has shown great power in multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs. Recently, embedding entities and queries with geometric shapes becomes a promising direction, as geometric shapes can naturally represent answer sets of queries and logical relationships among them. However, existing geometry-based models have difficulty in modeling queries with negation, which significantly limits their applicability. To address this challenge, we propose a novel query embedding model, namely \textbf{Con}e \textbf{E}mbeddings (ConE), which is the first geometry-based QE model that can handle all the FOL operations, including conjunction, disjunction, and negation. Specifically, ConE represents entities and queries as Cartesian products of two-dimensional cones, where the intersection and union of cones naturally model the conjunction and disjunction operations. By further noticing that the closure of complement of cones remains cones, we design geometric complement operators in the embedding space for the negation operations. Experiments demonstrate that ConE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Reasoning over a knowledge graph can involve combining several relationships and logical conditions to identify an answer set. Query embedding represents entities and queries in a compact mathematical space. Geometric representations are appealing because regions can describe sets of answers, but existing geometry-based approaches have difficulty expressing negation, limiting the queries they can model.

ConE represents entities and queries using Cartesian products of two-dimensional cones. Intersections and unions of cones provide geometric ways to express conjunction and disjunction: combining conditions with 'and' or 'or.' To express negation, the method uses the fact that taking the closure of a cone's complement again yields a cone, enabling a geometric complement operator.

The authors present ConE as the first geometry-based query-embedding model supporting all the first-order logical operations described in the paper, including negation. Experiments show significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets. The contribution is therefore both representational and empirical: the cone construction broadens the logical queries the geometry can express, while the evaluations demonstrate stronger reasoning performance on the tested benchmarks.
summary.tldr: ConE uses cone-shaped embeddings to support conjunction, disjunction, and negation in knowledge-graph queries, improving benchmark reasoning performance.

title: ConE: Cone Embeddings for Multi-Hop Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs

abstract: Predicting the most likely route from a source location to a destination is a core functionality in mapping services. Although the problem has been studied in the literature, two key limitations remain to be addressed. First, our study reveals that a significant portion of the routes recommended by existing methods fail to reach the destination. Second, existing techniques are transductive in nature; hence, they fail to recommend routes if unseen roads are encountered at inference time. In this paper, we address these limitations through an inductive algorithm called NeuroMLR. NeuroMLR learns a generative model from historical trajectories by conditioning on three explanatory factors: the current location, the destination, and real-time traffic conditions. The conditional distributions are learned through a novel combination of Lipschitz embedding with Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) using historical trajectory data. Through in-depth experiments on real-world datasets, we establish that NeuroMLR imparts significant improvement in accuracy over the state of the art. More importantly, NeuroMLR generalizes dramatically better to unseen data and the recommended routes reach the destination with much higher likelihood than existing techniques.

paragraphs: Predicting a likely route requires more than producing plausible road choices along the way. The authors find that a significant portion of routes recommended by existing methods fail to reach their destinations. They also identify a generalization problem: transductive methods cannot recommend routes when they encounter previously unseen roads at inference time.

NeuroMLR addresses these problems with an inductive generative model learned from historical trajectories. Its conditional distributions use the current location, the destination, and real-time traffic conditions as explanatory factors. The model combines Lipschitz embedding with graph convolutional networks to learn these distributions, bringing road-network structure into the route-generation process.

Experiments on real-world datasets show significant accuracy improvements over the state of the art. The authors also report substantially better generalization to unseen data and a much higher likelihood that recommended routes reach the destination. These findings address both the quality of route predictions and their practical completion. Destination arrival remains a probabilistic improvement in the stated results, rather than a guaranteed property.
summary.tldr: NeuroMLR learns an inductive route model that improves accuracy, unseen-data generalization, and the likelihood of reaching the destination.

title: NeuroMLR: Robust & Reliable Route Recommendation on Road Networks

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of fair sparse regression on a biased dataset where bias depends upon a hidden binary attribute. The presence of a hidden attribute adds an extra layer of complexity to the problem by combining sparse regression and clustering with unknown binary labels. The corresponding optimization problem is combinatorial, but we propose a novel relaxation of it as an invex optimization problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first invex relaxation for a combinatorial problem. We show that the inclusion of the debiasing/fairness constraint in our model has no adverse effect on the performance. Rather, it enables the recovery of the hidden attribute. The support of our recovered regression parameter vector matches exactly with the true parameter vector. Moreover, we simultaneously solve the clustering problem by recovering the exact value of the hidden attribute for each sample. Our method uses carefully constructed primal dual witnesses to provide theoretical guarantees for the combinatorial problem. To that end, we show that the sample complexity of our method is logarithmic in terms of the dimension of the regression parameter vector.

paragraphs: This paper studies sparse regression when dataset bias depends on an unobserved binary attribute. The learner must identify which regression features matter while also recovering the hidden group assignment of each sample. Combining these tasks produces a combinatorial optimization problem because the group labels are unknown discrete choices.

The authors replace that formulation with an invex relaxation and analyze it using carefully constructed primal-dual witnesses. Within their model, adding a fairness or debiasing constraint does not harm performance and enables recovery of the hidden attribute. Fairness therefore plays a constructive role in the recovery analysis rather than appearing only as an additional restriction.

The theoretical guarantees establish exact recovery of the regression vector's support, meaning the positions of its nonzero entries, together with the hidden binary label for every sample. They also show sample complexity logarithmic in the regression dimension. These are guarantees for the studied biased-data problem; the contribution connects fairness constraints, feature selection, and hidden-group recovery in one mathematically analyzed formulation.
summary.tldr: An invex relaxation jointly recovers relevant regression features and hidden binary groups, with a fairness constraint aiding recovery in the studied model.

title: Fair Sparse Regression with Clustering: An Invex Relaxation for a Combinatorial Problem

abstract: We derive information-theoretic generalization bounds for supervised learning algorithms based on the information contained in predictions rather than in the output of the training algorithm. These bounds improve over the existing information-theoretic bounds, are applicable to a wider range of algorithms, and solve two key challenges: (a) they give meaningful results for deterministic algorithms and (b) they are significantly easier to estimate. We show experimentally that the proposed bounds closely follow the generalization gap in practical scenarios for deep learning.

These bounds improve over the existing information-theoretic bounds, are applicable to a wider range of algorithms, and solve two key challenges: (a) they give meaningful results for deterministic algorithms and (b) they are significantly easier to estimate. We show experimentally that the proposed bounds closely follow the generalization gap in practical scenarios for deep learning.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds aim to describe how learning performance carries beyond the training data. This paper develops information-theoretic bounds for supervised learning by changing which information is measured. It focuses on the information contained in predictions, rather than the information in the output produced by the training algorithm.

That choice addresses two practical obstacles in earlier information-theoretic analyses. The new bounds provide meaningful results for deterministic algorithms, and they are substantially easier to estimate. The authors also establish improvements over existing bounds and applicability to a broader range of learning algorithms. Thus, the contribution concerns both the scope of the theory and how readily its quantities can be assessed.

Experiments in practical deep-learning settings show that the proposed bounds closely track the generalization gap. This empirical finding connects the theoretical quantities to observed differences in generalization behavior. The paper's central message is that predictions can provide a useful basis for analyzing generalization, with advantages for deterministic learning procedures and practical estimation.
summary.tldr: Prediction-based information bounds broaden generalization analysis, handle deterministic algorithms, and closely track observed deep-learning generalization gaps.

title: Information-theoretic generalization bounds for black-box learning algorithms

abstract: (Non-)robustness of neural networks to small, adversarial pixel-wise perturbations, and as more recently shown, to even random spatial transformations (e.g., translations, rotations) entreats both theoretical and empirical understanding. Spatial robustness to random translations and rotations is commonly attained via equivariant models (e.g., StdCNNs, GCNNs) and training augmentation, whereas adversarial robustness is typically achieved by adversarial training. In this paper, we prove a quantitative trade-off between spatial and adversarial robustness in a simple statistical setting. We complement this empirically by showing that: (a) as the spatial robustness of equivariant models improves by training augmentation with progressively larger transformations, their adversarial robustness worsens progressively, and (b) as the state-of-the-art robust models are adversarially trained with progressively larger pixel-wise perturbations, their spatial robustness drops progressively. Towards achieving Pareto-optimality in this trade-off, we propose a method based on curriculum learning that trains gradually on more difficult perturbations (both spatial and adversarial) to improve spatial and adversarial robustness simultaneously.

paragraphs: A vision model can be challenged by translating or rotating an image, or by applying small adversarial changes to its pixels. These perturbations motivate different training strategies. The paper asks how robustness to the two kinds of changes interacts, rather than assuming that strengthening one automatically strengthens the other.

The authors prove a quantitative trade-off in a simple statistical setting. They also find corresponding empirical patterns: training equivariant models with increasingly large spatial transformations improves spatial robustness while progressively worsening adversarial robustness. Conversely, adversarial training with increasingly large pixel perturbations progressively reduces spatial robustness in the robust models examined.

To seek better combinations of the two properties, the paper proposes a curriculum that gradually introduces harder spatial and adversarial perturbations. The method is intended to improve both kinds of robustness simultaneously and move toward Pareto-optimal trade-offs, where further improvement in one would cost the other. The theoretical result is specific to its statistical setting, while the experiments show the tension arising in the evaluated neural networks.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes a setting-dependent trade-off between spatial and adversarial robustness and proposes a curriculum to improve their balance.

title: Can we have it all? On the Trade-off between Spatial and Adversarial Robustness of Neural Networks

abstract: I consider the setting where reviewers offer very noisy scores for a number of items for the selection of high-quality ones (e.g., peer review of large conference proceedings) whereas the owner of these items knows the true underlying scores but prefers not to provide this information. To address this withholding of information, in this paper, I introduce the Isotonic Mechanism, a simple and efficient approach to improving on the imprecise raw scores by leveraging certain information that the owner is incentivized to provide. This mechanism takes as input the ranking of the items from best to worst provided by the owner, in addition to the raw scores provided by the reviewers. It reports adjusted scores for the items by solving a convex optimization problem. Under certain conditions, I show that the owner's optimal strategy is to honestly report the true ranking of the items to her best knowledge in order to maximize the expected utility. Moreover, I prove that the adjusted scores provided by this owner-assisted mechanism are indeed significantly moreaccurate than the raw scores provided by the reviewers. This paper concludes with several extensions of the Isotonic Mechanism and some refinements of the mechanism for practical considerations.

paragraphs: This paper studies selection when reviewers provide noisy scores and an item's owner has better information about underlying quality. The owner may prefer to withhold that information, so simply requesting it does not resolve the problem. The proposed Isotonic Mechanism aims to make useful disclosure compatible with the owner's incentives.

The mechanism combines reviewers' raw scores with an owner-provided ranking of items from best to worst. It then solves a convex optimization problem to produce adjusted scores. Asking for an ordering supplies information about relative quality that can be used to improve the noisy numerical assessments.

Under certain conditions, the author proves that honestly reporting the ranking to the best of the owner's knowledge maximizes expected utility. The paper also proves that adjusted scores are significantly more accurate than the original reviewer scores. The incentive result is conditional, which matters when interpreting the mechanism's applicability. Extensions and practical refinements round out an approach that joins score improvement with strategic reasons for owners to share information.
summary.tldr: The Isotonic Mechanism improves noisy reviewer scores using owner rankings and makes truthful ranking optimal under stated conditions.

title: You Are the Best Reviewer of Your Own Papers: An Owner-Assisted Scoring Mechanism

abstract: Most benchmark datasets targeting commonsense reasoning focus on everyday scenarios: physical knowledge like knowing that you could fill a cup under a waterfall, social knowledge like bumping into someone is awkward, and other generic situations. However, there is a rich space of commonsense inferences anchored to knowledge about specific entities: for example, deciding the truthfulness of a claim Harry Potter can teach classes on how to fly on a broomstick. Can models learn to combine entity knowledge with commonsense reasoning in this fashion? We introduce CREAK, a testbed for commonsense reasoning about entity knowledge, bridging fact-checking about entities (Harry Potter is a wizard and is skilled at riding a broomstick) with commonsense inferences (if you're good at a skill you can teach others how to do it). Our dataset consists of 13k human-authored English claims about entities that are either true or false, in addition to a small contrast set. Crowdworkers can easily come up with these statements and human performance on the dataset is high (high 90s); we argue that pre-trained language models (LMs) should be able to blend entity knowledge and commonsense reasoning to do well here. In our experiments, we focus on the closed-book setting and observe that a baseline model finetuned on existing fact verification benchmark struggles with the type of inferences in CREAK. Training a model on CREAK improves accuracy by a substantial margin, but still falls short of human performance. Our benchmark provides a unique probe into natural language understanding models, testing both its ability to retrieve facts (e.g., who teaches at the University of Chicago?) and unstated commonsense knowledge (e.g., butlers do not yell at guests).

paragraphs: CREAK tests whether language models can combine facts about particular entities with everyday reasoning. Knowing an entity's attributes is only part of the task: a model must also infer what those attributes imply. The paper places this combination between conventional fact verification and commonsense benchmarks centered on generic situations.

The dataset contains roughly 13,000 human-written English claims labeled true or false, plus a small contrast set. Human performance is in the high nineties. The experiments focus on a closed-book setting, asking models to judge claims using their learned knowledge rather than consulting external material during the evaluation.

The benchmark offers a focused way to study that combination.
summary.tldr: CREAK tests reasoning that combines entity facts with common sense, revealing a remaining human-model gap even after dataset-specific training.

title: CREAK: A Dataset for Commonsense Reasoning over Entity Knowledge

abstract: The rapid proliferation of machine learning models across domains and deployment settings has given rise to various communities (e.g. industry practitioners) which seek to benchmark models across tasks and objectives of personal value. Unfortunately, these users cannot use standard benchmark results to perform such value-driven comparisons as traditional benchmarks evaluate models on a single objective (e.g. average accuracy) and fail to facilitate a standardized training framework that controls for confounding variables (e.g. computational budget), making fair comparisons difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce the open-source Ludwig Benchmarking Toolkit (LBT), a personalized benchmarking toolkit for running end-to-end benchmark studies (from hyperparameter optimization to evaluation) across an easily extensible set of tasks, deep learning models, datasets and evaluation metrics. LBT provides a configurable interface for controlling training and customizing evaluation, a standardized training framework for eliminating confounding variables, and support for multi-objective evaluation. We demonstrate how LBT can be used to create personalized benchmark studies with a large-scale comparative analysis for text classification across 7 models and 9 datasets. We explore the trade-offs between inference latency and performance, relationships between dataset attributes and performance, and the effects of pretraining on convergence and robustness, showing how LBT can be used to satisfy various benchmarking objectives.
originalAbstract: The rapid proliferation of machine learning models across domains and deployment settings has given rise to various communities (e.g. industry practitioners) which seek to benchmark models across tasks and objectives of personal value. Unfortunately, these users cannot use standard benchmark results to perform such value-driven comparisons as traditional benchmarks evaluate models on a single objective (e.g. average accuracy) and fail to facilitate a standardized training framework that controls for confounding variables (e.g. computational budget), making fair comparisons difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce the open-source Ludwig Benchmarking Toolkit (LBT), a personalized benchmarking toolkit for running end-to-end benchmark studies (from hyperparameter optimization to evaluation) across an easily extensible set of tasks, deep learning models, datasets and evaluation metrics. LBT provides a configurable interface for controlling training and customizing evaluation, a standardized training framework for eliminating confounding variables, and support for multi-objective evaluation. We demonstrate how LBT can be used to create personalized benchmark studies with a large-scale comparative analysis for text classification across 7 models and 9 datasets. We explore the trade-offs between inference latency and performance, relationships between dataset attributes and performance, and the effects of pretraining on convergence and robustness, showing how LBT can be used to satisfy various benchmarking objectives.

A benchmark centered on average accuracy may be insufficient when other objectives matter, and differences in training resources can complicate comparisons. LBT provides a configurable way to run benchmark studies with explicit training controls and multiple evaluation objectives.

The toolkit covers the process from hyperparameter optimization through evaluation. Users can extend its tasks, models, datasets, and metrics while using a standardized training framework intended to control confounding variables. This makes the conditions of comparison part of the study’s design, alongside the choice of what outcomes to measure.

The authors demonstrate the toolkit through text classification experiments covering seven models and nine datasets. They examine prediction speed versus performance, relationships between dataset properties and results, and how pretraining affects convergence and robustness. These studies illustrate how the same toolkit can answer different practical benchmarking questions, depending on the objectives and constraints a user chooses.
summary.tldr: LBT enables customizable, controlled model comparisons that account for multiple objectives such as prediction performance and inference latency.

title: Personalized Benchmarking with the Ludwig Benchmarking Toolkit

abstract: The Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameters optimization (CASH) problem is one of the fundamental problems in Automated Machine Learning (AutoML). Motivated by the success of ensemble learning, recent AutoML systems build post-hoc ensembles to output the final predictions instead of using the best single learner. However, while most CASH methods focus on searching for a single learner with the best performance, they neglect the diversity among base learners (i.e., they may suggest similar configurations to previously evaluated ones), which is also a crucial consideration when building an ensemble. To tackle this issue and further enhance the ensemble performance, we propose DivBO, a diversity-aware framework to inject explicit search of diversity into the CASH problems. In the framework, we propose to use a diversity surrogate to predict the pair-wise diversity of two unseen configurations. Furthermore, we introduce a temporary pool and a weighted acquisition function to guide the search of both performance and diversity based on Bayesian optimization. Empirical results on 15 public datasets show that DivBO achieves the best average ranks (1.82 and 1.73) on both validation and test errors among 10 compared methods, including post-hoc designs in recent AutoML systems and state-of-the-art baselines for ensemble learning on CASH problems.

DivBO makes diversity an explicit part of this search. It introduces a surrogate model that predicts the pairwise diversity of two configurations that have not yet been evaluated. These aggregate results support choosing models with their eventual ensemble role in mind, while average rank does not imply winning on every individual dataset.
summary.tldr: DivBO guides automated model search using both predictive performance and model diversity, achieving the best average ranks in the reported comparison.

title: DivBO: Diversity-aware CASH for Ensemble Learning

abstract: Scaling up model sizes can lead to fundamentally new capabilities in many machine learning (ML) tasks. However, training big models requires strong distributed system expertise to carefully design model-parallel execution strategies that suit the model architectures and cluster setups. In this paper, we develop AMP, a framework that automatically derives such strategies. AMP identifies a valid space of model parallelism strategies and efficiently searches the space for high-performed strategies, by leveraging a cost model designed to capture the heterogeneity of the model and cluster specifications. Unlike existing methods, AMP is specifically tailored to support complex models composed of uneven layers and cluster setups with more heterogeneous accelerators and bandwidth. We evaluate AMP on popular modelsand cluster setups from public clouds and show that AMP returns parallel strategies that match the expert-tuned strategies on typical cluster setups. On heterogeneous clusters or models with heterogeneous architectures, AMP finds strategies with 1.54$\times$ and 1.77$\times$ higher throughput than state-of-the-art model-parallel systems, respectively.

paragraphs: Training a large model across multiple accelerators requires deciding how to distribute its computation. Good choices depend on both the model architecture and the available machines, making manual strategy design a specialized systems task. AMP automates this process by searching for effective model-parallel execution strategies.

AMP first identifies valid strategies, then searches them efficiently using a cost model that accounts for differences within the model and the cluster. These differences include uneven layers, heterogeneous accelerators, and varying communication bandwidth. Accounting for them matters because a strategy suited to uniform layers and hardware may use an uneven setup poorly.

On the evaluated public-cloud configurations, AMP finds strategies that match expert tuning for typical clusters. For heterogeneous clusters and heterogeneous model architectures, the reported throughput improvements over state-of-the-art model-parallel systems are 1.54 times and 1.77 times, respectively. These results support using automated, heterogeneity-aware planning to reduce the expertise required for distributed training while improving throughput in the tested uneven settings.
summary.tldr: AMP automatically searches for model-parallel training strategies that account for uneven model layers, accelerators, and communication bandwidth.

title: AMP: Automatically Finding Model Parallel Strategies with Heterogeneity Awareness

abstract: Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO), which aims to find an optimal decision that minimizes the worst case cost over the ambiguity set of probability distribution, has been applied in diverse applications, e.g., network behavior analysis, risk management, etc. However, existing DRO techniques face three key challenges: 1) how to deal with the asynchronous updating in a distributed environment; 2) how to leverage the prior distribution effectively; 3) how to properly adjust the degree of robustness according to difference scenarios. To this end, we propose an asynchronous distributed algorithm, named Asynchronous Single-looP alternatIve gRadient projEction (ASPIRE) algorithm with the itErative Active SEt method (EASE) to tackle the distributed distributionally robust optimization (DDRO) problem. Furthermore, a new uncertainty set, i.e., constrained $D$-norm uncertainty set, is developed to effectively leverage the prior distribution and flexibly control the degree of robustness. Finally, our theoretical analysis elucidates that the proposed algorithm is guaranteed to converge and the iteration complexity is also analyzed. Extensive empirical studies on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can not only achieve fast convergence, remain robust against data heterogeneity and malicious attacks, but also tradeoff robustness with performance.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization chooses decisions by considering the worst cost over a specified collection of possible data distributions. In distributed settings, that objective must coexist with workers updating asynchronously, prior knowledge about the distribution, and different preferences for robustness. This paper addresses those issues for distributed optimization with non-convex objectives.

The proposed algorithm, ASPIRE, combines asynchronous gradient projection with an iterative active-set method called EASE. The authors also introduce a constrained D-norm uncertainty set. This set determines which distributions the method protects against, while incorporating a prior distribution and allowing the degree of robustness to be adjusted. The uncertainty model is therefore part of the contribution, alongside the distributed optimization procedure.

The theoretical analysis establishes convergence and studies iteration complexity. Experiments on real-world datasets report fast convergence and robustness to heterogeneous data and malicious attacks. They also show a tradeoff between robustness and performance. These findings support the framework as a way to tune protection while learning across distributed data, rather than treating the desired robustness level as fixed.
summary.tldr: ASPIRE combines asynchronous distributed optimization with a prior-informed uncertainty set that allows robustness to be adjusted.

title: Distributed Distributionally Robust Optimization with Non-Convex Objectives

abstract: Deep equilibrium models (DEQs) refrain from the traditional layer-stacking paradigm and turn to find the fixed point of a single layer. DEQs have achieved promising performance on different applications with featured memory efficiency. At the same time, the adversarial vulnerability of DEQs raises concerns. Several works propose to certify robustness for monotone DEQs. However, limited efforts are devoted to studying empirical robustness for general DEQs. To this end, we observe that an adversarially trained DEQ requires more forward steps to arrive at the equilibrium state, or even violates its fixed-point structure. Besides, the forward and backward tracks of DEQs are misaligned due to the black-box solvers. These facts cause gradient obfuscation when applying the ready-made attacks to evaluate or adversarially train DEQs. Given this, we develop approaches to estimate the intermediate gradients of DEQs and integrate them into the attacking pipelines. Our approaches facilitate fully white-box evaluations and lead to effective adversarial defense for DEQs. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 validate the adversarial robustness of DEQs competitive with deep networks of similar sizes.
