paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models represent computation by finding a fixed point of one layer, rather than passing inputs through a stack of distinct layers. This design offers memory efficiency, but it also complicates the evaluation of adversarial robustness: attacks need gradients that accurately reflect how the model produces its predictions.

The paper identifies two problems. Adversarial training can make the model require more forward steps to reach equilibrium, and can even disrupt its fixed-point structure. Meanwhile, the black-box solvers used by DEQs can make the forward computation and backward gradient calculation follow misaligned paths. Together, these effects can obscure gradients and undermine ready-made attacks used for evaluation or training.

The authors estimate gradients at intermediate stages and incorporate those estimates into attack pipelines. This supports white-box evaluations and more effective adversarial defense. Experiments on CIFAR-10 find robustness competitive with similarly sized deep networks. The contribution connects the reliability of robustness measurements to the numerical procedures that make equilibrium models work.
summary.tldr: Estimating intermediate gradients enables more reliable adversarial evaluation and training of deep equilibrium models.

title: A Closer Look at the Adversarial Robustness of Deep Equilibrium Models

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViT) have shown rapid progress in computer vision tasks, achieving promising results on various benchmarks. However, due to the massive number of parameters and model design, e.g., attention mechanism, ViT-based models are generally times slower than lightweight convolutional networks. Therefore, the deployment of ViT for real-time applications is particularly challenging, especially on resource-constrained hardware such as mobile devices. Recent efforts try to reduce the computation complexity of ViT through network architecture search or hybrid design with MobileNet block, yet the inference speed is still unsatisfactory. This leads to an important question: can transformers run as fast as MobileNet while obtaining high performance? To answer this, we first revisit the network architecture and operators used in ViT-based models and identify inefficient designs. Then we introduce a dimension-consistent pure transformer (without MobileNet blocks) as a design paradigm. Finally, we perform latency-driven slimming to get a series of final models dubbed EfficientFormer. Extensive experiments show the superiority of EfficientFormer in performance and speed on mobile devices. Our fastest model, EfficientFormer-L1, achieves $79.2\%$ top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with only $1.6$ ms inference latency on iPhone 12 (compiled with CoreML), which runs as fast as MobileNetV2$\times 1.4$ ($1.6$ ms, $74.7\%$ top-1), and our largest model, EfficientFormer-L7, obtains $83.3\%$ accuracy with only $7.0$ ms latency. Our work proves that properly designed transformers can reach extremely low latency on mobile devices while maintaining high performance.

EfficientFormer investigates whether transformer design can retain high accuracy while reaching the latency of MobileNet.

The authors first examine transformer architectures and operators to identify inefficient choices. They then introduce a dimension-consistent transformer design that does not incorporate MobileNet blocks. A latency-driven slimming procedure produces a family of models. Actual inference latency therefore guides the final architecture choices, connecting the design process directly to the deployment goal.

The stated MobileNetV2 comparison has the same latency and 74.7% accuracy. The larger EfficientFormer-L7 reaches 83.3% accuracy at 7.0 milliseconds. These results demonstrate that carefully designed transformers can combine strong accuracy with low mobile latency under the reported hardware and compilation setup, while offering multiple points along the accuracy–speed tradeoff.
summary.tldr: EfficientFormer combines transformer architecture changes and latency-driven slimming to achieve strong accuracy at mobile inference speeds.

title: EfficientFormer: Vision Transformers at MobileNet Speed

abstract: SATNet is a differentiable constraint solver with a custom backpropagation algorithm, which can be used as a layer in a deep-learning system. It is a promising proposal for bridging deep learning and logical reasoning. In fact, SATNet has been successfully applied to learn, among others, the rules of a complex logical puzzle, such as Sudoku, just from input and output pairs where inputs are given as images. In this paper, we show how to improve the learning of SATNet by exploiting symmetries in the target rules of a given but unknown logical puzzle or more generally a logical formula. We present SymSATNet, a variant of SATNet that translates the given symmetries of the target rules to a condition on the parameters of SATNet and requires that the parameters should have a particular parametric form that guarantees the condition. The requirement dramatically reduces the number of parameters to learn for the rules with enough symmetries, and makes the parameter learning of SymSATNet much easier than that of SATNet. We also describe a technique for automatically discovering symmetries of the target rules from examples. Our experiments with Sudoku and Rubik's cube show the substantial improvement of SymSATNet over the baseline SATNet.

It has been used to learn puzzle rules from input-output examples, including image inputs. This paper asks how known symmetries in the target rules can make that learning process easier.

The proposed SymSATNet translates rule symmetries into a condition on SATNet's parameters. It then restricts those parameters to a form that guarantees the condition. For rule systems with enough symmetry, this sharply reduces the number of parameters that must be learned. The model therefore incorporates shared structure directly into its parameterization instead of learning every part of the rule representation independently.

The paper also introduces a technique for discovering target-rule symmetries automatically from examples. Experiments on Sudoku and Rubik's cube show substantial improvements over baseline SATNet. Together, the results indicate that symmetry can help both define a smaller learning problem and improve practical rule learning in the tested puzzles.
summary.tldr: SymSATNet builds rule symmetries into a differentiable solver's parameters, simplifying learning and improving results on two puzzles.

title: Learning Symmetric Rules with SATNet

abstract: Aleatoric uncertainty captures the inherent randomness of the data, such as measurement noise. In Bayesian regression, we often use a Gaussian observation model, where we control the level of aleatoric uncertainty with a noise variance parameter. By contrast, for Bayesian classification we use a categorical distribution with no mechanism to represent our beliefs about aleatoric uncertainty. Our work shows that explicitly accounting for aleatoric uncertainty significantly improves the performance of Bayesian neural networks. We note that many standard benchmarks, such as CIFAR-10, have essentially no aleatoric uncertainty. Moreover, we show that data augmentation in approximate inference softens the likelihood, leading to underconfidence and misrepresenting our beliefs about aleatoric uncertainty. Accordingly, we find that a cold posterior, tempered by a power greater than one, often more honestly reflects our beliefs about aleatoric uncertainty than no tempering --- providing an explicit link between data augmentation and cold posteriors. We further show that we can match or exceed the performance of posterior tempering by using a Dirichlet observation model, where we explicitly control the level of aleatoric uncertainty, without any need for tempering.

The paper argues that standard categorical observation models for Bayesian classification lack a corresponding way to express beliefs about its level, and shows benefits from modeling it explicitly.

The authors connect this issue to data augmentation and cold posteriors. They find that augmentation during approximate inference softens the likelihood, producing underconfidence and misrepresenting assumptions about data randomness. They also note that many standard benchmarks, including CIFAR-10, have essentially no aleatoric uncertainty. The paper then uses a Dirichlet observation model to control aleatoric uncertainty directly. This approach matches or exceeds the performance of posterior tempering without requiring tempering itself. The findings give a concrete interpretation of why cold posteriors can help and identify an alternative that places the uncertainty assumption explicitly inside the observation model.
summary.tldr: Explicitly modeling aleatoric uncertainty helps explain cold-posterior benefits and can match or exceed tempering through a Dirichlet observation model.

title: On Uncertainty, Tempering, and Data Augmentation in Bayesian Classification

abstract: Equivariant neural networks, whose hidden features transform according to representations of a group $G$ acting on the data, exhibit training efficiency and an improved generalisation performance. In this work, we extend group invariant and equivariant representation learning to the field of unsupervised deep learning. We propose a general learning strategy based on an encoder-decoder framework in which the latent representation is separated in an invariant term and an equivariant group action component. The key idea is that the network learns to encode and decode data to and from a group-invariant representation by additionally learning to predict the appropriate group action to align input and output pose to solve the reconstruction task. We derive the necessary conditions on the equivariant encoder, and we present a construction valid for any $G$, both discrete and continuous. We describe explicitly our construction for rotations, translations and permutations. We test the validity and the robustness of our approach in a variety of experiments with diverse data types employing different network architectures.

The key idea is that the network learns to encode and decode data to and from a group-invariant representation by additionally learning to predict the appropriate group action to align input and output pose to solve the reconstruction task. We derive the necessary conditions on the equivariant encoder, and we present a construction valid for any $G$, both discrete and continuous. paragraphs: An invariant representation stays the same under a chosen transformation, while an equivariant representation changes in a corresponding, structured way. This paper brings both ideas into unsupervised learning. It asks how a network can preserve transformation-independent information while still retaining what is needed to reconstruct the original input.

The proposed encoder-decoder separates its latent representation into an invariant component and a component describing a group action. The network learns to predict the action needed to align the input and reconstructed output. Reconstruction therefore requires both a representation that ignores the relevant pose change and information that restores the appropriate pose.

The authors derive necessary conditions on the equivariant encoder and give a construction valid for any group, whether discrete or continuous. They explicitly describe rotations, translations, and permutations. Experiments across diverse data types and architectures test the method's validity and robustness. The contribution is a general construction for combining invariance with reconstruction, where transformation information has a distinct role rather than being lost when an invariant representation is learned.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised encoder-decoder separates invariant content from a learned group action, allowing reconstruction while respecting transformation structure.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Group Invariant and Equivariant Representations

abstract: We focus on the task of learning a single index model $\sigma(w^\star \cdot x)$ with respect to the isotropic Gaussian distribution in $d$ dimensions. Prior work has shown that the sample complexity of learning $w^\star$ is governed by the information exponent $k^\star$ of the link function $\sigma$, which is defined as the index of the first nonzero Hermite coefficient of $\sigma$. Ben Arous et al. (2021) showed that $n \gtrsim d^{k^\star-1}$ samples suffice for learning $w^\star$ and that this is tight for online SGD. However, the CSQ lower bound for gradient based methods only shows that $n \gtrsim d^{k^\star/2}$ samples are necessary. In this work, we close the gap between the upper and lower bounds by showing that online SGD on a smoothed loss learns $w^\star$ with $n \gtrsim d^{k^\star/2}$ samples. We also draw connections to statistical analyses of tensor PCA and to the implicit regularization effects of minibatch SGD on empirical losses.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a single-index model, where the output applies a link function to a projection of the input onto an unknown direction. Inputs follow an isotropic Gaussian distribution in d dimensions. The learning difficulty depends on the link function’s information exponent, defined by the position of its first nonzero Hermite coefficient.

Earlier analysis showed that online stochastic gradient descent could learn the direction with a sample count scaling as d raised to k* − 1, and that this rate was tight for that setting. A lower bound for gradient-based methods in the correlational statistical query framework instead gave the smaller scale d raised to k*/2. This left a gap between the bounds.

The authors close that gap by applying online stochastic gradient descent to a smoothed loss, achieving the d raised to k*/2 sample scale. Smoothing changes the learning landscape enough to reach the stated lower-bound rate. The paper also connects this analysis to tensor principal component analysis and to implicit regularization from minibatch stochastic gradient descent.
summary.tldr: For single-index models with isotropic Gaussian inputs, smoothing the loss lets online SGD match the stated gradient-based sample-complexity lower bound.

title: Smoothing the Landscape Boosts the Signal for SGD: Optimal Sample Complexity for Learning Single Index Models

abstract: For partially observable environments, imitation learning with observation histories (ILOH) assumes that control-relevant information is sufficiently captured in the observation histories for imitating the expert actions. In the offline setting wherethe agent is required to learn to imitate without interaction with the environment, behavior cloning (BC) has been shown to be a simple yet effective method for imitation learning. However, when the information about the actions executed in the past timesteps leaks into the observation histories, ILOH via BC often ends up imitating its own past actions. In this paper, we address this catastrophic failure by proposing a principled regularization for BC, which we name Past Action Leakage Regularization (PALR). The main idea behind our approach is to leverage the classical notion of conditional independence to mitigate the leakage. We compare different instances of our framework with natural choices of conditional independence metric and its estimator. The result of our comparison advocates the use of a particular kernel-based estimator for the conditional independence metric. We conduct an extensive set of experiments on benchmark datasets in order to assess the effectiveness of our regularization method. The experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms prior related approaches, highlighting its potential to successfully imitate expert actions when the past action information leaks into the observation histories.

In the offline setting wherethe agent is required to learn to imitate without interaction with the environment, behavior cloning (BC) has been shown to be a simple yet effective method for imitation learning. However, when the information about the actions executed in the past timesteps leaks into the observation histories, ILOH via BC often ends up imitating its own past actions. In this paper, we address this catastrophic failure by proposing a principled regularization for BC, which we name Past Action Leakage Regularization (PALR). The main idea behind our approach is to leverage the classical notion of conditional independence to mitigate the leakage. We compare different instances of our framework with natural choices of conditional independence metric and its estimator. The result of our comparison advocates the use of a particular kernel-based estimator for the conditional independence metric. We conduct an extensive set of experiments on benchmark datasets in order to assess the effectiveness of our regularization method. The experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms prior related approaches, highlighting its potential to successfully imitate expert actions when the past action information leaks into the observation histories.

paragraphs: The paper examines a failure of behavior cloning in partially observable environments. An agent learns from observation histories because a single observation may not contain enough information to choose an action. This setup assumes that the history sufficiently captures the information needed to imitate an expert.

Problems arise when the history also reveals previously executed actions. A cloned policy can end up copying its own past behavior instead of producing the appropriate expert action. The authors introduce Past Action Leakage Regularization, or PALR, which uses conditional independence to reduce this unwanted dependence on leaked action information.

The paper compares several versions of the framework using different conditional-independence measures and estimators. That comparison favors a particular kernel-based estimator. Extensive benchmark experiments show substantial improvements over earlier related methods. The findings support regularizing how a policy uses observation history in offline imitation learning, where it must learn without interacting with the environment, and specifically when past-action leakage interferes with learning expert behavior.
summary.tldr: PALR uses conditional-independence regularization to reduce behavior cloning’s tendency to copy past actions leaked through observation histories.

title: Regularized Behavior Cloning for Blocking the Leakage of Past Action Information

abstract: Inverse optimal control can be used to characterize behavior in sequential decision-making tasks. Most existing work, however, is limited to fully observable or linear systems, or requires the action signals to be known. Here, we introduce a probabilistic approach to inverse optimal control for partially observable stochastic non-linear systems with unobserved action signals, which unifies previous approaches to inverse optimal control with maximum causal entropy formulations. Using an explicit model of the noise characteristics of the sensory and motor systems of the agent in conjunction with local linearization techniques, we derive an approximate likelihood function for the model parameters, which can be computed within a single forward pass. We present quantitative evaluations on stochastic and partially observable versions of two classic control tasks and two human behavioral tasks. Importantly, we show that our method can disentangle perceptual factors and behavioral costs despite the fact that epistemic and pragmatic actions are intertwined in sequential decision-making under uncertainty, such as in active sensing and active learning. The proposed method has broad applicability, ranging from imitation learning to sensorimotor neuroscience.

paragraphs: Inverse optimal control works backward from behavior to characterize the factors governing sequential decisions. This becomes difficult when an agent sees the world imperfectly, the system is nonlinear and stochastic, and the actions themselves are unobserved. The paper develops a probabilistic approach that handles this combination while connecting earlier inverse-control approaches with maximum causal entropy formulations.

The method explicitly models noise in the agent's sensory and motor systems. Together with local linearization, this produces an approximate likelihood for the model parameters that can be computed in one forward pass. The approximation provides a way to evaluate explanations of behavior while accounting for both uncertain perception and noisy action generation.

The authors show that the method can separate perceptual factors from behavioral costs even when actions simultaneously gather information and pursue practical goals. This matters for interpreting active sensing and learning, where the same behavior may reflect both what an agent knows and what it seeks to achieve.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic inverse-control method separates perceptual uncertainty from behavioral costs in nonlinear, partially observable systems with unobserved actions.

title: Probabilistic inverse optimal control for non-linear partially observable systems disentangles perceptual uncertainty and behavioral costs

abstract: We study social learning dynamics motivated by reviews on online platforms. Theagents collectively follow a simple multi-armed bandit protocol, but each agentacts myopically, without regards to exploration. We allow a wide range of myopicbehaviors that are consistent with (parameterized) confidence intervals for the arms’expected rewards. We derive stark exploration failures for any such behavior, andprovide matching positive results. As a special case, we obtain the first generalresults on failure of the greedy algorithm in bandits, thus providing a theoreticalfoundation for why bandit algorithms should explore.

paragraphs: This paper studies how people learn collectively when each person chooses only what currently seems rewarding. Online reviews motivate the setting: earlier choices provide information that later users can draw on, but individual users do not deliberately try uncertain options to help the group learn. The collective process follows a multi-armed bandit protocol.

The analysis covers a broad family of short-sighted decision rules rather than a single algorithm. These rules must be consistent with parameterized confidence intervals around the options’ expected rewards. Within that framework, the authors derive pronounced failures of exploration and matching positive results. Together, these results characterize both difficulties and possibilities for learning under the behaviors studied.

A notable special case concerns the greedy algorithm, which acts on currently available reward estimates without explicitly encouraging exploration. The paper provides general theoretical results about its failures. This gives a mathematical basis for designing bandit algorithms that actively gather information: individually appealing choices can leave the collective learning process poorly informed.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when short-sighted bandit decisions fail to explore, providing theoretical support for deliberate exploration.

title: Bandit Social Learning under Myopic Behavior

abstract: Local SGD, a cornerstone algorithm in federated learning, is widely used in training deep neural networks and shown to have strong empirical performance. A theoretical understanding of such performance on nonconvex loss landscapes is currently lacking. Analysis of the global convergence of SGD is challenging, as the noise depends on the model parameters. Indeed, many works narrow their focus to GD and rely on injecting noise to enable convergence to the local or global optimum. When expanding the focus to local SGD, existing analyses in the nonconvex case can only guarantee finding stationary points or assume the neural network is overparameterized so as to guarantee convergence to the global minimum through neural tangent kernel analysis. In this work, we provide the first global convergence analysis of the vanilla local SGD for two-layer neural networks \emph{without overparameterization} and \textit{without injecting noise}, when the input data is Gaussian. The main technical ingredients of our proof are \textit{a self-correction mechanism} and \textit{a new exact recursive characterization of the direction of global model parameters}. The self-correction mechanism guarantees the algorithm reaches a good region even if the initialization is in a bad region. A good (bad) region means updating the model by gradient descent will move closer to (away from) the optimal solution. The main difficulty in establishing a self-correction mechanism is to cope with the gradient dependency between two layers. To address this challenge, we divide the landscape of the objective into several regions to carefully control the interference of two layers during the correction process. As a result, we show that local SGD can correct the two layers and enter the good region in polynomial time. After that, we establish a new exact recursive characterization of the direction of global parameters, which is the key to showing convergence to the global minimum with linear speedup in the number of machines and reduced communication rounds. Experiments on synthetic data confirm theoretical results.

paragraphs: Local stochastic gradient descent is widely used for distributed and federated training, but its success on nonconvex neural-network objectives is difficult to explain theoretically. This paper analyzes ordinary local SGD for two-layer networks with Gaussian inputs. It establishes global convergence without requiring overparameterization or adding artificial noise.

The proof first identifies a self-correction mechanism. Even when initialization puts the model in a region where gradient descent would move away from the optimum, local SGD can bring both layers into a favorable region in polynomial time. The analysis divides the objective landscape into regions to control how the two layers' dependent gradients interfere with this correction.

Once the model reaches a favorable region, an exact recursive description of the direction of its global parameters establishes convergence to the global minimum. The result also provides linear speedup with the number of machines and reduced communication rounds. Synthetic-data experiments support the theory. The contribution explains how correction and subsequent progress can arise under the paper's specific network and input assumptions.
summary.tldr: For two-layer networks with Gaussian inputs, the paper proves local SGD can reach a global minimum without overparameterization or injected noise.

title: Global Convergence Analysis of Local SGD for Two-layer Neural Network without Overparameterization

abstract: We study gradient descent under linearly correlated noise. Our work is motivated by recent practical methods for optimization with differential privacy (DP), such as DP-FTRL, which achieve strong performance in settings where privacy amplification techniques are infeasible (such as in federated learning). These methods inject privacy noise through a matrix factorization mechanism, making the noise *linearly correlated* over iterations. We propose a simplified setting that distills key facets of these methods and isolates the impact of linearly correlated noise. We analyze the behavior of gradient descent in this setting, for both convex and non-convex functions. Our analysis is demonstrably tighter than prior work and recovers multiple important special cases exactly (including anticorrelated perturbed gradient descent). We use our results to develop new, effective matrix factorizations for differentially private optimization, and highlight the benefits of these factorizations theoretically and empirically.

paragraphs: Noise added during optimization need not be independent from one training step to the next. Some practical methods for differential privacy, including DP-FTRL, use matrix factorizations that create linear correlations across iterations. These methods are particularly relevant when privacy amplification techniques are infeasible, as can occur in federated learning.

The paper develops a simplified setting that isolates the effect of this correlated noise on gradient descent. It analyzes both convex and non-convex objectives, providing tighter results than prior analyses. The analysis also recovers several important special cases exactly, including gradient descent with anticorrelated perturbations.

The authors then use these results to design new matrix factorizations for differentially private optimization and demonstrate their benefits theoretically and empirically. The contribution connects an explanation of noisy optimization dynamics to a concrete design choice in privacy-preserving training. Understanding how noise is related across steps can therefore help improve the optimization mechanisms that inject it, rather than treating noise solely through its magnitude.
summary.tldr: A tighter analysis of gradient descent with correlated noise guides new matrix factorizations for differentially private optimization.

title: Gradient Descent with Linearly Correlated Noise: Theory and Applications to Differential Privacy

abstract: Large transformer models trained on diverse datasets have shown a remarkable ability to learn in-context, achieving high few-shot performance on tasks they were not explicitly trained to solve. In this paper, we study the in-context learning capabilities of transformers in decision-making problems, i.e., reinforcement learning (RL) for bandits and Markov decision processes. To do so, we introduce and study the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT), a supervised pretraining method where a transformer predicts an optimal action given a query state and an in-context dataset of interactions from a diverse set of tasks. While simple, this procedure produces a model with several surprising capabilities. We find that the trained transformer can solve a range of RL problems in-context, exhibiting both exploration online and conservatism offline, despite not being explicitly trained to do so. The model also generalizes beyond the pretraining distribution to new tasks and automatically adapts its decision-making strategies to unknown structure. Theoretically, we show DPT can be viewed as an efficient implementation of Bayesian posterior sampling, a provably sample-efficient RL algorithm. We further leverage this connection to provide guarantees on the regret of the in-context algorithm yielded by DPT, and prove that it can learn faster than algorithms used to generate the pretraining data. These results suggest a promising yet simple path towards instilling strong in-context decision-making abilities in transformers.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether supervised pretraining can produce a transformer that learns to make decisions from interactions supplied in its context. The Decision-Pretrained Transformer learns to predict an optimal action from a query state and a collection of interactions drawn from diverse tasks. The study covers bandits and Markov decision processes.

Despite the simplicity of that objective, the trained model exhibits several reinforcement-learning behaviours. It explores when interacting online and behaves conservatively when working from offline data, without explicit training objectives for those behaviours. The authors also observe generalisation to new tasks beyond the pretraining distribution and adaptation to previously unknown task structure.

The theoretical analysis connects DPT to Bayesian posterior sampling, a sample-efficient reinforcement-learning algorithm. This connection yields regret guarantees for the resulting in-context decision procedure and establishes that it can learn faster than algorithms that generated its pretraining data. Together, the findings show how supervised prediction across varied tasks can support adaptive decision-making through context.
summary.tldr: Supervised action prediction trains a transformer that performs reinforcement learning in context, with empirical adaptive behaviours and theoretical links to posterior sampling.

title: Supervised Pretraining Can Learn In-Context Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large language models have demonstrated surprising ability to perform in-context learning, i.e., these models can be directly applied to solve numerous downstream tasks by conditioning on a prompt constructed by a few input-output examples. However, prior research has shown that in-context learning can suffer from high instability due to variations in training examples, example order, and prompt formats. Therefore, the construction of an appropriate prompt is essential for improving the performance of in-context learning. In this paper, we revisit this problem from the view of predictive bias. Specifically, we introduce a metric to evaluate the predictive bias of a fixed prompt against labels or a given attributes. Then we empirically show that prompts with higher bias always lead to unsatisfactory predictive quality. Based on this observation, we propose a novel search strategy based on the greedy search to identify the near-optimal prompt for improving the performance of in-context learning. We perform comprehensive experiments with state-of-the-art mainstream models such as GPT-3 on various downstream tasks. Our results indicate that our method can enhance the model's in-context learning performance in an effective and interpretable manner.

paragraphs: Few-shot prompting lets a language model learn a task from input-output examples included in its prompt. Its performance can change substantially with the examples chosen, their order, and the prompt format. This paper studies prompt construction through predictive bias: whether a fixed prompt skews the model’s predictions with respect to labels or specified attributes.

The authors introduce a metric for this bias and empirically find that highly biased prompts produce unsatisfactory predictions in their investigation. They then use that observation to guide a search for a near-optimal prompt. The search builds on a greedy strategy, making predictive bias a concrete signal for prompt selection.

Experiments across downstream tasks and mainstream models, including GPT-3, show improved in-context learning performance. The method also gives an interpretable reason for selecting one prompt over another through its measured predictive bias. The reported connection between bias and poor quality is empirical; the contribution is a practical selection strategy supported by those observations and the resulting task evaluations.
summary.tldr: A predictive-bias metric guides greedy prompt selection to improve few-shot language-model performance.

title: Fairness-guided Few-shot Prompting for Large Language Models

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based recommender systems (RSs) have garnered considerable attention due to their ability to learn optimal recommendation policies and maximize long-term user rewards. However, deploying RL models directly in online environments and generating authentic data through A/B tests can pose challenges and require substantial resources. Simulators offer an alternative approach by providing training and evaluation environments for RS models, reducing reliance on real-world data. Existing simulators have shown promising results but also have limitations such as simplified user feedback, lacking consistency with real-world data, the challenge of simulator evaluation, and difficulties in migration and expansion across RSs.To address these challenges, we propose KuaiSim, a comprehensive user environment that provides user feedback with multi-behavior and cross-session responses.The resulting simulator can support three levels of recommendation problems: the request level list-wise recommendation task, the whole-session level sequential recommendation task, and the cross-session level retention optimization task. For each task, KuaiSim also provides evaluation protocols and baseline recommendation algorithms that further serve as benchmarks for future research. We also restructure existing competitive simulators on the Kuairand Dataset and compare them against KuaiSim to future assess their performance and behavioral differences. Furthermore, to showcase KuaiSim's flexibility in accommodating different datasets, we demonstrate its versatility and robustness when deploying it on the ML-1m dataset. The implementation code is available online to ease reproducibility \footnote{https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/KuaiSim}.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can optimize recommendations for longer-term user rewards, but training and testing directly with users can require substantial resources. KuaiSim provides a simulated user environment for this work. It models multiple kinds of user behavior and responses across sessions, extending the scope beyond a simplified response to one recommendation.

The simulator supports three decision scales. A system can choose a recommendation list for an individual request, optimize a sequence of recommendations throughout a session, or work on retaining users across sessions. Each task comes with evaluation protocols and baseline recommendation algorithms, making the environment a benchmark as well as a place to train models.

The authors rebuild competing simulators on the Kuairand dataset and compare their performance and behavioral differences with KuaiSim. They also deploy KuaiSim on ML-1m to demonstrate flexibility across datasets. These contributions give researchers a common way to examine immediate recommendation behavior and longer-term interaction, with less reliance on online experiments for every stage of development.
summary.tldr: KuaiSim simulates multiple user behaviors across requests and sessions to support training and evaluating long-term recommendation policies.

title: KuaiSim: A Comprehensive Simulator for Recommender Systems

abstract: Learning with rejection is an important framework that can refrain from making predictions to avoid critical mispredictions by balancing between prediction and rejection. Previous studies on cost-based rejection only focused on the classification setting, which cannot handle the continuous and infinite target space in the regression setting. In this paper, we investigate a novel regression problem called regression with cost-based rejection, where the model can reject to make predictions on some examples given certain rejection costs. To solve this problem, we first formulate the expected risk for this problem and then derive the Bayes optimal solution, which shows that the optimal model should reject to make predictions on the examples whose variance is larger than the rejection cost when the mean squared error is used as the evaluation metric. Furthermore, we propose to train the model by a surrogate loss function that considers rejection as binary classification and we provide conditions for the model consistency, which implies that the Bayes optimal solution can be recovered by our proposed surrogate loss. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

paragraphs: A prediction system may sometimes benefit from declining to answer, especially when a wrong answer is costly. This paper studies that choice for regression, where the target is continuous. It gives rejection an explicit cost, so the learning objective balances the cost of predicting poorly against the cost of withholding a prediction.

The authors formulate the expected risk and derive its Bayes-optimal solution. With mean squared error as the evaluation metric, the optimal rule rejects examples whose target variance exceeds the rejection cost. This makes the decision depend on uncertainty in the outcome for an example and on how expensive rejection is within the specified objective.

To train a model, the paper proposes a surrogate loss that treats rejection as a binary classification decision. It supplies conditions for consistency, under which optimizing the surrogate can recover the Bayes-optimal solution. Experiments demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines a precise decision rule with a training approach, extending cost-based rejection to continuous predictions while making the role of the chosen loss explicit.
summary.tldr: For squared-error regression, the Bayes-optimal rejection rule compares target variance with rejection cost, and a surrogate loss can recover it under consistency conditions.

title: Regression with Cost-based Rejection

abstract: We introduce HT-Step, a large-scale dataset containing temporal annotations of instructional article steps in cooking videos. It includes 122k segment-level annotations over 20k narrated videos (approximately 2.3k hours) of the HowTo100M dataset.Each annotation provides a temporal interval, and a categorical step label from a taxonomy of 4,958 unique steps automatically mined from wikiHow articles which include rich descriptions of each step.Our dataset significantly surpasses existing labeled step datasets in terms of scale, number of tasks, and richness of natural language step descriptions. Based on these annotations, we introduce a strongly supervised benchmark for aligning instructional articles with how-to videos and present a comprehensive evaluation of baseline methods for this task.By publicly releasing these annotations and defining rigorous evaluation protocols and metrics,we hope to significantly accelerate research in the field of procedural activity understanding.

paragraphs: Connecting written instructions to video requires identifying when each described step occurs. HT-Step provides labeled examples for studying that alignment in cooking videos. Each annotation pairs a time interval with a step category, linking a segment of observed activity to a step described in an instructional article.

The dataset contains 122,000 segment annotations across 20,000 narrated HowTo100M videos, covering approximately 2,300 hours. Its taxonomy contains 4,958 distinct steps automatically mined from wikiHow articles, along with rich descriptions. The authors report that it exceeds existing labeled step datasets in scale, task coverage, and the richness of its natural-language descriptions.

Using these annotations, the paper establishes a strongly supervised benchmark and evaluates baseline alignment methods. It also releases the annotations and specifies evaluation protocols and metrics so that subsequent methods can be assessed on a common task. The contribution is research infrastructure for procedural activity understanding: a substantial collection of timed step labels and a defined way to evaluate connections between instructions and video.
summary.tldr: HT-Step supplies large-scale timed cooking-step annotations and a benchmark for aligning written instructions with videos.

title: HT-Step: Aligning Instructional Articles with How-To Videos

abstract: This paper studies the behaviour of two-layer fully connected networks with linear activations trained with gradient flow on the square loss. We show how the optimization process carries an implicit bias on the parameters that depends on the scale of its initialization. The main result of the paper is a variational characterization of the loss minimizers retrieved by the gradient flow for a specific initialization shape. This characterization reveals that, in the small scale initialization regime, the linear neural network's hidden layer is biased toward having a low-rank structure. To complement our results, we showcase a hidden mirror flow that tracks the dynamics of the singular values of the weights matrices and describe their time evolution. We support our findings with numerical experiments illustrating the phenomena.

paragraphs: This paper studies two-layer fully connected networks with linear activations, trained by gradient flow on squared loss. Even in this simplified setting, optimization can favor particular parameter structures. The authors examine how that implicit preference depends on the scale of the initial weights, connecting initialization to the solution eventually reached.

Their main result characterizes the loss minimizers selected by gradient flow for a specific initialization shape through a variational formulation. In the regime of small initialization scale, this characterization reveals a preference for a low-rank hidden-layer structure. Thus, the parameterization and training dynamics can favor a restricted internal representation without adding an explicit low-rank objective.

The authors also identify a hidden mirror flow that tracks the singular values of the weight matrices and describes how they evolve over time. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical phenomena. These results explain a concrete form of optimization bias within the stated linear-network setting, with the initialization shape and scale playing explicit roles in the analysis.
summary.tldr: For a specified initialization shape, small-scale initialization biases gradient-flow training of two-layer linear networks toward low-rank hidden representations.

title: On the spectral bias of two-layer linear networks

abstract: In this work we explore recent advances in instruction-tuning language models on a range of open instruction-following datasets. Despite recent claims that open models can be on par with state-of-the-art proprietary models, these claims are often accompanied by limited evaluation, making it difficult to compare models across the board and determine the utility of various resources. We provide a large set of instruction-tuned models from 6.7B to 65B parameters in size, trained on 12 instruction datasets ranging from manually curated (e.g., OpenAssistant) to synthetic and distilled (e.g., Alpaca) and systematically evaluate them on their factual knowledge, reasoning, multilinguality, coding, safety, and open-ended instruction following abilities through a collection of automatic, model-based, and human-based metrics. We further introduce Tülu, our best performing instruction-tuned model suite finetuned on a combination of high-quality open resources.Our experiments show that different instruction-tuning datasets can uncover or enhance specific skills, while no single dataset (or combination) provides the best performance across all evaluations. Interestingly, we find that model and human preference-based evaluations fail to reflect differences in model capabilities exposed by benchmark-based evaluations, suggesting the need for the type of systemic evaluation performed in this work. Our evaluations show that the best model in any given evaluation reaches on average 87% of ChatGPT performance, and 73% of GPT-4 performance, suggesting that further investment in building better base models and instruction-tuning data is required to close the gap. We release our instruction-tuned models, including a fully finetuned 65B Tülu, along with our code, data, and evaluation framework to facilitate future research.

abstract: Molecular representation learning lays the foundation for drug discovery. However, existing methods suffer from poor out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, particularly when data for training and testing originate from different environments. To address this issue, we propose a new framework for learning molecular representations that exhibit invariance and robustness against distribution shifts. Specifically, we propose a strategy called ``first-encoding-then-separation'' to identify invariant molecule features in the latent space, which deviates from conventional practices. Prior to the separation step, we introduce a residual vector quantization module that mitigates the over-fitting to training data distributions while preserving the expressivity of encoders. Furthermore, we design a task-agnostic self-supervised learning objective to encourage precise invariance identification, which enables our method widely applicable to a variety of tasks, such as regression and multi-label classification. Extensive experiments on 18 real-world molecular datasets demonstrate that our model achieves stronger generalization against state-of-the-art baselines in the presence of various distribution shifts. Our code is available at https://github.com/HICAI-ZJU/iMoLD.

paragraphs: Molecular representation learning produces features used in tasks relevant to drug discovery. A central difficulty is that representations learned in one data environment may perform poorly in another. This paper proposes learning features that remain useful under distribution shifts, with the aim of improving generalization beyond the training environment.

The framework first encodes molecules and then separates invariant features within the latent representation. Before separation, it applies residual vector quantization, introducing a discrete latent representation intended to reduce overfitting to training distributions while preserving the encoder's expressiveness. A task-agnostic self-supervised objective encourages more accurate identification of invariant information, allowing the approach to support tasks such as regression and multi-label classification.

The authors evaluate the method on 18 real-world molecular datasets under various distribution shifts. They report stronger generalization than state-of-the-art baselines. These results support the combination of encoding before separation, latent quantization, and self-supervised invariance learning as a way to improve molecular representations across the tested shifts and tasks.
summary.tldr: The framework combines discrete latent encoding and invariant-feature separation to improve molecular prediction under distribution shifts.

title: Learning Invariant Molecular Representation in Latent Discrete Space

abstract: A crucial problem in reinforcement learning is learning the optimal policy. We study this in tabular infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision processes under the online setting. The existing algorithms either fail to achieve regret optimality or have to incur a high memory and computational cost. In addition, existing optimal algorithms all require a long burn-in time in order to achieve optimal sample efficiency, i.e., their optimality is not guaranteed unless sample size surpasses a high threshold. We address both open problems by introducing a model-free algorithm that employs variance reduction and a novel technique that switches the execution policy in a slow-yet-adaptive manner. This is the first regret-optimal model-free algorithm in the discounted setting, with the additional benefit of a low burn-in time.

paragraphs: This paper studies an agent learning through ongoing interaction with a tabular environment, where future rewards receive progressively less weight. Its target is regret-optimal learning: controlling the accumulated performance gap relative to optimal behavior. The setting is an infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision process, so the result concerns this particular mathematical formulation of reinforcement learning.

The authors identify two obstacles in prior approaches. Existing algorithms either miss optimal regret or require substantial memory and computation. Moreover, existing optimal algorithms need a long burn-in period before their optimal sample-efficiency guarantees apply. That threshold matters because a favorable eventual guarantee may only become relevant after considerable experience.

The proposed model-free algorithm combines variance reduction with a new way of changing the policy used to act. Policy changes occur slowly but adaptively, rather than following an entirely fixed schedule. The authors establish the first regret-optimal model-free result in the discounted setting, together with a shorter burn-in time. This means the optimality guarantee becomes applicable after a lower sample threshold, not that optimal behavior is available immediately.
summary.tldr: A model-free reinforcement-learning algorithm achieves optimal regret with a shorter burn-in period in tabular discounted environments.

title: Regret-Optimal Model-Free Reinforcement Learning for Discounted MDPs with Short Burn-In Time

abstract: We propose a novel method, \textbf{TwinAct}, to tackle the challenge of decoupling actions and actors in order to customize the text-guided diffusion models (TGDMs) for few-shot action image generation. TwinAct addresses the limitations of existing methods that struggle to decouple actions from other semantics (e.g., the actor's appearance) due to the lack of an effective inductive bias with few exemplar images. Our approach introduces a common action space, which is a textual embedding space focused solely on actions, enabling precise customization without actor-related details. Specifically, TwinAct involves three key steps: 1) Building common action space based on a set of representative action phrases; 2) Imitating the customized action within the action space; and 3) Generating highly adaptable customized action images in diverse contexts with action similarity loss. To comprehensively evaluate TwinAct, we construct a novel benchmark, which provides sample images with various forms of actions. Extensive experiments demonstrate TwinAct's superiority in generating accurate, context-independent customized actions while maintaining the identity consistency of different subjects, including animals, humans, and even customized actors.

paragraphs: Learning an action from a few example images is difficult because those images also show an actor, an appearance, and surrounding context. A text-guided diffusion model can entangle these details with the action being customized. TwinAct addresses this separation problem so that a learned action can be generated with different subjects and in different contexts.

The method constructs a common action space from representative action phrases. This textual embedding space is designed to emphasize actions while excluding actor-related details. TwinAct then imitates the desired action within that space and uses an action similarity loss when generating customized images. The action space supplies the organizing bias that the authors argue is missing from existing few-shot approaches.

The paper also introduces a benchmark containing varied forms of actions. Experiments report better action accuracy and independence from context while preserving subject identity across animals, humans, and customized actors. The findings support using an explicit action-focused representation to transfer what a subject is doing without tying that behavior to the subject shown in the examples.
summary.tldr: TwinAct learns customized actions in an action-focused text space so they can be generated across different subjects and contexts.

title: Action Imitation in Common Action Space for Customized Action Image Synthesis

abstract: Finding specific preference-guided Pareto solutions that represent different trade-offs among multiple objectives is critical yet challenging in multi-objective problems. Existing methods are restrictive in preference definitions and/or their theoretical guarantees.In this work, we introduce a Flexible framEwork for pREfeRence-guided multi-Objective learning (**FERERO**) by casting it as a constrained vector optimization problem.Specifically, two types of preferences are incorporated into this formulation -- the *relative preference* defined by the partial ordering induced by a polyhedral cone, and the *absolute preference* defined by constraints that are linear functions of the objectives. To solve this problem, convergent algorithms are developed with both single-loop and stochastic variants. Notably, this is the *first single-loop primal algorithm* for constrained optimization to our knowledge. The proposed algorithms adaptively adjust to both constraint and objective values, eliminating the need to solve different subproblems at different stages of constraint satisfaction. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the proposed method is very competitive in finding preference-guided optimal solutions.Code is available at https://github.com/lisha-chen/FERERO/.

paragraphs: Multi-objective learning must navigate trade-offs among several goals. A Pareto solution represents a trade-off where improving one objective requires sacrificing another, but users may prefer only particular parts of that solution space. FERERO addresses how to express those preferences flexibly and develop algorithms with convergence guarantees for finding the corresponding solutions.

The framework formulates the task as constrained vector optimization. It supports relative preferences through a partial ordering defined by a polyhedral cone, and absolute preferences through constraints that are linear functions of the objectives. These two mechanisms let the formulation encode both how outcomes should be compared and which combinations of objective values are acceptable.

The authors develop convergent algorithms, including single-loop and stochastic variants. The algorithms adapt to both objective and constraint values, avoiding separate subproblems for different stages of constraint satisfaction. The authors identify their method as the first single-loop primal algorithm for constrained optimization to their knowledge. Benchmark experiments show competitive performance in finding preference-guided optimal solutions.
summary.tldr: FERERO expresses relative and absolute preferences within constrained multi-objective optimization and provides convergent algorithms for finding preferred trade-offs.

title: FERERO: A Flexible Framework for Preference-Guided Multi-Objective Learning

abstract: When learning vision-language models (VLM) for the fashion domain, most existing works design new architectures from vanilla BERT with additional objectives, or perform dense multi-task learning with fashion-specific tasks. Though progress has been made, their architecture or objectives are often intricate and the extendibility is limited.By contrast, with simple architecture (comprising only two unimodal encoders) and just the contrastive objective, popular pre-trained VL models (e.g., CLIP) achieve superior performance in general domains, which are further easily extended to downstream tasks.However, inheriting such benefits of CLIP in the fashion domain is non-trivial in the presence of the notable domain gap. Empirically, we find that directly finetuning on fashion data leads CLIP to frequently ignore minor yet important details such as logos and composition, which are critical in fashion tasks such as retrieval and captioning.In this work, to maintain CLIP's simple architecture and objective while explicitly attending to fashion details, we propose $E^2$: Easy Regional Contrastive Learning of Expressive Fashion Representations.$E^2$ introduces only a few selection tokens and fusion blocks (just 1.9\% additional parameters in total) with only contrastive losses. Despite lightweight, in our primary focus, cross-modal retrieval, $E^2$ notably outperforms existing fashion VLMs with various fashion-specific objectives.Moreover, thanks to CLIP's widespread use in downstream tasks in general domains (e.g., zero-shot composed image retrieval and image captioning), our model can easily extend these models from general domain to the fashion domain with notable improvement.To conduct a comprehensive evaluation, we further collect data from Amazon Reviews to build a new dataset for cross-modal retrieval in the fashion domain.

paragraphs: Fashion understanding depends on details that a general vision-language model may overlook. The authors find that directly fine-tuning CLIP on fashion data often neglects small but consequential features, including logos and composition. These omissions matter for tasks such as finding an item from a description or producing a caption that captures its distinguishing characteristics.

Their method, E², adapts CLIP through regional contrastive learning while keeping a relatively simple architecture and contrastive training objectives. It adds selection tokens and fusion blocks, increasing the parameter count by just 1.9%. The purpose is to direct representation learning toward fashion details without adopting the intricate task-specific architectures and objectives used by many existing fashion models.

For its primary task, retrieval across images and text, E² substantially outperforms the existing fashion models considered in the paper. It also helps extend general-domain approaches for zero-shot composed image retrieval and image captioning into fashion. The authors additionally build a fashion retrieval dataset from Amazon Reviews, supporting a broader evaluation of whether representations capture the details needed for these applications.
summary.tldr: E² adds lightweight regional learning components to CLIP to better capture fashion details and improve retrieval and related tasks.

title: Easy Regional Contrastive Learning of Expressive Fashion Representations

abstract: Diffusion models have obtained substantial progress in image-to-video generation. However, in this paper, we find that these models tend to generate videos with less motion than expected. We attribute this to the issue called conditional image leakage, where the image-to-video diffusion models (I2V-DMs) tend to over-rely on the conditional image at large time steps. We further address this challenge from both inference and training aspects. First, we propose to start the generation process from an earlier time step to avoid the unreliable large-time steps of I2V-DMs, as well as an initial noise distribution with optimal analytic expressions (Analytic-Init) by minimizing the KL divergence between it and the actual marginal distribution to bridge the training-inference gap. Second, we design a time-dependent noise distribution (TimeNoise) for the conditional image during training, applying higher noise levels at larger time steps to disrupt it and reduce the model's dependency on it. We validate these general strategies on various I2V-DMs on our collected open-domain image benchmark and the UCF101 dataset. Extensive results show that our methods outperform baselines by producing higher motion scores with lower errors while maintaining image alignment and temporal consistency, thereby yielding superior overall performance and enabling more accurate motion control. The project page: \url{https://cond-image-leak.github.io/}.

paragraphs: Image-to-video diffusion models can generate less motion than intended. The authors attribute this tendency to conditional image leakage: at large diffusion time steps, the model relies too heavily on the input image. They address that dependency both when generating videos and when training the model.

At inference time, generation begins at an earlier time step to bypass unreliable large-time-step behavior. Analytic-Init supplies an initial noise distribution derived by minimizing its KL divergence from the actual marginal distribution, reducing the mismatch between training and generation. During training, TimeNoise applies noise to the conditioning image according to the diffusion step, using more noise at larger steps to weaken excessive dependence on that image.

The strategies are evaluated across several image-to-video models using an open-domain image benchmark collected by the authors and UCF101. Reported results combine higher motion scores with lower errors while preserving alignment with the input image and consistency over time. The findings suggest that controlling reliance on the conditioning image can improve both overall video quality and the accuracy of motion control.
summary.tldr: Changing diffusion initialization and conditioning-image noise reduces excessive image dependence and improves motion in image-to-video generation.

title: Identifying and Solving Conditional Image Leakage in Image-to-Video Diffusion Model

abstract: In online bilateral trade, a platform posts prices to incoming pairs of buyers and sellers that have private valuations for a certain good. If the price is lower than the buyers' valuation and higher than the sellers' valuation, then a trade takes place. Previous work focused on the platform perspective, with the goal of setting prices maximizing the *gain from trade* (the sum of sellers' and buyers' utilities). Gain from trade is, however, potentially unfair to traders, as they may receive highly uneven shares of the total utility. In this work we enforce fairness by rewarding the platform with the _fair gain from trade_, defined as the minimum between sellers' and buyers' utilities.After showing that any no-regret learning algorithm designed to maximize the sum of the utilities may fail badly with fair gain from trade, we present our main contribution: a complete characterization of the regret regimes for fair gain from trade when, after each interaction, the platform only learns whether each trader accepted the current price. Specifically, we prove the following regret bounds: $\Theta(\ln T)$ in the deterministic setting, $\Omega(T)$ in the stochastic setting, and $\tilde{\Theta}(T^{2/3})$ in the stochastic setting when sellers' and buyers' valuations are independent of each other. We conclude by providing tight regret bounds when, after each interaction, the platform is allowed to observe the true traders' valuations.

paragraphs: This paper studies a platform that repeatedly posts a price to a buyer and seller whose valuations are private. A trade happens when both accept. Maximizing their combined utility can leave one participant with a very small share, so the authors instead reward the platform according to the smaller of the two participants’ utilities.

They first show that an algorithm with no regret for total utility can perform badly under this fairness objective. They then characterize what can be learned when feedback reveals only whether each participant accepted the price. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to the comparison used in the learning problem.

For T interactions, the regret is Θ(log T) in the deterministic setting. In the general stochastic setting, an Ω(T) lower bound rules out sublinear regret. When buyer and seller valuations are independent, the rate becomes Θ(T^(2/3)) up to logarithmic factors. The paper also gives tight bounds when valuations are fully observed. These results show how the fairness objective, feedback, and dependence between valuations jointly shape learnability.
summary.tldr: Using the smaller trader utility as a fairness objective produces sharply different learning guarantees depending on feedback and valuation independence.

title: Fair Online Bilateral Trade

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel across various applications but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, particularly Graph Injection Attacks (GIAs), which inject malicious nodes into the original graph and pose realistic threats.Text-attributed graphs (TAGs), where nodes are associated with textual features, are crucial due to their prevalence in real-world applications and are commonly used to evaluate these vulnerabilities.However, existing research only focuses on embedding-level GIAs, which inject node embeddings rather than actual textual content, limiting their applicability and simplifying detection.In this paper, we pioneer the exploration of GIAs at the text level, presenting three novel attack designs that inject textual content into the graph.Through theoretical and empirical analysis, we demonstrate that text interpretability, a factor previously overlooked at the embedding level, plays a crucial role in attack strength. Among the designs we investigate, the Word-frequency-based Text-level GIA (WTGIA) is particularly notable for its balance between performance and interpretability. Despite the success of WTGIA, we discover that defenders can easily enhance their defenses with customized text embedding methods or large language model (LLM)--based predictors. These insights underscore the necessity for further research into the potential and practical significance of text-level GIAs.

paragraphs: Graph injection attacks add malicious nodes to a graph to disrupt a graph neural network. In text-attributed graphs, nodes carry textual content, yet previous attacks often operated directly on numerical embeddings. This paper studies attacks that inject actual text, bringing the attack representation closer to the information these graphs contain in practice.

The authors introduce three text-level attack designs and analyze them theoretically and empirically. They find that text interpretability plays an important role in attack strength, adding a consideration that embedding-only attacks overlook. Among the designs, a word-frequency-based method called WTGIA offers a notable balance between attack performance and interpretable text.

The study also identifies a practical counterweight: customized text-embedding methods or predictors based on large language models can readily strengthen defenses against the investigated attacks. The findings therefore connect attack effectiveness to how text is represented and processed. They establish text-level graph injection as a meaningful research problem while showing that changes to the defender’s text-processing approach can materially affect its vulnerability.
summary.tldr: Text-level graph injection reveals a tradeoff involving interpretability and attack strength, while alternative text processing can strengthen defenses.

title: Intruding with Words: Towards Understanding Graph Injection Attacks at the Text Level

abstract: In the U.S. historically, local newspapers drew their content largely from newswires like the Associated Press. Historians argue that newswires played a pivotal role in creating a national identity and shared understanding of the world, but there is no comprehensive archive of the content sent over newswires. We reconstruct such an archive by applying a customized deep learning pipeline to hundreds of terabytes of raw image scans from thousands of local newspapers. The resulting dataset contains 2.7 million unique public domain U.S. news wire articles, written between 1878 and 1977. Locations in these articles are georeferenced, topics are tagged using customized neural topic classification, named entities are recognized, and individuals are disambiguated to Wikipedia using a novel entity disambiguation model. To construct the Newswire dataset, we first recognize newspaper layouts and transcribe around 138 millions structured article texts from raw image scans. We then use a customized neural bi-encoder model to de-duplicate reproduced articles, in the presence of considerable abridgement and noise, quantifying how widely each article was reproduced. A text classifier is used to ensure that we only include newswire articles, which historically are in the public domain. The structured data that accompany the texts provide rich information about the who (disambiguated individuals), what (topics), and where (georeferencing) of the news that millions of Americans read over the course of a century. We also include Library of Congress metadata information about the newspapers that ran the articles on their front pages. The Newswire dataset is useful both for large language modeling - expanding training data beyond what is available from modern web texts - and for studying a diversity of questions in computational linguistics, social science, and the digital humanities.

A text classifier is used to ensure that we only include newswire articles, which historically are in the public domain. The structured data that accompany the texts provide rich information about the who (disambiguated individuals), what (topics), and where (georeferencing) of the news that millions of Americans read over the course of a century. We also include Library of Congress metadata information about the newspapers that ran the articles on their front pages. The Newswire dataset is useful both for large language modeling - expanding training data beyond what is available from modern web texts - and for studying a diversity of questions in computational linguistics, social science, and the digital humanities.

paragraphs: Newswire reconstructs a historical archive of syndicated news from local newspapers, addressing the absence of a comprehensive collection of material distributed by newswires. Its resulting dataset contains 2.7 million unique public-domain U.S. newswire articles written between 1878 and 1977, assembled from scans of thousands of newspapers.

The pipeline first recognizes newspaper layouts and transcribes around 138 million structured article texts. A customized neural bi-encoder then identifies reproduced articles despite abridgment and noisy text, while recording how widely each article circulated. A classifier selects newswire material. This process turns scattered newspaper reproductions into a deduplicated collection with information about their distribution.

The dataset adds topic tags, geographic references, recognized entities, and links that disambiguate people to Wikipedia. It also includes Library of Congress metadata for newspapers carrying the articles on their front pages. These structured fields support questions about who appeared in the news, what was covered, and where events occurred. The collection also expands the historical material available for language modeling beyond modern web text.
summary.tldr: Newswire reconstructs 2.7 million historical newswire articles from newspaper scans and enriches them with searchable information about people, topics, places, and circulation.

title: Newswire: A Large-Scale Structured Database of a Century of Historical News

abstract: Deep neural networks are ubiquitously adopted in many applications, such as computer vision, natural language processing, and graph analytics. However, well-trained neural networks can make prediction errors after deployment as the world changes. \textit{Model editing} involves updating the base model to correct prediction errors with less accessible training data and computational resources.Despite recent advances in model editors in computer vision and natural language processing, editable training in graph neural networks (GNNs) is rarely explored. The challenge with editable GNN training lies in the inherent information aggregation across neighbors, which can lead model editors to affect the predictions of other nodes unintentionally. In this paper, we first observe the gradient of cross-entropy loss for the target node and training nodes with significant inconsistency, which indicates that directly fine-tuning the base model using the loss on the target node deteriorates the performance on training nodes. Motivated by the gradient inconsistency observation, we propose a simple yet effective \underline{G}radient \underline{R}ewiring method for \underline{E}ditable graph neural network training, named \textbf{GRE}. Specifically, we first store the anchor gradient of the loss on training nodes to preserve the locality. Subsequently, we rewire the gradient of the loss on the target node to preserve performance on the training node using anchor gradient. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of GRE on various model architectures and graph datasets in terms of multiple editing situations. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/zhimengj0326/Gradient_rewiring_editing}.

paragraphs: Model editing corrects errors in a deployed network when retraining resources or access to training data are limited. Graph neural networks create a particular challenge because they aggregate information across neighboring nodes. An update intended to fix one node can therefore unintentionally change predictions elsewhere in the graph.

The authors observe substantial disagreement between the loss gradient for a target node and gradients associated with training nodes. In their analysis, directly fine-tuning on the target can consequently degrade training-node performance. Their method, Gradient Rewiring for Editable graph neural network training, stores an anchor gradient computed from the training-node loss and uses it to modify the target-node update.

The anchor supplies information about preserving existing predictions while the target gradient supplies the desired correction. Experiments across graph datasets, model architectures, and multiple editing situations demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a gradient-based mechanism for making localized corrections more compatible with maintaining broader model behavior, addressing the interference that arises when graph predictions share information.
summary.tldr: GRE adjusts target-node editing gradients using a stored training gradient to help correct graph predictions while preserving other performance.

title: Gradient Rewiring for Editable Graph Neural Network Training

abstract: We introduce a novel framework for analyzing reinforcement learning (RL) in continuous state-action spaces, and use it to prove fast rates of convergence in both off-line and on-line settings. Our analysis highlights two key stability properties, relating to how changes in value functions and/or policies affect the Bellman operator and occupation measures. We argue that these properties are satisfied in many continuous state-action Markov decision processes. Our analysis also offers fresh perspectives on the roles of pessimism and optimism in off-line and on-line RL.
