paragraphs: This paper introduces a variational inference framework for text models with hidden, or latent, variables. Such models require approximations to distributions that are difficult to compute directly. The authors use an inference network that takes discrete text as input and produces the variational distribution, making the approximation itself a learned component of the model.

The framework supports both generative and conditional text modeling. For document generation, the authors combine a continuous stochastic representation of a document with a bag-of-words generative model. This application learns a probabilistic document representation and uses it within a model of word content. It achieves the lowest reported perplexities on two standard test corpora.

The second application is supervised answer selection. Here, a stochastic representation layer sits within an attention mechanism to capture the semantic relationship between a question and an answer. The model exceeds previously published benchmark results on two question-answering datasets. These two applications demonstrate the framework’s usefulness across distinct text tasks, with reported improvements in both document modeling and answer selection.
summary.tldr: Text-conditioned inference networks support probabilistic document modeling and answer selection, with leading reported results on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Neural Variational Inference for Text Processing

abstract: Many of the recent Trajectory Optimization algorithms alternate between local approximation of the dynamics and conservative policy update. However, linearly approximating the dynamics in order to derive the new policy can bias the update and prevent convergence to the optimal policy. In this article, we propose a new model-free algorithm that backpropagates a local quadratic time-dependent Q-Function, allowing the derivation of the policy update in closed form. Our policy update ensures exact KL-constraint satisfaction without simplifying assumptions on the system dynamics demonstrating improved performance in comparison to related Trajectory Optimization algorithms linearizing the dynamics.

paragraphs: Trajectory optimization methods often alternate between approximating a system's dynamics locally and making a conservative policy update. The paper identifies a potential problem with using a linear approximation of those dynamics: it can bias the policy update and prevent convergence to the optimal policy. The proposed method changes the quantity used to derive the update.

The authors introduce a model-free algorithm that backpropagates a local, time-dependent quadratic Q-function. This local description of action value allows the policy update to be obtained in closed form. The method therefore uses an approximation of the value function to construct its update without relying on the simplifying dynamics assumptions highlighted in the abstract.

A central stated property is exact satisfaction of the KL constraint that controls the policy update. The paper reports improved performance relative to related trajectory optimization algorithms that linearize dynamics. This supports the usefulness of the alternative update construction while keeping the guarantee precise: exact constraint satisfaction is the stated guarantee, rather than a general claim of convergence to a globally optimal policy.
summary.tldr: A model-free trajectory optimizer derives closed-form policy updates from local quadratic Q-functions while exactly satisfying a KL constraint.

title: Model-Free Trajectory Optimization for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: One of the key challenges of artificial intelligence is to learn models that are effective in the context of planning. In this document we introduce the predictron architecture. The predictron consists of a fully abstract model, represented by a Markov reward process, that can be rolled forward multiple “imagined” planning steps. Each forward pass of the predictron accumulates internal rewards and values over multiple planning depths. The predictron is trained end-to-end so as to make these accumulated values accurately approximate the true value function. We applied the predictron to procedurally generated random mazes and a simulator for the game of pool. The predictron yielded significantly more accurate predictions than conventional deep neural network architectures.

paragraphs: A model used for planning needs to support useful predictions about what lies ahead. This paper introduces the predictron, an architecture that learns an abstract internal model and rolls it forward through several imagined steps. The model is represented as a Markov reward process, making internal rewards and values part of its computation.

Each forward pass accumulates rewards and values over multiple planning depths. The architecture is trained end-to-end so that these accumulated quantities approximate the true value function accurately. This connects the internal planning computation directly to the prediction objective: the learned abstract process is shaped by the values it needs to estimate.

The authors evaluate the predictron on procedurally generated random mazes and a pool simulator. It produces significantly more accurate predictions than the conventional deep neural network architectures used for comparison. These findings support embedding learned, multi-step planning computations inside a value-prediction architecture. The reported benefit is improved prediction in those environments, with the internal model and its planning operations learned together.
summary.tldr: The predictron learns an abstract internal planning process end-to-end to improve value predictions.

title: The Predictron: End-To-End Learning and Planning

abstract: We propose a new approximate inference algorithm for graphical models, tensor belief propagation, based on approximating the messages passed in the junction tree algorithm. Our algorithm represents the potential functions of the graphical model and all messages on the junction tree compactly as mixtures of rank-1 tensors. Using this representation, we show how to perform the operations required for inference on the junction tree efficiently: marginalisation can be computed quickly due to the factored form of rank-1 tensors while multiplication can be approximated using sampling. Our analysis gives sufficient conditions for the algorithm to perform well, including for the case of high-treewidth graphs, for which exact inference is intractable. We compare our algorithm experimentally with several approximate inference algorithms and show that it performs well.

Our algorithm represents the potential functions of the graphical model and all messages on the junction tree compactly as mixtures of rank-1 tensors. Using this representation, we show how to perform the operations required for inference on the junction tree efficiently: marginalisation can be computed quickly due to the factored form of rank-1 tensors while multiplication can be approximated using sampling. Our analysis gives sufficient conditions for the algorithm to perform well, including for the case of high-treewidth graphs, for which exact inference is intractable. We compare our algorithm experimentally with several approximate inference algorithms and show that it performs well.

paragraphs: Graphical-model inference can involve passing messages that become too large to handle efficiently. Tensor belief propagation tackles this problem by approximating messages within the junction tree algorithm. The paper's main idea is to use a compact representation for both the model's potential functions and the messages exchanged during inference.

Each is represented as a mixture of rank-one tensors. Their factored structure makes marginalization, which combines information over variables being removed, quick to compute. Multiplication is handled approximately through sampling. This pairing adapts the required inference operations to the compact representation, rather than relying on unrestricted message tables.

The authors derive sufficient conditions under which the algorithm performs well. These include cases involving high-treewidth graphs, where exact inference is intractable. The conditions establish favorable settings rather than a guarantee for every difficult graph. Experimental comparisons with several approximate inference methods show good performance, supporting the practicality of tensor representations for the inference problems examined.
summary.tldr: Compact tensor mixtures and sampled multiplication enable approximate junction-tree inference, with sufficient performance conditions and supporting experiments.

title: Tensor Belief Propagation

abstract: We consider the multi-agent reinforcement learning setting with imperfect information. The reward function depends on the hidden goals of both agents, so the agents must infer the other players’ goals from their observed behavior in order to maximize their returns. We propose a new approach for learning in these domains: Self Other-Modeling (SOM), in which an agent uses its own policy to predict the other agent’s actions and update its belief of their hidden goal in an online manner. We evaluate this approach on three different tasks and show that the agents are able to learn better policies using their estimate of the other players’ goals, in both cooperative and competitive settings.

paragraphs: In multiagent reinforcement learning, another player's goals may be hidden even though those goals affect rewards. An agent must therefore use observed behavior to infer what the other player wants. This paper studies that imperfect-information setting, where successful decisions depend on the hidden goals of both interacting agents.

The proposed Self Other-Modeling method uses an agent's own policy to predict the other agent's actions. It updates a belief about the other's hidden goal as interaction unfolds. The policy thus serves two purposes: guiding the agent's behavior and helping it interpret another player's behavior in terms of possible goals.

The authors evaluate the approach on three tasks spanning cooperation and competition. They find that agents learn better policies when they use their estimates of other players' goals. These results support online goal inference as a useful component of decision-making in the tested settings, and show how an agent's own policy can contribute to that inference.
summary.tldr: Self Other-Modeling uses an agent's own policy to infer another player's hidden goal and improve decisions in cooperative and competitive tasks.

title: Modeling Others using Oneself in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper develops a novel methodology for using symbolic knowledge in deep learning. From first principles, we derive a semantic loss function that bridges between neural output vectors and logical constraints. This loss function captures how close the neural network is to satisfying the constraints on its output. An experimental evaluation shows that it effectively guides the learner to achieve (near-)state-of-the-art results on semi-supervised multi-class classification. Moreover, it significantly increases the ability of the neural network to predict structured objects, such as rankings and paths. These discrete concepts are tremendously difficult to learn, and benefit from a tight integration of deep learning and symbolic reasoning methods.

This loss function captures how close the neural network is to satisfying the constraints on its output. An experimental evaluation shows that it effectively guides the learner to achieve (near-)state-of-the-art results on semi-supervised multi-class classification. Moreover, it significantly increases the ability of the neural network to predict structured objects, such as rankings and paths. These discrete concepts are tremendously difficult to learn, and benefit from a tight integration of deep learning and symbolic reasoning methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to make logical knowledge useful during neural network training. A network produces numerical outputs, while symbolic knowledge describes rules that those outputs should satisfy. The authors derive a semantic loss from first principles to connect these two forms of information. This loss measures how close the network's outputs are to satisfying the supplied logical constraints.

The central idea is to turn knowledge about acceptable outputs into a training signal. Instead of leaving logical requirements separate from learning, the method gives the learner feedback about whether its predictions respect those requirements. This is particularly relevant for structured predictions, where an output must represent a coherent object such as a ranking or a path.

Experiments show that the loss guides semi-supervised multiclass classification toward results at or near the state of the art. The authors also report substantial improvements in predicting structured objects. These findings support integrating symbolic reasoning with neural learning when discrete structure is difficult to learn from the available training signal alone.
summary.tldr: A semantic loss turns logical output constraints into a training signal that improves classification and structured prediction.

title: A Semantic Loss Function for Deep Learning with Symbolic Knowledge

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning algorithms have been successfully applied to a range of challenging control tasks. However, these methods typically struggle with achieving effective exploration and are extremely sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters. One reason is that most approaches use a noisy version of their operating policy to explore - thereby limiting the range of exploration. In this paper, we introduce Collaborative Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (CERL), a scalable framework that comprises a portfolio of policies that simultaneously explore and exploit diverse regions of the solution space. A collection of learners - typically proven algorithms like TD3 - optimize over varying time-horizons leading to this diverse portfolio. All learners contribute to and use a shared replay buffer to achieve greater sample efficiency. Computational resources are dynamically distributed to favor the best learners as a form of online algorithm selection. Neuroevolution binds this entire process to generate a single emergent learner that exceeds the capabilities of any individual learner. Experiments in a range of continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that the emergent learner significantly outperforms its composite learners while remaining overall more sample-efficient - notably solving the Mujoco Humanoid benchmark where all of its composite learners (TD3) fail entirely in isolation.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can struggle to explore effectively and can be sensitive to hyperparameter choices. Adding noise to a single operating policy may leave exploration confined to a limited range of behavior. Collaborative Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning, or CERL, instead maintains a portfolio of policies that explore and exploit different parts of the solution space.

The portfolio contains learners, such as TD3, that optimize over different time horizons. They share a replay buffer, allowing experience collected by one learner to support others. Computational resources are reassigned toward better-performing learners, providing online algorithm selection. Neuroevolution connects these components into an emergent learner whose behavior reflects their collaboration.

Across continuous-control benchmarks, the authors report that this combined learner significantly outperforms its constituent learners while using samples more efficiently overall. A highlighted result is solving the MuJoCo Humanoid benchmark when every constituent TD3 learner fails in isolation. The finding supports the value of combining diverse learning processes and shared experience in the evaluated tasks, rather than relying solely on exploration around one policy.
summary.tldr: CERL combines diverse learners, shared experience, adaptive resource allocation, and neuroevolution to improve exploration and sample efficiency in continuous control.

title: Collaborative Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of unsupervised domain adaption from theoretical and algorithmic perspectives. Existing domain adaptation theories naturally imply minimax optimization algorithms, which connect well with the domain adaptation methods based on adversarial learning. However, several disconnections still exist and form the gap between theory and algorithm. We extend previous theories (Mansour et al., 2009c; Ben-David et al., 2010) to multiclass classification in domain adaptation, where classifiers based on the scoring functions and margin loss are standard choices in algorithm design. We introduce Margin Disparity Discrepancy, a novel measurement with rigorous generalization bounds, tailored to the distribution comparison with the asymmetric margin loss, and to the minimax optimization for easier training. Our theory can be seamlessly transformed into an adversarial learning algorithm for domain adaptation, successfully bridging the gap between theory and algorithm. A series of empirical studies show that our algorithm achieves the state of the art accuracies on challenging domain adaptation tasks.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation seeks to transfer a classifier between domains without target-domain labels. Existing theory points toward minimax optimization, which fits naturally with adversarial learning. The paper argues that this broad connection still leaves gaps between theoretical formulations and the scoring functions and margin losses used in practical multiclass classifiers.

The authors extend domain adaptation theory to this multiclass setting and introduce Margin Disparity Discrepancy. This quantity compares distributions in a way tailored to an asymmetric margin loss. They establish generalization bounds for it and design the formulation to fit minimax optimization, making the theoretical comparison directly useful for constructing a training algorithm.

The resulting theory leads to an adversarial domain adaptation method. This matters because the distribution comparison, predictive loss, and optimization procedure are developed together, giving the algorithm a clearer theoretical foundation. Empirical studies report state-of-the-art accuracy on challenging adaptation tasks. Those experiments support the practical value of the approach, while the generalization analysis supplies the formal connection between domain discrepancy and predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Margin Disparity Discrepancy connects multiclass domain adaptation bounds to a practical adversarial training algorithm.

title: Bridging Theory and Algorithm for Domain Adaptation

abstract: A well-documented weakness of neural networks is the fact that they suffer from catastrophic forgetting when trained on data provided by a non-stationary distribution. Recent work in the field of continual learning attempts to understand and overcome this issue. Unfortunately, the majority of relevant work embraces the implicit assumption that the distribution of observed data is perfectly balanced, despite the fact that, in the real world, humans and animals learn from observations that are temporally correlated and severely imbalanced. Motivated by this remark, we aim to evaluate memory population methods that are used in online continual learning, when dealing with highly imbalanced and temporally correlated streams of data. More importantly, we introduce a new memory population approach, which we call class-balancing reservoir sampling (CBRS). We demonstrate that CBRS outperforms the state-of-the-art memory population algorithms in a considerably challenging learning setting, over a range of different datasets, and for multiple architectures.

paragraphs: Neural networks can forget earlier knowledge when trained on a changing stream of data. Many continual-learning studies assume balanced observations, although real streams may contain long correlated runs and very uneven class frequencies. This paper examines how those conditions affect the memory buffers used in online continual learning.

The authors evaluate methods for selecting which examples populate memory and propose class-balancing reservoir sampling, or CBRS. Its purpose is to account for class imbalance when retaining examples for later learning. Memory selection matters because the retained sample determines which past observations remain available as the stream moves on.

Across several datasets and model architectures, CBRS outperforms the compared state-of-the-art memory-population algorithms in the challenging streaming setting. The paper’s contribution concerns managing a limited record of past experience under imbalance and temporal correlation. The abstract does not give the buffer sizes or numerical improvements, so the results should be understood as comparative evidence in the evaluated conditions.
summary.tldr: Class-balancing reservoir sampling improves continual-learning memory selection for imbalanced, temporally correlated data streams.

title: Online Continual Learning from Imbalanced Data

abstract: We present distribution augmentation (DistAug), a simple and powerful method of regularizing generative models. Our approach applies augmentation functions to data and, importantly, conditions the generative model on the specific function used. Unlike typical data augmentation, DistAug allows usage of functions which modify the target density, enabling aggressive augmentations more commonly seen in supervised and self-supervised learning. We demonstrate this is a more effective regularizer than standard methods, and use it to train a 152M parameter autoregressive model on CIFAR-10 to 2.56 bits per dim (relative to the state-of-the-art 2.80). Samples from this model attain FID 12.75 and IS 8.40, outperforming the majority of GANs. We further demonstrate the technique is broadly applicable across model architectures and problem domains.

paragraphs: Data augmentation changes training examples, but generative modeling must also account for how those changes affect the distribution being learned. Distribution augmentation, or DistAug, applies a transformation and conditions the generative model on which transformation was used. The transformation therefore becomes explicit information available to the model.

This design permits augmentations that alter the target density, expanding the set of usable transformations beyond typical data augmentation. It enables aggressive transformations of the kind used in supervised and self-supervised learning. The authors demonstrate that this approach regularizes generative models more effectively than the standard methods considered in their study.

One reported result is a 152-million-parameter autoregressive model on CIFAR-10 reaching 2.56 bits per dimension, compared with the stated previous best of 2.80. Its samples achieve FID 12.75 and IS 8.40, outperforming a majority of GANs in the reported comparison. Additional demonstrations span architectures and problem domains, supporting the method's broader applicability beyond that single model.
summary.tldr: DistAug conditions generative models on applied transformations, enabling stronger augmentation and improving reported density modeling and sample quality.

title: Distribution Augmentation for Generative Modeling

abstract: We describe a new approach for managing aleatoric uncertainty in the Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm. Instead of selecting actions according to a single statistic, we propose a distributional method based on the second-order stochastic dominance (SSD) relation. This compares the inherent dispersion of random returns induced by actions, producing a comprehensive evaluation of the environment’s uncertainty. The necessary conditions for SSD require estimators to predict accurate second moments. To accommodate this, we map the distributional RL problem to a Wasserstein gradient flow, treating the distributional Bellman residual as a potential energy functional. We propose a particle-based algorithm for which we prove optimality and convergence. Our experiments characterize the algorithm’s performance and demonstrate how uncertainty and performance are better balanced using an SSD policy than with other risk measures.

The necessary conditions for SSD require estimators to predict accurate second moments. paragraphs: This paper addresses aleatoric uncertainty, the randomness inherent in the returns an environment produces. It proposes selecting actions through second-order stochastic dominance, or SSD, rather than relying on a single summary statistic. Comparing return distributions in this way accounts for their dispersion when evaluating actions.

The necessary conditions for SSD require accurate estimates of second moments. To support that requirement, the authors formulate distributional reinforcement learning as a Wasserstein gradient flow. In this construction, the distributional Bellman residual acts as a potential energy functional, providing the mathematical basis for their approach to learning return distributions.

They develop a particle-based algorithm and prove optimality and convergence results for it. Experiments characterize its performance and show a better balance between uncertainty and performance with an SSD policy than with the other risk measures considered. The contribution connects distribution estimation to an action-selection rule whose assessment of uncertainty depends on more of the return distribution than a single statistic captures.
summary.tldr: A distributional reinforcement-learning method uses second-order stochastic dominance to balance return performance and inherent uncertainty.

title: Stochastically Dominant Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models have been the dominating approach to conditional sequence generation, but are suffering from the issue of high inference latency. Non-autoregressive (NAR) models have been recently proposed to reduce the latency by generating all output tokens in parallel but could only achieve inferior accuracy compared to their autoregressive counterparts, primarily due to a difficulty in dealing with the multi-modality in sequence generation. This paper proposes a new approach that jointly optimizes both AR and NAR models in a unified Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework. In the E-step, an AR model learns to approximate the regularized posterior of the NAR model. In the M-step, the NAR model is updated on the new posterior and selects the training examples for the next AR model. This iterative process can effectively guide the system to remove the multi-modality in the output sequences. To our knowledge, this is the first EM approach to NAR sequence generation. We evaluate our method on the task of machine translation. Experimental results on benchmark data sets show that the proposed approach achieves competitive, if not better, performance with existing NAR models and significantly reduces the inference latency.

paragraphs: Generating a sequence one token at a time can make prediction slow. Non-autoregressive models reduce that delay by generating tokens in parallel, but handling several valid outputs for the same input is difficult. The paper addresses this tension by training an autoregressive model and a non-autoregressive model together.

The training procedure alternates between two steps in an Expectation-Maximization framework. First, the autoregressive model learns to approximate a regularized posterior belonging to the non-autoregressive model. Then the non-autoregressive model learns from that updated posterior and selects examples for the next round of autoregressive training. Each model therefore helps shape the other's next update.

summary.tldr: Joint EM training lets autoregressive and parallel sequence models guide each other, yielding competitive non-autoregressive translation with lower inference latency.

title: An EM Approach to Non-autoregressive Conditional Sequence Generation

abstract: \emph{Contrastive learning} (CL) pretrains models in a pairwise manner, where given a data point, other data points are all regarded as dissimilar, including some that are \emph{semantically} similar. The issue has been addressed by properly weighting similar and dissimilar pairs as in \emph{positive-unlabeled learning}, so that the objective of CL is \emph{unbiased} and CL is \emph{consistent}. However, in this paper, we argue that this great solution is still not enough: its weighted objective \emph{hides} the issue where the semantically similar pairs are still pushed away; as CL is pretraining, this phenomenon is not our desideratum and might affect downstream tasks. To this end, we propose \emph{large-margin contrastive learning} (LMCL) with \emph{distance polarization regularizer}, motivated by the distribution characteristic of pairwise distances in \emph{metric learning}. In LMCL, we can distinguish between \emph{intra-cluster} and \emph{inter-cluster} pairs, and then only push away inter-cluster pairs, which \emph{solves} the above issue explicitly. Theoretically, we prove a tighter error bound for LMCL; empirically, the superiority of LMCL is demonstrated across multiple domains, \emph{i.e.}, image classification, sentence representation, and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Contrastive pretraining can treat other data points as dissimilar even when they share semantic meaning with the current point. Weighting pairs through positive-unlabeled learning can make the objective unbiased and the learning procedure consistent. The authors argue that this still leaves an undesirable effect: semantically similar pairs can continue to be pushed apart, potentially affecting downstream tasks.

Large-margin contrastive learning addresses this behavior with a distance polarization regularizer, motivated by patterns in pairwise distances from metric learning. The method distinguishes pairs within a cluster from pairs across clusters. It then applies separation only to the latter, explicitly changing which relationships the representation learning process pushes apart.

The paper proves a tighter error bound for the proposed method and reports empirical advantages in image classification, sentence representation, and reinforcement learning. These findings provide both theoretical and experimental support for the approach. The central distinction is between correcting the aggregate training objective and controlling the treatment of individual pairs: the paper argues that the second remains important even after the first is addressed.
summary.tldr: Large-margin contrastive learning separates pairs across clusters while avoiding repulsion within clusters, with a tighter error bound and gains across several domains.

title: Large-Margin Contrastive Learning with Distance Polarization Regularizer

abstract: We propose a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm inspired by the popular randomized least squares value iteration (RLSVI) algorithm as well as the optimism principle. Unlike existing upper-confidence-bound (UCB) based approaches, which are often computationally intractable, our algorithm drives exploration by simply perturbing the training data with judiciously chosen i.i.d. scalar noises. To attain optimistic value function estimation without resorting to a UCB-style bonus, we introduce an optimistic reward sampling procedure. When the value functions can be represented by a function class $\mathcal{F}$, our algorithm achieves a worst-case regret bound of $\tilde{O}(\mathrm{poly}(d_EH)\sqrt{T})$ where $T$ is the time elapsed, $H$ is the planning horizon and $d_E$ is the \emph{eluder dimension} of $\mathcal{F}$. In the linear setting, our algorithm reduces to LSVI-PHE, a variant of RLSVI, that enjoys an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d^3H^3T})$ regret. We complement the theory with an empirical evaluation across known difficult exploration tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning needs exploration to discover valuable actions, but some approaches based on upper confidence bounds are computationally difficult. This paper proposes a model-free alternative inspired by randomized least squares value iteration and optimism. It encourages exploration by perturbing training data with carefully chosen independent scalar noise.

An optimistic reward-sampling procedure helps produce optimistic value estimates without adding a conventional upper-confidence-bound bonus. The theoretical analysis applies when the value functions are representable by a specified function class. Its worst-case regret bound grows with the square root of elapsed time, up to logarithmic factors, and polynomially with the planning horizon and the class’s eluder dimension.

For linear value functions, the algorithm becomes LSVI-PHE, a variant of randomized least squares value iteration, with regret bounded by Õ(√(d³H³T)). Here d is the linear dimension, H the horizon, and T elapsed time. Experiments on difficult exploration tasks complement the analysis. The contribution connects a simple perturbation mechanism to formal exploration guarantees for general function approximation.
summary.tldr: Carefully randomized training data and optimistic reward sampling provide exploration guarantees without conventional upper-confidence-bound bonuses.

title: Randomized Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with General Value Function Approximation

abstract: We consider a popular family of constrained optimization problems arising in machine learning that involve optimizing a non-decomposable evaluation metric with a certain thresholded form, while constraining another metric of interest. Examples of such problems include optimizing false negative rate at a fixed false positive rate, optimizing precision at a fixed recall, optimizing the area under the precision-recall or ROC curves, etc. Our key idea is to formulate a rate-constrained optimization that expresses the threshold parameter as a function of the model parameters via the Implicit Function theorem. We show how the resulting optimization problem can be solved using standard gradient based methods. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method over existing state-of-the-art approaches for these problems.

paragraphs: Many evaluation goals involve jointly controlling rates computed across a set of predictions. Examples include improving false negatives at a fixed false positive rate or maximizing precision at a fixed recall. These objectives are non-decomposable: they cannot be treated simply as independent losses for individual examples. Their dependence on a decision threshold further couples the optimization choices.

The paper formulates the task as rate-constrained optimization and uses the Implicit Function theorem to express the threshold as a function of the model parameters. This makes the threshold's relationship to the constraint part of the optimization formulation. The resulting problem can then be handled with standard gradient-based methods.

The approach also covers objectives involving areas under precision-recall or ROC curves. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness relative to existing state-of-the-art approaches for these problems. The contribution is a way to bring threshold-dependent evaluation criteria into a familiar optimization framework, so model training can address the desired operating rates and evaluation objectives more directly.
summary.tldr: Expressing decision thresholds implicitly through model parameters enables gradient-based optimization of constrained, non-decomposable evaluation metrics.

title: Implicit rate-constrained optimization of non-decomposable objectives

abstract: Reconstructing continuous surfaces from 3D point clouds is a fundamental operation in 3D geometry processing. Several recent state-of-the-art methods address this problem using neural networks to learn signed distance functions (SDFs). In this paper, we introduce Neural-Pull, a new approach that is simple and leads to high quality SDFs. Specifically, we train a neural network to pull query 3D locations to their closest points on the surface using the predicted signed distance values and the gradient at the query locations, both of which are computed by the network itself. The pulling operation moves each query location with a stride given by the distance predicted by the network. Based on the sign of the distance, this may move the query location along or against the direction of the gradient of the SDF. This is a differentiable operation that allows us to update the signed distance value and the gradient simultaneously during training. Our outperforming results under widely used benchmarks demonstrate that we can learn SDFs more accurately and flexibly for surface reconstruction and single image reconstruction than the state-of-the-art methods. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/mabaorui/NeuralPull.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a continuous surface from a collection of 3D points requires a representation that fills in the geometry between observations. Neural-Pull learns a signed distance function with a neural network. Its training task is to move query locations toward their closest surface points using quantities that the network itself predicts.

For each query location, the predicted distance determines how far to move, while the function's gradient provides the direction. The sign of the distance determines whether movement follows or opposes that gradient. Because the pulling operation is differentiable, training can update the predicted distance and the gradient together through the same operation.

This connects learning the surface representation to the geometric action of pulling space onto the surface. On widely used benchmarks, the authors report more accurate and flexible signed distance learning than the compared state-of-the-art methods for surface reconstruction and single-image reconstruction. The stated results support using the predicted function and its gradient jointly as the basis of reconstruction training.
summary.tldr: Neural-Pull learns surface distance functions by differentiably moving 3D queries toward the surface using predicted distances and gradients.

title: Neural-Pull: Learning Signed Distance Function from Point clouds by Learning to Pull Space onto Surface

abstract: Can a neural network minimizing cross-entropy learn linearly separable data? Despite progress in the theory of deep learning, this question remains unsolved. Here we prove that SGD globally optimizes this learning problem for a two-layer network with Leaky ReLU activations. The learned network can in principle be very complex. However, empirical evidence suggests that it often turns out to be approximately linear. We provide theoretical support for this phenomenon by proving that if network weights converge to two weight clusters, this will imply an approximately linear decision boundary. Finally, we show a condition on the optimization that leads to weight clustering. We provide empirical results that validate our theoretical analysis.

However, empirical evidence suggests that it often turns out to be approximately linear. paragraphs: This paper studies whether a neural network trained with cross-entropy can learn linearly separable data. For a two-layer network with Leaky ReLU activations, the authors prove that stochastic gradient descent globally optimizes the learning problem. This gives a theoretical result for a specific architecture and data setting.

The paper then examines the shape of the learned solution. Although the network could represent a complex decision boundary, empirical evidence suggests that its boundary is often approximately linear. The authors prove a conditional explanation: if the network weights converge into two clusters, the resulting decision boundary is approximately linear. The clustering premise is essential to that implication.

They also identify a condition on the optimization that leads to weight clustering and provide experiments validating their analysis. Together, the results connect optimization success, the organization of learned weights, and the simplicity of the resulting classifier. They offer an explanation for observed near-linear behavior without claiming that every trained network must develop two weight clusters.
summary.tldr: The paper proves SGD optimization for a two-layer Leaky ReLU network and conditionally explains near-linear boundaries through weight clustering.

title: Towards Understanding Learning in Neural Networks with Linear Teachers

abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) has shown great promise for the global optimization of functions that are expensive to evaluate, but despite many successes, standard approaches can struggle in high dimensions. To improve the performance of BO, prior work suggested incorporating gradient information into a Gaussian process surrogate of the objective, giving rise to kernel matrices of size $nd$ {\texttimes} $nd$ for $n$ observations in $d$ dimensions. Naı̈vely multiplying with (resp. inverting) these matrices requires $O(n^2d^2)$ (resp. $O(n^3d^3)$) operations, which becomes infeasible for moderate dimensions and sample sizes. Here, we observe that a wide range of kernels gives rise to structured matrices, enabling an exact $O(n^2d)$ matrix-vector multiply for gradient observations and $O(n^2d^2)$ for Hessian observations. Beyond canonical kernel classes, we derive a programmatic approach to leveraging this type of structure for transformations and combinations of the discussed kernel classes, which constitutes a structure-aware automatic differentiation algorithm. Our methods apply to virtually all canonical kernels and automatically extend to complex kernels, like the neural network, radial basis function network, and spectral mixture kernels without any additional derivations, enabling flexible, problem-dependent modeling while scaling first-order BO to high $d$.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a surrogate model to guide the search for good values of an expensive function. Gradient observations can enrich a Gaussian-process surrogate, but they also make its kernel matrices much larger. With n observations in d dimensions, naive multiplication costs O(n²d²), while naive inversion costs O(n³d³), creating a substantial high-dimensional bottleneck.

This paper identifies matrix structure arising from a wide range of kernels. Exploiting it permits exact matrix-vector multiplication in O(n²d) for gradient observations and O(n²d²) for Hessian observations. The improvement concerns the cost of these matrix operations, preserving exactness while avoiding the corresponding naive computation.

The authors also develop a structure-aware automatic differentiation method that carries these benefits through transformations and combinations of kernels. It applies to virtually all canonical kernels and extends automatically to more complex examples, including neural-network and spectral-mixture kernels. This matters because computational scalability need not require restricting modeling to one specially derived kernel. The approach supports flexible, problem-dependent surrogate design while making gradient-informed Bayesian optimization more practical at high dimension.
summary.tldr: Structure-aware automatic differentiation enables exact, cheaper kernel matrix operations for gradient-informed Bayesian optimization across many kernel families.

title: Scalable First-Order Bayesian Optimization via Structured Automatic Differentiation

abstract: Deep models are designed to operate on huge volumes of high dimensional data such as images. In order to reduce the volume of data these models must process, we propose a set-based two-stage end-to-end neural subsampling model that is jointly optimized with an arbitrary downstream task network (e.g. classifier). In the first stage, we efficiently subsample candidate elements using conditionally independent Bernoulli random variables by capturing coarse grained global information using set encoding functions, followed by conditionally dependent autoregressive subsampling of the candidate elements using Categorical random variables by modeling pair-wise interactions using set attention networks in the second stage. We apply our method to feature and instance selection and show that it outperforms the relevant baselines under low subsampling rates on a variety of tasks including image classification, image reconstruction, function reconstruction and few-shot classification. Additionally, for nonparametric models such as Neural Processes that require to leverage the whole training data at inference time, we show that our method enhances the scalability of these models.

paragraphs: Large, high-dimensional inputs can make deep learning expensive because the model must process so much data. This paper learns which elements to retain through a two-stage stochastic subsampling model. The selector is trained end to end together with a downstream network, so selection can serve the task being solved.

The first stage captures coarse global information using set encodings and efficiently selects candidate elements through conditionally independent Bernoulli decisions. The second stage refines that candidate set through autoregressive categorical selections. Set attention models pairwise interactions during this refinement, allowing later selection decisions to depend on other elements rather than treating all choices independently.

The authors apply the approach to both feature and instance selection. At low sampling rates, it outperforms relevant baselines on image classification, image reconstruction, function reconstruction, and few-shot classification. They also show improved scalability for nonparametric models such as Neural Processes that use the training data at inference time. The two-stage design combines inexpensive initial filtering with more interaction-aware selection when only a small portion of the data can be retained.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained two-stage selector reduces data processing and improves task performance over relevant baselines at low sampling rates.

title: Set Based Stochastic Subsampling

abstract: Unsupervised black-box models are challenging to interpret. Indeed, most existing explainability methods require labels to select which component(s) of the black-box’s output to interpret. In the absence of labels, black-box outputs often are representation vectors whose components do not correspond to any meaningful quantity. Hence, choosing which component(s) to interpret in a label-free unsupervised/self-supervised setting is an important, yet unsolved problem. To bridge this gap in the literature, we introduce two crucial extensions of post-hoc explanation techniques: (1) label-free feature importance and (2) label-free example importance that respectively highlight influential features and training examples for a black-box to construct representations at inference time. We demonstrate that our extensions can be successfully implemented as simple wrappers around many existing feature and example importance methods. We illustrate the utility of our label-free explainability paradigm through a qualitative and quantitative comparison of representation spaces learned by various autoencoders trained on distinct unsupervised tasks.

paragraphs: Many explanation methods need a label to decide which model output to explain. Unsupervised and self-supervised models often produce representation vectors instead, whose individual coordinates have no obvious meaning. Selecting a coordinate to interpret therefore becomes a problem before an explanation method can even be applied.

This paper introduces label-free versions of feature importance and example importance. Feature importance highlights input features that influence the representation constructed at inference time. Example importance highlights influential training examples. Together, these extensions provide two ways to investigate representation formation without requiring a labeled output as the explanation target.

The authors show that the extensions can be implemented as simple wrappers around many existing importance methods. They demonstrate the approach through qualitative and quantitative comparisons of representation spaces from autoencoders trained on different unsupervised tasks. The contribution makes established explanation techniques usable in a setting where meaningful output labels are unavailable, while preserving the distinction between explaining input features and explaining training-example influence.
summary.tldr: Label-free wrappers extend feature and training-example importance methods to explain representations learned without labels.

title: Label-Free Explainability for Unsupervised Models

abstract: Transfer-learning methods aim to improve performance in a data-scarce target domain using a model pretrained on a data-rich source domain. A cost-efficient strategy, linear probing, involves freezing the source model and training a new classification head for the target domain. This strategy is outperformed by a more costly but state-of-the-art method – fine-tuning all parameters of the source model to the target domain – possibly because fine-tuning allows the model to leverage useful information from intermediate layers which is otherwise discarded by the later previously trained layers. We explore the hypothesis that these intermediate layers might be directly exploited. We propose a method, Head-to-Toe probing (Head2Toe), that selects features from all layers of the source model to train a classification head for the target-domain. In evaluations on the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark-1k, Head2Toe matches performance obtained with fine-tuning on average while reducing training and storage cost hundred folds or more, but critically, for out-of-distribution transfer, Head2Toe outperforms fine-tuning. Code used in our experiments can be found in supplementary materials.

paragraphs: Transfer learning adapts a model trained on abundant source data to a target task with little data. Linear probing keeps the pretrained model fixed and trains a classification head, making adaptation inexpensive. Fine-tuning every parameter usually performs better but costs more. This paper investigates whether useful intermediate representations explain part of that difference.

The proposed Head2Toe method selects features from all layers of the source model to train the target classification head. The motivation is that later layers may discard information that remains useful for the new task. Accessing intermediate features directly could therefore improve transfer without requiring updates throughout the pretrained model.

On the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark-1k, Head2Toe matches fine-tuning performance on average while reducing training and storage costs by at least a factor of one hundred. For out-of-distribution transfer in the evaluation, it outperforms fine-tuning. These findings support intermediate-layer feature selection as a powerful, economical adaptation strategy. The average-performance result is distinct from claiming a match on every target task.
summary.tldr: Head2Toe selects features across pretrained layers, matching fine-tuning on average on VTAB-1k at much lower cost and improving evaluated out-of-distribution transfer.

title: Head2Toe: Utilizing Intermediate Representations for Better Transfer Learning

abstract: Generalising robustly to distribution shift is a major challenge that is pervasive across most real-world applications of machine learning. A recent study highlighted that many advanced algorithms proposed to tackle such domain generalisation (DG) fail to outperform a properly tuned empirical risk minimisation (ERM) baseline. We take a different approach, and explore the impact of the ERM loss function on out-of-domain generalisation. In particular, we introduce a novel meta-learning approach to loss function search based on implicit gradient. This enables us to discover a general purpose parametric loss function that provides a drop-in replacement for cross-entropy. Our loss can be used in standard training pipelines to efficiently train robust models using any neural architecture on new datasets. The results show that it clearly surpasses cross-entropy, enables simple ERM to outperform some more complicated prior DG methods, and provides state-of-the-art performance across a variety of DG benchmarks. Furthermore, unlike most existing DG approaches, our setup applies to the most practical setting of single-source domain generalisation, on which we show significant improvement.

paragraphs: Domain generalization concerns models that must work when deployment data differs from training data. This paper starts from evidence that carefully tuned empirical risk minimization can rival more elaborate approaches. It investigates a basic part of that training procedure: whether changing the loss function can improve performance on unseen domains.

The authors introduce a meta-learning method that searches for a parametric loss using implicit gradients. The resulting loss serves as a replacement for cross-entropy in standard training pipelines. It is designed for reuse with different neural architectures and new datasets, making the learned training objective the main transferable component.

Across the reported domain generalization benchmarks, the loss outperforms cross-entropy, enables ordinary empirical risk minimization to beat some more complicated prior methods, and achieves state-of-the-art results. The approach also applies when training data comes from only one source domain, where the authors report substantial improvement. These findings support loss design as a practical route to better generalization under distribution shift.
summary.tldr: An implicitly differentiated meta-learning procedure discovers a reusable loss that improves domain generalization in standard training pipelines.

title: Loss Function Learning for Domain Generalization by Implicit Gradient

abstract: In this work, we argue for the importance of an online evaluation budget for a reliable comparison of deep offline RL algorithms. First, we delineate that the online evaluation budget is problem-dependent, where some problems allow for less but others for more. And second, we demonstrate that the preference between algorithms is budget-dependent across a diverse range of decision-making domains such as Robotics, Finance, and Energy Management. Following the points above, we suggest reporting the performance of deep offline RL algorithms under varying online evaluation budgets. To facilitate this, we propose to use a reporting tool from the NLP field, Expected Validation Performance. This technique makes it possible to reliably estimate expected maximum performance under different budgets while not requiring any additional computation beyond hyperparameter search. By employing this tool, we also show that Behavioral Cloning is often more favorable to offline RL algorithms when working within a limited budget.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning algorithms are trained from existing data, but comparing them can still involve online evaluations during model selection. This paper argues that the available evaluation budget is part of a meaningful comparison. Different problems permit different amounts of evaluation, and the preferred algorithm can change with that budget.

The authors demonstrate this budget dependence across robotics, finance, and energy management. They recommend reporting performance over varying online evaluation budgets. To support that reporting, they adopt Expected Validation Performance, a tool from natural language processing that estimates expected maximum performance at different budgets using results already produced by hyperparameter search.

The method requires no additional computation beyond that search. Applying it also reveals that Behavioral Cloning is often more favorable than offline reinforcement learning algorithms when the evaluation budget is limited. The finding does not establish a universally preferred method; it shows why the resources available for selecting a model can affect practical conclusions about algorithm quality and should be visible in reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: Offline reinforcement learning rankings can change with online evaluation budgets, making budget-aware performance reporting essential to the paper’s proposed comparisons.

title: Showing Your Offline Reinforcement Learning Work: Online Evaluation Budget Matters

abstract: How do we compare between hypotheses that are entirely consistent with observations? The marginal likelihood (aka Bayesian evidence), which represents the probability of generating our observations from a prior, provides a distinctive approach to this foundational question, automatically encoding Occam’s razor. Although it has been observed that the marginal likelihood can overfit and is sensitive to prior assumptions, its limitations for hyperparameter learning and discrete model comparison have not been thoroughly investigated. We first revisit the appealing properties of the marginal likelihood for learning constraints and hypothesis testing. We then highlight the conceptual and practical issues in using the marginal likelihood as a proxy for generalization. Namely, we show how marginal likelihood can be negatively correlated with generalization, with implications for neural architecture search, and can lead to both underfitting and overfitting in hyperparameter learning. We provide a partial remedy through a conditional marginal likelihood, which we show is more aligned with generalization, and practically valuable for large-scale hyperparameter learning, such as in deep kernel learning.

paragraphs: Marginal likelihood evaluates how probable the observed data are under a model's prior assumptions. It offers a principled way to compare hypotheses that fit the observations and incorporates a preference for simpler explanations. This paper examines whether those attractive properties also make it a reliable guide to predictive performance on new data.

The authors distinguish its value for learning constraints and testing hypotheses from its use as a proxy for generalization. They show that marginal likelihood can be negatively correlated with generalization, making a better evidence score potentially accompany worse prediction. They also show that using it to learn hyperparameters can produce either underfitting or overfitting, with consequences for applications such as neural architecture search.

As a partial remedy, the paper studies conditional marginal likelihood and finds it better aligned with generalization. It also demonstrates practical value for large-scale hyperparameter learning, including deep kernel learning. The conclusion is qualified: marginal likelihood retains useful roles, but its model-comparison appeal does not by itself establish that optimizing it will improve predictions.
summary.tldr: Marginal likelihood can favor worse generalization, while a conditional version offers a partial remedy for model and hyperparameter selection.

title: Bayesian Model Selection, the Marginal Likelihood, and Generalization

abstract: Designing biological sequences is an important challenge that requires satisfying complex constraints and thus is a natural problem to address with deep generative modeling. Diffusion generative models have achieved considerable success in many applications. Score-based generative stochastic differential equations (SDE) model is a continuous-time diffusion model framework that enjoys many benefits, but the originally proposed SDEs are not naturally designed for modeling discrete data. To develop generative SDE models for discrete data such as biological sequences, here we introduce a diffusion process defined in the probability simplex space with stationary distribution being the Dirichlet distribution. This makes diffusion in continuous space natural for modeling discrete data. We refer to this approach as Dirchlet diffusion score model. We demonstrate that this technique can generate samples that satisfy hard constraints using a Sudoku generation task. This generative model can also solve Sudoku, including hard puzzles, without additional training. Finally, we applied this approach to develop the first human promoter DNA sequence design model and showed that designed sequences share similar properties with natural promoter sequences.

The originally proposed processes are not naturally suited to discrete data. This paper introduces a diffusion construction that connects these settings by operating on the probability simplex, the space of probability assignments over possible symbols.

The diffusion has a Dirichlet stationary distribution, giving the resulting Dirichlet diffusion score model a continuous space suited to representing discrete choices. This design matters for sequence generation because the model must handle categorical outputs while accommodating complex constraints. The approach changes the underlying diffusion process to fit that structure.

The authors demonstrate constrained generation with Sudoku, showing that generated samples can satisfy hard constraints. They also report that the model can solve Sudoku puzzles, including hard ones, without additional training. For biology, they apply the method to human promoter DNA design and report that designed sequences share properties with natural promoters. These findings demonstrate applications of the construction without establishing that all generated biological sequences meet every desired functional requirement.
summary.tldr: A diffusion process over symbol probabilities supports discrete generation, with demonstrations on constrained Sudoku tasks and human promoter DNA design.

title: Dirichlet Diffusion Score Model for Biological Sequence Generation

abstract: We initiate a principled study of algorithmic collective action on digital platforms that deploy machine learning algorithms. We propose a simple theoretical model of a collective interacting with a firm’s learning algorithm. The collective pools the data of participating individuals and executes an algorithmic strategy by instructing participants how to modify their own data to achieve a collective goal. We investigate the consequences of this model in three fundamental learning-theoretic settings: nonparametric optimal learning, parametric risk minimization, and gradient-based optimization. In each setting, we come up with coordinated algorithmic strategies and characterize natural success criteria as a function of the collective’s size. Complementing our theory, we conduct systematic experiments on a skill classification task involving tens of thousands of resumes from a gig platform for freelancers. Through more than two thousand model training runs of a BERT-like language model, we see a striking correspondence emerge between our empirical observations and the predictions made by our theory. Taken together, our theory and experiments broadly support the conclusion that algorithmic collectives of exceedingly small fractional size can exert significant control over a platform’s learning algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies how people acting together can influence a digital platform through the data its machine learning system uses. The authors model a collective that pools participants’ data and coordinates changes to their own contributions. The central question is how much influence such a group can achieve relative to its size.

The analysis covers three learning settings: nonparametric optimal learning, parametric risk minimization, and gradient-based optimization. For each setting, the authors develop coordinated strategies and describe success criteria as a function of collective size. This connects the organization of participants with properties of the platform’s learning procedure.

The authors also test their ideas on skill classification using tens of thousands of freelancer resumes. Across more than two thousand training runs of a BERT-like model, observed behavior closely corresponds to theoretical predictions. Together, these results support the possibility that collectives representing a very small fraction of participants can substantially influence a platform’s learning algorithm. The conclusion concerns the studied strategies and settings, rather than guaranteeing influence for every collective.
summary.tldr: Coordinated changes to participants’ data can give even very small collectives substantial influence over a platform’s learning algorithm.

title: Algorithmic Collective Action in Machine Learning

abstract: Nowadays, state-of-the-art learning-to-rank methods are based on gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT). The most well-known algorithm is LambdaMART which was proposed more than a decade ago. Recently, several other GBDT-based ranking algorithms were proposed. In this paper, we thoroughly analyze these methods in a unified setup. In particular, we address the following questions. Is direct optimization of a smoothed ranking loss preferable over optimizing a convex surrogate? How to properly construct and smooth surrogate ranking losses? To address these questions, we compare LambdaMART with YetiRank and StochasticRank methods and their modifications. We also propose a simple improvement of the YetiRank approach that allows for optimizing specific ranking loss functions. As a result, we gain insights into learning-to-rank techniques and obtain a new state-of-the-art algorithm.

paragraphs: Learning to rank trains a model to place items in a useful order. This paper examines gradient-boosted decision tree approaches, including LambdaMART, YetiRank, and StochasticRank. Its aim is to understand which choices in the training objective account for effective ranking, using a unified setup to compare the methods and their modifications.

The comparison focuses on two related questions. One is whether directly optimizing a smoothed ranking loss is preferable to optimizing a convex surrogate. The other is how surrogate ranking losses should be constructed and smoothed. These choices matter because the objective used during training determines how the model is encouraged to improve its ordering.

The authors also propose a simple change to YetiRank that allows optimization of specific ranking loss functions. Their study produces insights into ranking techniques and an algorithm they report as achieving a new state of the art. The abstract does not identify a universal winner between all direct and surrogate objectives; its concrete contribution combines controlled comparison with a targeted improvement to YetiRank.
summary.tldr: A unified study of boosted-tree ranking losses leads to a YetiRank improvement that targets specific ranking objectives and achieves reported state-of-the-art performance.

title: Which Tricks are Important for Learning to Rank?

abstract: Certified_Watermarks is the first to provide a watermark certificate against $l_2$-norm watermark removal attacks, by leveraging the randomized smoothing techniques for certified robustness to adversarial attacks. However, the randomized smoothing techniques suffer from hardness of certified robustness in high-dimensional space against $l_p$-norm attacks for large $p$ ($p>2$). The certified watermark method based on the randomized smoothing is no exception, i.e., fails to provide meaningful certificates in high-dimensional space against the $l_p$-norm watermark removal attacks ($p>2$). By leveraging mollifier theory, this paper proposes a mollifier smoothing method with dimension-independent certified radius of our proposed smooth classifier, for conducting the certified watermark problem against the $l_p$-norm watermark removal attacks ($1 \leq p \leq \infty$) for high parameter dimension $d$. Based on partial differential equation (PDE) theory, an approximation of mollifier smoothing is developed to alleviate the inefficiency of sampling and prediction in the randomized smoothing as well as numerical integration in the mollifier smoothing, while maintaining the certified watermark against the $l_p$-norm watermark removal attacks ($1 \leq p \leq \infty$).

paragraphs: A certified neural-network watermark comes with a mathematical guarantee against a defined class of removal attacks. Earlier work used randomized smoothing to obtain guarantees for attacks bounded in the l2 norm. The difficulty is that this approach can fail to give meaningful certificates in high-dimensional parameter spaces when attacks are measured using lp norms with p greater than two.

This paper replaces that smoothing approach with one based on mollifier theory. For the proposed smooth classifier, the authors obtain a certified radius that does not depend on parameter dimension. Their formulation covers lp-norm watermark removal attacks throughout the range from p equal to one through infinity, extending the range of attack measurements addressed by the certificate.

The paper also develops an approximation using partial differential equation theory. Its purpose is to ease the sampling and prediction costs associated with randomized smoothing and the numerical integration costs of mollifier smoothing, while retaining the watermark certification. The contribution therefore joins a broader dimensional robustness guarantee with a method intended to make the required smoothing computation more practical.
summary.tldr: Mollifier smoothing provides dimension-independent watermark certificates across lp attack norms, with a PDE-based approximation to reduce computational difficulty.

title: Dimension-independent Certified Neural Network Watermarks via Mollifier Smoothing

abstract: This paper introduces a new principled approach for off-policy learning in contextual bandits. Unlike previous work, our approach does not derive learning principles from intractable or loose bounds. We analyse the problem through the PAC-Bayesian lens, interpreting policies as mixtures of decision rules. This allows us to propose novel generalization bounds and provide tractable algorithms to optimize them. We prove that the derived bounds are tighter than their competitors, and can be optimized directly to confidently improve upon the logging policy offline. Our approach learns policies with guarantees, uses all available data and does not require tuning additional hyperparameters on held-out sets. We demonstrate through extensive experiments the effectiveness of our approach in providing performance guarantees in practical scenarios.

We prove that the derived bounds are tighter than their competitors, and can be optimized directly to confidently improve upon the logging policy offline. paragraphs: Offline contextual-bandit learning seeks a better decision policy using data already collected by a logging policy. A central challenge is turning that data into a reliable claim about the new policy's performance. This paper develops a learning approach around generalization bounds that are both tighter than competing bounds and tractable to optimize.

The authors use a PAC-Bayesian perspective, representing policies as mixtures of decision rules. This representation supports new bounds and algorithms that optimize those bounds directly. The approach connects the learning objective to a performance guarantee, allowing the method to seek confident improvement over the logging policy using offline observations.

The method uses all available data and does not require tuning extra hyperparameters on held-out sets. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in providing performance guarantees in practical settings. The significance lies in bringing the statistical guarantee into the optimization procedure itself, so that policy learning is guided by an actionable bound rather than by a bound too loose or computationally difficult to use.
summary.tldr: Tractable PAC-Bayesian bounds guide offline contextual-bandit learning toward policies with performance guarantees.

title: PAC-Bayesian Offline Contextual Bandits With Guarantees

abstract: There is a growing interest in designing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for seeded graph matching, which aims to match two unlabeled graphs using only topological information and a small set of seed nodes. However, most previous GNNs for this task use a semi-supervised approach, which requires a large number of seeds and cannot learn knowledge that is transferable to unseen graphs. In contrast, this paper proposes a new supervised approach that can learn from a training set how to match unseen graphs with only a few seeds. Our SeedGNN architecture incorporates several novel designs, inspired by theoretical studies of seeded graph matching: 1) it can learn to compute and use witness-like information from different hops, in a way that can be generalized to graphs of different sizes; 2) it can use easily-matched node-pairs as new seeds to improve the matching in subsequent layers. We evaluate SeedGNN on synthetic and real-world graphs and demonstrate significant performance improvements over both non-learning and learning algorithms in the existing literature. Furthermore, our experiments confirm that the knowledge learned by SeedGNN from training graphs can be generalized to test graphs of different sizes and categories.

paragraphs: Seeded graph matching identifies corresponding nodes in two unlabeled graphs using their connectivity and a small set of known matches. Previous neural approaches often require many seeds and do not learn knowledge transferable to new graphs. SeedGNN instead uses supervised training to learn how to match unseen graphs from only a few seeds.

The architecture incorporates two ideas inspired by graph-matching theory. It learns to compute and use witness-like structural evidence from different hop distances in a form that can transfer across graph sizes. It also treats easily matched node pairs as additional seeds, allowing later layers to build on matches established earlier.

Evaluations on synthetic and real-world graphs show substantial improvements over the learning and non-learning methods compared. The experiments also demonstrate transfer from training graphs to test graphs with different sizes and categories. These findings support learning a reusable matching procedure, where structural evidence and progressively expanded seed information work together to identify correspondences beyond the graphs seen during training.
summary.tldr: SeedGNN learns transferable graph matching from few seeds by combining multi-hop evidence with progressively discovered matches.

title: SeedGNN: Graph Neural Network for Supervised Seeded Graph Matching

abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) samples is essential when deploying machine learning models in open-world scenarios. Zero-shot OOD detection, requiring no training on in-distribution (ID) data, has been possible with the advent of vision-language models like CLIP. Existing methods build a text-based classifier with only closed-set labels. However, this largely restricts the inherent capability of CLIP to recognize samples from large and open label space. In this paper, we propose to tackle this constraint by leveraging the expert knowledge and reasoning capability of large language models (LLM) to Envision potential Outlier Exposure, termed EOE, without access to any actual OOD data. Owing to better adaptation to open-world scenarios, EOE can be generalized to different tasks, including far, near, and fine-grained OOD detection. Technically, we design (1) LLM prompts based on visual similarity to generate potential outlier class labels specialized for OOD detection, as well as (2) a new score function based on potential outlier penalty to distinguish hard OOD samples effectively. Empirically, EOE achieves state-of-the-art performance across different OOD tasks and can be effectively scaled to the ImageNet-1K dataset. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/EOE.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the categories a system is meant to handle. Vision-language models such as CLIP enable this without training on in-distribution data. However, building a text classifier using only the accepted class labels restricts how much of the model’s broader recognition ability can contribute to detecting unfamiliar inputs.

The proposed EOE method uses a large language model to imagine potential outlier categories without accessing actual outlier data. Prompts based on visual similarity produce labels tailored to the detection problem. A new scoring function then incorporates a penalty associated with these potential outliers, helping distinguish difficult unfamiliar samples from accepted ones.

This expands the text descriptions available to the detector beyond its closed set of target classes. The authors evaluate the approach on far, near, and fine-grained out-of-distribution detection, reporting state-of-the-art performance across these tasks. They also demonstrate effective scaling to ImageNet-1K. The stated results support using generated category descriptions as useful detection evidence even when real outlier examples are unavailable.
summary.tldr: EOE uses language-model-generated outlier labels to improve zero-shot detection without accessing actual outlier data.

title: Envisioning Outlier Exposure by Large Language Models for Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: Molecular modeling, a central topic in quantum mechanics, aims to accurately calculate the properties and simulate the behaviors of molecular systems. The molecular model is governed by physical laws, which impose geometric constraints such as invariance and equivariance to coordinate rotation and translation. While numerous deep learning approaches have been developed to learn molecular representations under these constraints, most of them are built upon heuristic and costly modules. We argue that there is a strong need for a general and flexible framework for learning both invariant and equivariant features. In this work, we introduce a novel Transformer-based molecular model called GeoMFormer to achieve this goal. Using the standard Transformer modules, two separate streams are developed to maintain and learn invariant and equivariant representations. Carefully designed cross-attention modules bridge the two streams, allowing information fusion and enhancing geometric modeling in each stream. As a general and flexible architecture, we show that many previous architectures can be viewed as special instantiations of GeoMFormer. Extensive experiments are conducted to demonstrate the power of GeoMFormer. All empirical results show that GeoMFormer achieves strong performance on both invariant and equivariant tasks of different types and scales. Code and models will be made publicly available at https://github.com/c-tl/GeoMFormer.
