paragraphs: Molecular models must respect how physical quantities behave when coordinates are rotated or translated. Invariant features remain unchanged, while equivariant features transform consistently with the coordinate change. GeoMFormer provides a common architecture for learning both kinds of representation, addressing the authors’ concern that existing approaches often depend on specialized, costly modules.

The model uses standard Transformer components arranged into two streams, one for invariant representations and one for equivariant representations. Carefully designed cross-attention passes information between them. This lets the streams enrich each other while maintaining their different geometric roles, bringing both types of information into the same molecular modeling framework.

The authors show that many earlier architectures can be understood as particular instances of GeoMFormer, supporting its claim to generality. Experiments report strong results on invariant and equivariant tasks across different types and scales. These findings support the usefulness of a flexible shared design for molecular learning, rather than requiring an unrelated architecture for each kind of geometric prediction.
summary.tldr: GeoMFormer links invariant and equivariant Transformer streams to learn molecular representations that respect geometric constraints.

title: GeoMFormer: A General Architecture for Geometric Molecular Representation Learning

abstract: The current paradigm of training deep neural networks for classification tasks includes minimizing the empirical risk, pushing the training loss value towards zero even after the training classification error has vanished. In this terminal phase of training, it has been observed that the last-layer features collapse to their class-means and these class-means converge to the vertices of a simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF). This phenomenon is termed as Neural Collapse ($\mathcal{NC}$). However, this characterization only holds in class-balanced datasets where every class has the same number of training samples. When the training dataset is class-imbalanced, some $\mathcal{NC}$ properties will no longer hold true, for example, the geometry of class-means will skew away from the simplex ETF. In this paper, we generalize $\mathcal{NC}$ to imbalanced regime for cross-entropy loss under the unconstrained ReLU features model. We demonstrate that while the within-class features collapse property still holds in this setting, the class-means will converge to a structure consisting of orthogonal vectors with lengths dependent on the number of training samples. Furthermore, we find that the classifier weights (i.e., the last-layer linear classifier) are aligned to the scaled and centered class-means, with scaling factors dependent on the number of training samples of each class. This generalizes $\mathcal{NC}$ in the class-balanced setting. We empirically validate our results through experiments on practical architectures and dataset.

Features from the same class converge toward their class mean, and in the balanced setting the means form a symmetric geometric arrangement. This paper investigates how that picture changes when classes have different numbers of training examples.

The analysis uses cross-entropy loss under an unconstrained ReLU features model. Within this setting, examples within each class still collapse to a common representation. However, the class means converge to orthogonal vectors whose lengths depend on class sample counts, replacing the balanced characterization with geometry that reflects the imbalance.

The classifier weights also follow a structured relationship: they align with scaled and centered class means, with scaling determined by each class's sample count. The authors validate the results empirically using practical architectures and data. The contribution clarifies which parts of neural collapse persist under imbalance and how both feature geometry and classifier alignment change, with the theoretical conclusions tied to the stated model.
summary.tldr: Under an unconstrained ReLU features model, class imbalance preserves within-class collapse while changing class-mean geometry and classifier alignment according to class counts.

title: Neural Collapse for Cross-entropy Class-Imbalanced Learning with Unconstrained ReLU Features Model

abstract: We present evidence of substantial benefit from efficient exploration in gathering human feedback to improve large language models. In our experiments, an agent sequentially generates queries while fitting a reward model to the feedback received. Our best-performing agent generates queries using double Thompson sampling, with uncertainty represented by an epistemic neural network. Our results demonstrate that efficient exploration enables high levels of performance with far fewer queries. Further, both uncertainty estimation and the choice of exploration scheme play critical roles.

This paper studies an agent that gathers feedback sequentially while learning a reward model. Each round provides evidence that can influence subsequent queries, making feedback collection an exploration problem rather than a fixed sequence of requests.

The strongest agent in the experiments combines double Thompson sampling for query generation with an epistemic neural network for representing uncertainty. These components address related decisions: what the reward model remains unsure about, and how that uncertainty should guide the next query. The study examines both as parts of an effective feedback-gathering process.

The experiments show that efficient exploration can reach high performance using far fewer queries. They also indicate that uncertainty estimation and the exploration scheme each play critical roles. The practical message is that feedback efficiency depends on the strategy for acquiring information as well as the model that learns from the resulting responses.
summary.tldr: Experiments show that uncertainty-aware exploration can substantially reduce the human-feedback queries needed to improve language models.

title: Efficient Exploration for LLMs

abstract: The stochastic proximal gradient method is a powerful generalization of the widely used stochastic gradient descent (SGD) method and has found numerous applications in Machine Learning. However, it is notoriously known that this method fails to converge in non-convex settings where the stochastic noise is significant (i.e. when only small or bounded batch sizes are used). In this paper, we focus on the stochastic proximal gradient method with Polyak momentum. We prove this method attains an optimal convergence rate for non-convex composite optimization problems, regardless of batch size. Additionally, we rigorously analyze the variance reduction effect of the Polyak momentum in the composite optimization setting and we show the method also converges when the proximal step can only be solved inexactly. Finally, we provide numerical experiments to validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Stochastic proximal gradient methods extend stochastic gradient descent to composite optimization problems. Their usefulness is limited in nonconvex settings when gradient noise remains substantial, as can happen with small or bounded batch sizes. The paper addresses this convergence problem by adding Polyak momentum to the stochastic proximal gradient method.

The authors prove that the resulting method achieves an optimal convergence rate for the nonconvex composite problems studied, regardless of batch size. They also analyze how Polyak momentum reduces variance in this setting. This connects the convergence guarantee to the behavior of the noisy optimization updates, rather than treating momentum only as an empirical enhancement.

The analysis additionally permits the proximal step to be solved approximately, and establishes convergence even with that inexact computation. This matters because a convergence argument requiring an exact proximal solution would impose a stricter computational requirement. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical results, supporting momentum as a way to handle stochastic noise while retaining flexibility in how the proximal step is computed.
summary.tldr: Polyak momentum gives stochastic proximal gradient methods optimal nonconvex convergence rates across batch sizes, with convergence also established for inexact proximal steps.

title: Non-convex Stochastic Composite Optimization with Polyak Momentum

abstract: The vast applications of deep generative models are anchored in three core capabilities—generating new instances, reconstructing inputs, and learning compact representations—across various data types, such as discrete text/protein sequences and continuous images. Existing model families, like variational autoencoders (VAEs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), autoregressive models, and (latent) diffusion models, generally excel in specific capabilities and data types but fall short in others. We introduce Generalized Encoding-Decoding Diffusion Probabilistic Models (EDDPMs) which integrate the core capabilities for broad applicability and enhanced performance. EDDPMs generalize the Gaussian noising-denoising in standard diffusion by introducing parameterized encoding-decoding. Crucially, EDDPMs are compatible with the well-established diffusion model objective and training recipes, allowing effective learning of the encoder-decoder parameters jointly with diffusion. By choosing appropriate encoder/decoder (e.g., large language models), EDDPMs naturally apply to different data types. Extensive experiments on text, proteins, and images demonstrate the flexibility to handle diverse data and tasks and the strong improvement over various existing models. Code is available at https://github.com/guangyliu/EDDPM .

The encoder and decoder are learned jointly with diffusion while remaining compatible with established diffusion objectives and training recipes. The findings support jointly adapting encoding, decoding, and diffusion as a way to bring generation, reconstruction, and representation learning into one model family.
summary.tldr: EDDPMs jointly learn encoding, decoding, and diffusion to support generation, reconstruction, and representation learning across text, proteins, and images.

title: Unified Generation, Reconstruction, and Representation: Generalized Diffusion with Adaptive Latent Encoding-Decoding

abstract: An open scientific challenge is how to classify events with reliable measures of uncertainty, when we have a mechanistic model of the data-generating process but the distribution over both labels and latent nuisance parameters is different between train and target data. We refer to this type of distributional shift as generalized label shift (GLS). Direct classification using observed data $\mathbf{X}$ as covariates leads to biased predictions and invalid uncertainty estimates of labels $Y$. We overcome these biases by proposing a new method for robust uncertainty quantification that casts classification as a hypothesis testing problem under nuisance parameters. The key idea is to estimate the classifier’s receiver operating characteristic (ROC) across the entire nuisance parameter space, which allows us to devise cutoffs that are invariant under GLS. Our method effectively endows a pre-trained classifier with domain adaptation capabilities and returns valid prediction sets while maintaining high power. We demonstrate its performance on two challenging scientific problems in biology and astroparticle physics with data from realistic mechanistic models.

paragraphs: Scientific classification can involve a mechanistic model of how observations arise, alongside hidden nuisance parameters that affect those observations. This paper addresses situations where the distribution of both labels and nuisance parameters changes between training and deployment. The authors call this generalized label shift and explain that direct classification can then produce biased predictions and invalid uncertainty estimates.

Their approach treats classification as hypothesis testing in the presence of nuisance parameters. It estimates how a classifier’s true-positive and false-positive behavior varies across the entire nuisance parameter space. That information is used to construct decision cutoffs that remain invariant under the specified distributional shift.

The method equips a pretrained classifier with adaptation capabilities and produces prediction sets with valid uncertainty while maintaining high statistical power. Its value is that uncertainty assessment explicitly accounts for the nuisance variation responsible for the shift. The authors demonstrate the approach on biology and astroparticle physics problems using data from realistic mechanistic models, connecting the statistical construction to scientific classification tasks.
summary.tldr: A hypothesis-testing approach gives pretrained classifiers valid prediction sets under shifts in both labels and latent nuisance parameters.

title: Classification under Nuisance Parameters and Generalized Label Shift in Likelihood-Free Inference

abstract: Distributed learning is an effective approach to accelerate model training by using parallel computing power of multiple workers. However, substantial communication delays arise between workers and a parameter server due to the massive costs associated with communicating gradients. SignSGD with majority voting (signSGD-MV) is a simple yet effective optimizer that reduces communication costs through sign quantization, but its convergence rate significantly decreases when adversarial workers arbitrarily manipulate datasets or local gradient updates. In this paper, we consider a distributed learning problem where the workforce comprises a mixture of honest and adversarial workers. In this setting, we show that the convergence rate can remain invariant as long as the number of honest workers providing trustworthy local updates to the parameter server exceeds the number of adversarial workers. The key idea behind this counter-intuitive result is our novel aggregation method, signSGD with federated defense (signSGD-FD). Unlike traditional approaches, signSGD-FD utilizes the gradient information sent by adversarial workers with appropriate weights, obtained through gradient sign decoding. Experimental results demonstrate that signSGD-FD achieves superior convergence rates compared to traditional algorithms in various adversarial attack scenarios.

paragraphs: Distributed learning divides training across workers, but sending their gradients to a central server can create substantial communication costs. SignSGD reduces this burden by transmitting gradient signs and combining them through majority voting. Its convergence can deteriorate when adversarial workers manipulate their data or updates.

The paper proposes signSGD with federated defense, which aggregates signs using weights obtained through gradient sign decoding. A distinctive feature is that it uses information sent by adversarial workers with appropriate weighting. The method therefore seeks useful aggregate information even when some messages originate from compromised participants.

The authors show that convergence speed can remain invariant provided honest workers supplying trustworthy updates outnumber adversarial workers. This majority condition is essential to the stated result. Experiments across several adversarial attack scenarios report better convergence rates than traditional algorithms. The theoretical and empirical contributions together support weighted sign decoding as a way to retain communication efficiency while improving training behavior in the presence of adversarial workers.
summary.tldr: SignSGD-FD weights decoded gradient signs, allowing convergence rates to remain invariant when trustworthy honest workers outnumber adversarial workers.

title: SignSGD with Federated Defense: Harnessing Adversarial Attacks through Gradient Sign Decoding

abstract: This paper proposes two different models for equitable resource allocation in online settings. The first one is called external equity promotion, where sequentially arriving agents are heterogeneous in their external attributes, namely how many resources they demand, which are drawn from a probability distribution (accessible to the algorithm). The focus is then to devise an allocation policy such that every requester can get a fair share of resources proportional to their demands, regardless of their arrival time. The second is called internal equity promotion, where arriving requesters can be treated homogeneously in external attributes (demands) but are heterogeneous in internal traits such as demographics. In particular, each requester can be identified as belonging to one or several groups, and an allocation of resources is regarded as equitable when every group of requesters can receive a fair share of resources proportional to the percentage of that group in the whole population. For both models above, we consider as the benchmark a clairvoyant optimal solution that has the privilege to access all random demand realizations in advance. We consider two equity metrics, namely ex-post and ex-ante, and discuss the challenges under the two metrics in detail. Specifically, we present two linear program (LP)-based policies for external equity promotion under ex-ante with independent demands, each achieving an optimal CR of $1/2$ with respect to the benchmark LP. For internal equity promotion, we present optimal policies under both ex-ante and ex-post metrics.

paragraphs: Allocating resources as requests arrive creates a fairness problem because later requests remain unknown. The paper distinguishes external equity, where allocations should be proportional to differing demands regardless of arrival time, from internal equity, where groups should receive shares proportional to their population representation. A requester may belong to multiple groups.

For external equity, demand distributions are accessible to the algorithm. The authors compare online policies with a clairvoyant solution that knows all realized demands in advance. They examine both ex-ante equity, assessed in expectation, and ex-post equity, assessed after outcomes are realized. These perspectives create different requirements for what a fair allocation policy must accomplish.

Under independent demands and the ex-ante metric, two linear-programming-based external-equity policies achieve an optimal competitive ratio of one-half relative to the benchmark linear program. For internal equity, the authors present optimal policies under both metrics. The results provide separate guarantees for distinct meanings of fairness, with the external-equity guarantee explicitly tied to independence and ex-ante evaluation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops optimal online allocation policies for specified demand-based and group-based fairness objectives under different equity metrics.

title: Promoting External and Internal Equities Under Ex-Ante/Ex-Post Metrics in Online Resource Allocation

abstract: We establish the first finite-time logarithmic regret bounds for the self-tuning regulation problem. We introduce a modified version of the certainty equivalence algorithm, which we call PIECE, that clips inputs in addition to utilizing probing inputs for exploration. We show that it has a $C \log T$ upper bound on the regret after $T$ time-steps for bounded noise, and $C\log^3 T$ in the case of sub-Gaussian noise, unlike the LQ problem where logarithmic regret is shown to be not possible. The PIECE algorithm is also designed to address the critical challenge of poor initial transient performance of reinforcement learning algorithms for linear systems. Comparative simulation results illustrate the improved performance of PIECE.

We introduce a modified version of the certainty equivalence algorithm, which we call PIECE, that clips inputs in addition to utilizing probing inputs for exploration. We show that it has a $C \log T$ upper bound on the regret after $T$ time-steps for bounded noise, and $C\log^3 T$ in the case of sub-Gaussian noise, unlike the LQ problem where logarithmic regret is shown to be not possible. paragraphs: Self-tuning regulation concerns controlling a system while learning how to regulate it. This paper studies regret, which tracks the accumulated performance cost of learning while acting. Its focus is a finite-time guarantee: a bound that describes performance after a specified number of steps, rather than only eventual behavior.

The authors introduce PIECE, a modified certainty-equivalence algorithm. It combines probing inputs for exploration with input clipping. The algorithm also targets poor initial transient performance, the difficult early period during which learning-based controllers can behave poorly before they have gathered sufficient information about the system.

The regret guarantee depends on the noise assumption. For bounded noise, the authors prove an upper bound of C log T after T steps; for sub-Gaussian noise, the bound is C(log T)^3. They identify the logarithmic result as the first finite-time bound of this kind for self-tuning regulation. Comparative simulations illustrate improved performance, complementing the theoretical results. The distinction between noise settings matters because the stronger logarithmic guarantee is stated for bounded noise.
summary.tldr: PIECE combines probing and input clipping to achieve logarithmic regret for self-tuning regulation under bounded noise, with a different bound for sub-Gaussian noise.

title: Finite Time Logarithmic Regret Bounds for Self-Tuning Regulation

abstract: Fourier features based positional encoding (PE) is commonly used in machine learning tasks that involve learning high-frequency features from low-dimensional inputs, such as 3D view synthesis and time series regression with neural tangent kernels. Despite their effectiveness, existing PEs require manual, empirical adjustment of crucial hyperparameters, specifically the Fourier features, tailored to each unique task. Further, PEs face challenges in efficiently learning high-frequency functions, particularly in tasks with limited data. In this paper, we introduce sinusoidal PE (SPE), designed to efficiently learn adaptive frequency features closely aligned with the true underlying function. Our experiments demonstrate that SPE, without hyperparameter tuning, consistently achieves enhanced fidelity and faster training across various tasks, including 3D view synthesis, Text-to-Speech generation, and 1D regression. SPE is implemented as a direct replacement for existing PEs. Its plug-and-play nature lets numerous tasks easily adopt and benefit from SPE.

paragraphs: Learning rapidly varying functions from low-dimensional inputs is important in tasks such as view synthesis and time-series regression. Fourier-feature positional encodings help with this problem, but their frequency choices often require manual adjustment for each task. Existing encodings can also struggle to learn high-frequency functions efficiently when data is limited.

The paper introduces sinusoidal positional encoding, or SPE, to learn adaptive frequency features that closely match the underlying function. Frequency adaptation is the central design goal: the representation should adjust to the function being learned instead of depending on a manually selected set of Fourier features. SPE is designed as a direct replacement for existing positional encodings.

Across experiments in 3D view synthesis, text-to-speech generation, and one-dimensional regression, SPE achieves better fidelity and faster training without hyperparameter tuning. These are empirical results across the evaluated tasks. The combination of adaptive features and a drop-in implementation matters because it offers improvements at a component already used in many learning systems, with less task-specific adjustment in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: SPE learns adaptive frequency features as a drop-in positional encoding, improving fidelity and training speed without hyperparameter tuning in the reported experiments.

title: Learning High-Frequency Functions Made Easy with Sinusoidal Positional Encoding

abstract: Modeling symmetry breaking is essential for understanding the fundamental changes in the behaviors and properties of physical systems, from microscopic particle interactions to macroscopic phenomena like fluid dynamics and cosmic structures. Thus, identifying sources of asymmetry is an important tool for understanding physical systems. In this paper, we focus on learning asymmetries of data using relaxed group convolutions. We provide both theoretical and empirical evidence that this flexible convolution technique allows the model to maintain the highest level of equivariance that is consistent with data and discover the subtle symmetry-breaking factors in various physical systems. We employ various relaxed group convolution architectures to uncover various symmetry-breaking factors that are interpretable and physically meaningful in different physical systems, including the phase transition of crystal structure, the isotropy and homogeneity breaking in turbulent flow, and the time-reversal symmetry breaking in pendulum systems.

paragraphs: Physical symmetries describe how a system's behavior relates across transformations. Departures from those symmetries can reveal meaningful changes in the system. This paper studies how neural networks can learn such departures from data, making asymmetry something to investigate rather than simply treating it as an obstacle to modeling.

The authors use relaxed group convolutions, which allow flexibility in how strongly a network respects a symmetry. They provide theoretical and empirical evidence that this approach can preserve the greatest degree of equivariance compatible with the observations. Equivariance means that a transformation of the input produces a corresponding transformation of the output. Relaxing it allows data to reveal where that relationship breaks.

The paper applies several architectures to crystal phase transitions, broken isotropy and homogeneity in turbulent flow, and broken time-reversal symmetry in pendulum systems. The discovered factors are reported to be interpretable and physically meaningful. The contribution is therefore both a modeling technique and a way to identify subtle departures from symmetry in the physical systems examined.
summary.tldr: Relaxed group convolutions learn physically meaningful symmetry breaking while retaining the degree of equivariance supported by the data.

title: Discovering Symmetry Breaking in Physical Systems with Relaxed Group Convolution

abstract: The availability of a wide range of large language models (LLMs) embedded in various agentic systems has significantly increased the potential of model selection strategies to improve the cost-performance tradeoff. Existing strategies involve either routing, where a single model is chosen per query, or cascading, which sequentially runs increasingly larger models until a satisfactory answer is found. However, current approaches face three key limitations: they (1) lack formal proofs of optimality, (2) fail to identify the conditions under which these strategies are most effective to improve the cost-performance tradeoff, and (3) are unable to combine both paradigms for further improvements. To address these issues, we first derive a novel optimal strategy for cascading and prove the optimality of an existing routing strategy. Further, we propose cascade routing, a unified framework that integrates routing and cascading into a theoretically optimal strategy. Through our analysis, we identify good quality estimators as the critical factor for the success of model selection paradigms. Finally, in our experiments, we show that cascade routing consistently outperforms the individual approaches by a large margin and we analyze quality estimators to determine when routing and/or cascading are useful paradigms for model selection.

paragraphs: Choosing which language model handles a query can change both answer quality and computational cost. Routing makes that choice once, selecting a single model. Cascading instead tries models sequentially, moving to larger ones until an answer is considered satisfactory. This paper studies how to make these decisions within a common framework.

The authors derive an optimal cascading strategy and prove the optimality of an existing routing strategy. They then introduce cascade routing, which combines both forms of selection into a strategy with a theoretical optimality result. The contribution therefore includes both decision rules and an analysis of why those rules work within the studied formulation.

A central finding is that model selection depends critically on good quality estimators: the system needs useful estimates of how well models will answer. In the reported experiments, cascade routing consistently surpasses either approach alone by a large margin. The analysis of quality estimators also helps identify when routing, cascading, or their combination can improve the cost-performance tradeoff.
summary.tldr: Cascade routing combines model routing and sequential escalation, with theoretical optimality results and strong experimental gains tied to quality estimation.

title: A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs

abstract: Deriving insights from experimentally generated datasets requires methods that can account for random and systematic measurement errors and remove them in order to accurately represent the underlying effects of the conditions being tested. Here we present a framework for pretraining on large-scale microscopy datasets that includes three steps: (1) curating a set of diverse and self-consistent training samples, (2) scaling training of an appropriate foundation model architecture on this dataset, (3) evaluating intermediate layers of the trained model to identify the best representation for downstream tasks. Using this strategy, we present the largest foundation model for cell microscopy data to our knowledge, a new 1.9 billion-parameter ViT-G/8 MAE trained on over 8 billion microscopy image crops. Compared to a previous published ViT-L/8 MAE, our new model achieves a 60% improvement in linear separability of genetic perturbations and obtains the best overall performance on whole-genome relationship recall, batch correction replicate consistency, and compound-gene activity prediction benchmarks.

paragraphs: Cell microscopy representations need to capture biological effects despite random and systematic measurement errors. This paper presents a three-part pretraining strategy: curate diverse, internally consistent samples, scale an appropriate foundation model on them, and inspect intermediate layers to identify the representations most useful for downstream tasks.

Using this strategy, the authors train a 1.9-billion-parameter ViT-G/8 masked autoencoder on more than eight billion microscopy image crops. They describe it as the largest cell-microscopy foundation model to their knowledge. The framework treats data consistency and representation selection as explicit parts of scaling, alongside the model’s size and training dataset.

Compared with a previously published ViT-L/8 masked autoencoder, the model improves linear separability of genetic perturbations by 60%, meaning the learned representations better support separating those perturbations with a linear decision rule. It also achieves the best overall performance on the reported whole-genome relationship recall, batch-correction replicate consistency, and compound–gene activity prediction benchmarks. These results connect the pretraining strategy to several distinct tests of biological usefulness.
summary.tldr: A microscopy pretraining framework combining consistent data, model scaling, and layer selection improves biological representations across several benchmarks.

title: ViTally Consistent: Scaling Biological Representation Learning for Cell Microscopy

abstract: In a neural network with ReLU activations, the number of piecewise linear regions in the output can grow exponentially with depth. However, this is highly unlikely to happen when the initial parameters are sampled randomly, which therefore often leads to the use of networks that are unnecessarily large. To address this problem, we introduce a novel parameterization of the network that restricts its weights so that a depth $d$ network produces exactly $2^d$ linear regions at initialization and maintains those regions throughout training under the parameterization. This approach allows us to learn approximations of convex, one-dimensional functions that are several orders of magnitude more accurate than their randomly initialized counterparts. We further demonstrate a preliminary extension of our construction to multidimensional and non-convex functions, allowing the technique to replace traditional dense layers in various architectures.
originalAbstract: In a neural network with ReLU activations, the number of piecewise linear regions in the output can grow exponentially with depth. However, this is highly unlikely to happen when the initial parameters are sampled randomly, which therefore often leads to the use of networks that are unnecessarily large. To address this problem, we introduce a novel parameterization of the network that restricts its weights so that a depth $d$ network produces exactly $2^d$ linear regions at initialization and maintains those regions throughout training under the parameterization. This approach allows us to learn approximations of convex, one-dimensional functions that are several orders of magnitude more accurate than their randomly initialized counterparts. We further demonstrate a preliminary extension of our construction to multidimensional and non-convex functions, allowing the technique to replace traditional dense layers in various architectures.

paragraphs: A network with ReLU activations represents a function through pieces that are individually linear. The number of such regions can grow exponentially with depth, but randomly chosen initial parameters are highly unlikely to realize that potential. The paper argues that this gap between possible and realized complexity can contribute to using unnecessarily large networks.

The authors introduce a parameterization that restricts network weights so a depth-d network has exactly 2^d linear regions at initialization. Those regions remain present throughout training under the parameterization. The method therefore makes a particular form of expressive structure available from the beginning and preserves it as the network learns.

For approximating convex functions of one variable, the resulting networks achieve accuracy several orders of magnitude better than randomly initialized counterparts. The authors also present a preliminary extension to functions that are multidimensional or non-convex, supporting replacement of traditional dense layers in various architectures. The strongest demonstrated approximation result concerns the convex, one-dimensional setting.
summary.tldr: A constrained parameterization preserves exactly 2^d linear regions in depth-d ReLU networks and greatly improves convex one-dimensional function approximation.

title: Compelling ReLU Networks to Exhibit Exponentially Many Linear Regions at Initialization and During Training

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (Multimodal LLMs) have shown their strength in Video Question Answering (VideoQA). However, due to the black-box nature of end-to-end training strategies, existing approaches based on Multimodal LLMs suffer from the lack of interpretability for VideoQA: they can neither present reasoning paths nor indicate where the answers are derived from the video. To address this issue, we propose MSR-ViR (Modularized Self-Reflected Video Reasoner), which for the first time integrates modular networks to Multimodal LLMs, capable of providing VideoQA with explicit reasoning paths for more interpretability. Specifically, a MoST-Grounding (Modularized Spatial-Temporal Grounding) network is proposed to decompose complex questions via tree-structured policies, localizing relevant temporal and spatial segments within videos through step-by-step reasoning. The proposed MoST-Grounding network provides explicit visually grounded information for Multimodal LLMs with clear reasoning paths, thus enhancing interpretability for the predicted answers. To further improve the reasoning quality, we design an Alternate Self-reflection Training Strategy to jointly optimize policy generation and Multimodal LLMs. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed MSR-ViR framework in video understanding, reasoning transparency, and providing explicit localization evidence for answers.

paragraphs: A video question-answering system may provide an answer without revealing its reasoning or the video evidence behind it. This paper addresses that interpretability problem in multimodal language models. MSR-ViR integrates modular networks into the answering process so that the system can expose explicit reasoning paths and identify relevant parts of the video.

Its MoST-Grounding network breaks complex questions into steps using tree-structured policies. These steps locate relevant intervals in time and regions in space, producing visually grounded information for the multimodal language model. The resulting reasoning path links the question’s decomposition to the video segments used in constructing an answer.

An alternating self-reflection training strategy jointly optimizes policy generation and the multimodal language model to improve reasoning quality. Experiments on real-world datasets report stronger video understanding, greater reasoning transparency, and explicit localization evidence for answers. The approach makes evidence selection part of the system’s visible reasoning process, giving users more information about how an answer relates to the observed video.
summary.tldr: MSR-ViR answers video questions through modular reasoning that explicitly locates supporting video evidence and exposes the reasoning path.

title: Modularized Self-Reflected Video Reasoner for Multimodal LLM with Application to Video Question Answering

abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly proficient at solving web-based tasks. With this capability comes a greater risk of misuse for malicious purposes, such as posting misinformation in an online forum or selling illicit substances on a website. To evaluate these risks, we propose SafeArena, a benchmark focused on the deliberate misuse of web agents. SafeArena comprises 250 safe and 250 harmful tasks across four websites. We classify the harmful tasks into five harm categories—misinformation, illegal activity, harassment, cybercrime, and social bias, designed to assess realistic misuses of web agents. We evaluate leading LLM-based web agents, including GPT-4o, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, Qwen-2-VL 72B, and Llama-3.2 90B, on our benchmark. To systematically assess their susceptibility to harmful tasks, we introduce the Agent Risk Assessment framework that categorizes agent behavior across four risk levels. We find agents are surprisingly compliant with malicious requests, with GPT-4o and Qwen-2 completing 34.7% and 27.3% of harmful requests, respectively. Our findings highlight the urgent need for safety alignment procedures for web agents.

paragraphs: SafeArena evaluates whether autonomous web agents comply with deliberately harmful requests. The benchmark focuses on that risk by testing agent behavior on concrete web tasks, including both legitimate requests and requests intended to cause harm.

It contains 250 safe tasks and 250 harmful tasks across four websites. Harmful tasks cover misinformation, illegal activity, harassment, cybercrime, and social bias. These benchmark findings show substantial compliance with malicious instructions among tested agents and motivate safety alignment procedures aimed specifically at agents that can act on websites.
summary.tldr: SafeArena tests deliberate misuse of web agents and finds substantial harmful-request completion among evaluated systems.

title: SafeArena: Evaluating the Safety of Autonomous Web Agents

abstract: Post-hoc calibration of pre-trained models is critical for ensuring reliable inference, especially in safety-critical domains such as healthcare. Conformal Prediction (CP) offers a robust post-hoc calibration framework, providing distribution-free statistical coverage guarantees for prediction sets by leveraging held-out datasets. In this work, we address a decentralized setting where each device has limited calibration data and can communicate only with its neighbors over an arbitrary graph topology. We propose two message-passing-based approaches for achieving reliable inference via CP: quantile-based distributed conformal prediction (Q-DCP) and histogram-based distributed conformal prediction (H-DCP). Q-DCP employs distributed quantile regression enhanced with tailored smoothing and regularization terms to accelerate convergence, while H-DCP uses a consensus-based histogram estimation approach. Through extensive experiments, we investigate the trade-offs between hyperparameter tuning requirements, communication overhead, coverage guarantees, and prediction set sizes across different network topologies. The code of our work is released on: https://github.com/HaifengWen/Distributed-Conformal-Prediction.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction uses held-out calibration data to turn model outputs into prediction sets with statistical coverage guarantees. This paper considers a decentralized setting where individual devices have little calibration data and can communicate only with neighboring devices. The challenge is to support reliable prediction through local exchanges over a graph rather than centralized calibration.

The authors propose two message-passing methods. Quantile-based distributed conformal prediction, Q-DCP, uses distributed quantile regression, with tailored smoothing and regularization to accelerate convergence. Histogram-based distributed conformal prediction, H-DCP, instead uses consensus to estimate a histogram. These approaches offer different ways for devices to collectively obtain the information needed for calibration.

Experiments examine their behavior across network topologies, comparing tuning requirements, communication costs, coverage guarantees, and prediction-set sizes. These dimensions matter together: a method’s calibration behavior must be considered alongside the exchanges and tuning it requires. The paper’s contribution is a pair of decentralized approaches and an investigation of their tradeoffs, rather than a stated single winner for every network.
summary.tldr: Two message-passing methods enable decentralized conformal calibration while exposing tradeoffs among communication, tuning, coverage, and prediction-set size.

title: Distributed Conformal Prediction via Message Passing

abstract: To learn from data collected in diverse dynamics, Imitation from Observation (IfO) methods leverage expert state trajectories based on the premise that recovering expert state distributions in other dynamics facilitates policy learning in the current one. However, Imitation Learning inherently imposes a performance upper bound of learned policies. Additionally, as the environment dynamics change, certain expert states may become inaccessible, rendering their distributions less valuable for imitation. To address this, we propose a novel framework that integrates reward maximization with IfO, employing F-distance regularized policy optimization. This framework enforces constraints on globally accessible states—those with nonzero visitation frequency across all considered dynamics—mitigating the challenge posed by inaccessible states. By instantiating F-distance in different ways, we derive two theoretical analysis and develop a practical algorithm called Accessible State Oriented Policy Regularization (ASOR). ASOR serves as a general-purpose module that can be incorporated into various RL approaches, including offline RL and off-policy RL. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate ASOR’s effectiveness in enhancing state-of-the-art cross-domain policy transfer algorithms, significantly improving their performance.

paragraphs: Learning from expert state trajectories can help transfer policies between environments with different dynamics. However, imitation can constrain the learned policy's performance, and changed dynamics can make some expert states unreachable. The paper addresses both problems by combining reward maximization with imitation from observation while focusing regularization on shared accessible states.

The framework uses F-distance regularized policy optimization. Its constraints apply to globally accessible states, defined as states with nonzero visitation frequency across every considered dynamics setting. This directs the imitation-related constraint toward states that remain relevant across environments. Different choices of F-distance lead to theoretical analyses and a practical algorithm called Accessible State Oriented Policy Regularization, or ASOR.

ASOR is designed as a module that can be incorporated into reinforcement learning approaches, including offline and off-policy methods. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report significant improvements to state-of-the-art cross-domain policy transfer algorithms. The findings support combining reward-driven learning with accessibility-aware regularization when expert experience comes from different dynamics.
summary.tldr: ASOR improves cross-dynamics policy transfer by combining reward maximization with regularization on states accessible across the considered environments.

title: Policy Regularization on Globally Accessible States in Cross-Dynamics Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Mixtures of Bernoulli product distributions are a simple and widely used latent-variable model, with applications in e.g. recommendation systems, crowdsourcing, and medical data analysis. We consider the problem of reconstructing the mixture parameters from oracle access to its probability generating polynomial (PGP), for instance represented by a probabilistic generating circuit (PGC). We show that the parameters are uniquely identifiable for almost all mixtures, and give a randomized algorithm that exactly recovers the mixture weights and component marginals for mixtures of $r$ Bernoulli product distributions over $n$ variables using only $O(nr^2)$ oracle queries. The algorithm repeatedly applies restrictions to $O(r)$ variables, extracts low-degree coefficients, and then recovers the parameters using a moment-based tensor decomposition. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exact reconstruction algorithm in this PGP oracle model with query complexity linear in $n$ and polynomial in $r$.

paragraphs: A mixture of Bernoulli product distributions models binary data through hidden components, each with its own probabilities for the variables. This paper studies recovering those component probabilities and mixture weights from access to a probability generating polynomial. That polynomial may be represented by a probabilistic generating circuit.

The authors establish that parameters are uniquely identifiable for almost all mixtures. They provide a randomized exact-reconstruction algorithm requiring O(nr²) oracle queries for n variables and r components. The procedure repeatedly restricts attention to O(r) variables, extracts low-degree coefficients, and uses a moment-based tensor decomposition to recover the parameters.

The query bound grows linearly with the number of variables and polynomially with the number of components. According to the authors, this is the first exact reconstruction algorithm with those query-complexity properties in this oracle model. The result concerns the stated polynomial-access setting, and its identifiability claim applies to almost all mixtures rather than every possible mixture.
summary.tldr: A randomized algorithm exactly reconstructs Bernoulli mixture parameters using O(nr²) generating-polynomial oracle queries, with identifiability established for almost all mixtures.

title: Fast Reconstruction of Mixtures of Bernoulli Product Distributions

abstract: Standard conformal prediction (CP) procedures are typically formulated in terms of p-values, but reliance on p-values alone limits flexibility, for example, when combining dependent evidence across models or data splits. Recent work has explored e-value formulations for conformal inference, yet a direct connection between p- and e-value formulations in CP has been missing, especially regarding their statistical efficiency. We first identify limitations of classical p-to-e calibrators in the CP setting, showing that they are not set-preserving and can lead to overly conservative prediction sets. To address this, we propose a novel P2E calibrator that converts conformal p-values into e-values without altering the prediction set induced by the original conformal p-value. We establish both theoretically and empirically that our calibrator can yield significant efficiency gains over existing p-to-e calibrators. This e-value formulation enables principled use of recent advances in e-value merging and randomization, where we demonstrate its impact in two applications: cross-conformal prediction (CCP), whose variants typically provide only approximate $1-2\alpha$ coverage, and conformal aggregation (CA). In both cases, our e-value-based methods satisfy the desired $1-\alpha$ coverage guarantee while improving efficiency over standard baselines. More broadly, our approach expands the flexibility of CP and opens new directions for efficient, distribution-free uncertainty quantification.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction commonly uses p-values to construct prediction sets, but combining dependent evidence across models or data splits can be restrictive in that formulation. E-values offer additional ways to combine evidence. This paper examines how to move between the two formulations without needlessly enlarging the resulting prediction sets.

The authors show that classical p-to-e conversions do not preserve conformal prediction sets and can make them overly conservative. Their P2E calibrator converts a conformal p-value into an e-value while keeping the original induced prediction set unchanged. Theory and experiments establish that this can produce substantial efficiency gains over existing conversion methods.

The formulation also enables e-value merging and randomization in cross-conformal prediction and conformal aggregation. For both applications, the proposed methods achieve the desired 1−α coverage guarantee while improving efficiency over standard baselines. This strengthens the coverage available from typical cross-conformal variants, which provide only approximate 1−2α coverage. The contribution connects flexible evidence combination with preservation of useful prediction sets.
summary.tldr: A set-preserving p-to-e calibrator enables efficient conformal evidence combination with 1−α coverage guarantees in two applications.

title: Set-Preserving Calibration from Conformal P-Values to E-Values

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in visual understanding tasks such as visual grounding, segmentation, and captioning. However, their ability to perceive perceptual-level image features remains limited. In this work, we present UniPercept-Bench, a unified framework for perceptual-level image understanding across three key domains: Aesthetics, Quality, Structure and Texture. We establish a hierarchical definition system and construct large-scale datasets to evaluate perceptual-level image understanding. Based on this foundation, we develop a strong baseline UniPercept trained via Domain-Adaptive Pre-Training and Task-Aligned RL, enabling robust generalization across both Visual Rating (VR) and Visual Question Answering (VQA) tasks. UniPercept outperforms existing MLLMs on perceptual-level image understanding and can serve as a plug-and-play reward model for text-to-image generation. This work defines perceptual-level image understanding in the era of MLLMs and, through the introduction of a comprehensive benchmark together with a strong baseline, provides a solid foundation for advancing perceptual-level multimodal image understanding.

This paper focuses on aesthetics, quality, structure, and texture. It introduces UniPercept-Bench to organize and evaluate those aspects of image understanding within a common framework.

The authors establish a hierarchical definition system and construct large-scale datasets for evaluation. They then train UniPercept through domain-adaptive pretraining and task-aligned reinforcement learning. The resulting model is designed to generalize across both visual rating, which assigns assessments to images, and visual question answering, which responds to questions about them.

summary.tldr: UniPercept combines a perceptual image benchmark with a trained model for visual ratings, question answering, and image-generation rewards.

title: UniPercept: Towards Unified Perceptual-Level Image Understanding across Aesthetics, Quality, Structure, and Texture

abstract: Parameter Sharing (PS) is widely used to improve efficiency in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but it can limit behavioral diversity and degrade performance. This limitation stems from gradient conflicts among agents on shared weights, which hinders effective policy learning. To fully characterize this phenomenon, we propose Geometric Gradient Decomposition Analysis that decomposes gradients with respect to weight vector into radial (scale) and tangential (direction) components and uncover a key insight: agents largely agree on directional updates but substantially disagree on scale updates. Consequently, while recent methods split the shared network into agent-specific subnetworks to mitigate conflicts, they also discard shared directional updates, limiting training efficiency. To address this issue, we propose Hyperspherical Parameter Sharing (HPS), which explicitly decouples direction and scale in parameter sharing. Specifically, HPS constrains the shared backbone weights onto a Riemannian manifold(unit hypersphere), enforcing purely directional learning. Building on this, an agent-specific scale generator outputs multiplicative modulation factors to adjust each agent’s scales, thus preserving heterogeneous response magnitudes without disrupting the shared directions. Experiments on SMAC, SMACv2, VMAS and Predator Prey demonstrate that HPS effectively resolves the scale conflict, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Sharing network parameters makes multi-agent reinforcement learning more efficient, but agents can push the same weights toward conflicting updates. HPS analyzes those updates geometrically, separating changes to a weight vector’s direction from changes to its magnitude. The authors find that agents largely agree on directional changes while disagreeing substantially on scale.

That finding motivates sharing directions while allowing agent-specific scales. HPS constrains the shared backbone weights to a unit hypersphere, so shared learning changes their direction. A separate scale generator supplies multiplicative factors for each agent. This lets agents express different response magnitudes while retaining the directional learning they have in common.

The paper argues that splitting a shared network into agent-specific subnetworks can lose useful shared directional updates along with the conflicts. HPS instead targets the identified scale conflict directly. Experiments on SMAC, SMACv2, VMAS, and Predator Prey report significant gains over state-of-the-art methods, supporting this separation as an effective way to combine parameter sharing with behavioral diversity.
summary.tldr: HPS shares weight directions across agents while learning individual scales to reduce gradient conflict without discarding common learning.

title: HPS: Hyperspherical Parameter Sharing for Efficient Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Fine-tuning-as-a-Service (FaaS) enables personalization of large language models (LLMs), but it can weaken safety-alignment under harmful fine-tuning attacks. Recent work has shown that activating harmful-behavior modules during fine-tuning can prevent models from learning undesired behaviors, but its mechanism remains unclear. In this paper, we revisit temporary jailbreaking as a defense against harmful fine-tuning and provide a gradient-level analysis showing that it saturates safety-degrading gradients while preserving benign task-relevant gradients. Based on this insight, we propose a Buffer-and-Reinforce fine-tuning framework that buffers harmful updates during user fine-tuning and reinforces safety after adaptation. Specifically, BufferLoRA induces temporary jailbreaking as a removable adapter to reduce harmful updates during user fine-tuning. After adaptation, ReinforceLoRA, trained to recover refusal behavior under the temporarily jailbroken state, is integrated with UserLoRA via QR decomposition-based merging to reinforce safety while preserving user-task performance. Extensive experiments show that our framework achieves superior safety and utility with no additional safety data during user fine-tuning and minimal computational cost.

paragraphs: Personalizing a language model through fine-tuning can weaken its safety behavior when the training includes harmful examples. This paper studies a counterintuitive defense: temporarily activating harmful behavior during adaptation. Its gradient-level analysis finds that this temporary state saturates gradients that would degrade safety while preserving gradients relevant to benign tasks.

The resulting Buffer-and-Reinforce framework divides protection into two parts. BufferLoRA supplies a removable adapter that induces the temporary jailbroken state and reduces harmful updates during user fine-tuning. After adaptation, ReinforceLoRA strengthens refusal behavior. That adapter is trained to restore refusals while the temporary jailbreak is active, preparing it to counter the disrupted safety behavior.

ReinforceLoRA is then combined with the user adapter using a merging procedure based on QR decomposition, aiming to preserve task performance while reinforcing safety. Experiments report superior safety and utility with minimal computational cost. The framework requires no additional safety data during user fine-tuning, a scope-specific benefit that concerns the adaptation stage rather than every stage of preparing the defense.
summary.tldr: Buffer-and-Reinforce uses a temporary jailbreak adapter to reduce harmful fine-tuning updates, then merges in an adapter that strengthens refusal behavior.

title: Jailbreak to Protect: Buffering and Reinforcing via Temporary Jailbreaking for Safe Fine-Tuning in Large Language Models

abstract: Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) must often support preferences that change online or are specified only after data collection. We study finite-horizon MORL with vector feedback in linear MDPs under two protocols: (i) predictable adversarial preferences revealed before each episode, and (ii) reward-free preference-free exploration (PFE), where exploration observes only transitions and must later answer arbitrary preference queries. Standard reductions are protocol-unsafe: re-scalarizing past stochastic rewards with future weights breaks the martingale structure needed for self-normalized confidence bounds, and hypervolume evaluation must account for episode-start randomization, which yields a deployable convex hull of return vectors. We propose a protocol-safe reward interface that estimates each reward coordinate via regression and performs scalarization only at query time, and we formalize deployable hypervolume semantics with a stability chain from support-function error to hypervolume error. Consequently, we obtain filtration-safe regret bounds for any predictable preference sequence without discretizing the simplex (only $\log m$ dependence) and matching near-minimax rates in linear MDPs, as well as sharp reward-free PFE guarantees: a (near-)minimax decision-optimal query answering rate $\tilde{O}(d^2 U_{\mathrm{ret}}^2/\varepsilon^2)$ and a tight separation from explicit transition-model recovery $\Theta(d(|\mathcal{S}|-1)/\varepsilon_P^2)$. These results connect online learning, preference-free deployment, and hypervolume-aware evaluation through a single protocol-aligned theory.
originalAbstract: Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) must often support preferences that change online or are specified only after data collection. We study finite-horizon MORL with vector feedback in linear MDPs under two protocols: (i) predictable adversarial preferences revealed before each episode, and (ii) reward-free preference-free exploration (PFE), where exploration observes only transitions and must later answer arbitrary preference queries. Standard reductions are protocol-unsafe: re-scalarizing past stochastic rewards with future weights breaks the martingale structure needed for self-normalized confidence bounds, and hypervolume evaluation must account for episode-start randomization, which yields a deployable convex hull of return vectors. We propose a protocol-safe reward interface that estimates each reward coordinate via regression and performs scalarization only at query time, and we formalize deployable hypervolume semantics with a stability chain from support-function error to hypervolume error. Consequently, we obtain filtration-safe regret bounds for any predictable preference sequence without discretizing the simplex (only $\log m$ dependence) and matching near-minimax rates in linear MDPs, as well as sharp reward-free PFE guarantees: a (near-)minimax decision-optimal query answering rate $\tilde{O}(d^2 U_{\mathrm{ret}}^2/\varepsilon^2)$ and a tight separation from explicit transition-model recovery $\Theta(d(|\mathcal{S}|-1)/\varepsilon_P^2)$. These results connect online learning, preference-free deployment, and hypervolume-aware evaluation through a single protocol-aligned theory.

paragraphs: This paper studies finite-horizon multi-objective reinforcement learning in linear Markov decision processes under two information protocols. In one, potentially adversarial preference weights are revealed before each episode. In the other, exploration observes transitions without rewards or preferences, and the collected information must later support arbitrary preference queries.

The analysis identifies why standard shortcuts can break guarantees. Applying future weights to past stochastic rewards disrupts the probabilistic structure used for confidence bounds. The proposed reward interface instead estimates each reward coordinate separately and combines them only when answering a query. The paper also formalizes evaluation when policies may be randomized at episode start, accounting for the resulting convex combinations of returns.

The results give protocol-safe regret bounds with only logarithmic dependence on the number of objectives and near-minimax rates under the stated linear setting. For preference-free exploration, the theory separates learning enough to answer decision queries from explicitly recovering the transition model. This distinction clarifies how the information required for good decisions can differ from the information required for full model reconstruction.
summary.tldr: The paper develops near-minimax multi-objective learning guarantees that respect when preferences and rewards become available.

title: Near-Minimax Multi-Objective RL under Predictable Adversarial Preferences and Preference-Free Exploration in Linear MDPs

abstract: Evolutionary algorithms for adversarial attacks leverage population-based search to discover perturbations without gradient information, but suffer from inefficient crossover operations that destroy adversarial properties through discrete interpolation. We introduce Mode Connectivity Evolutionary Attack (MoCo-EA), which replaces traditional crossover with a novel Bézier crossover operator that optimizes perturbations along a continuous Bézier curve between parent perturbations. Our key insight is that adversarial examples lie on connected manifolds where intermediate points maintain and often enhance attack effectiveness. We demonstrate three findings: (1) Successful adversarial perturbations exhibit mode connectivity; (2) Intermediate points along optimized paths achieve higher transferability than endpoints; (3) Bézier crossover dramatically outperforms discrete genetic operations while reducing convergence time and query requirements. By exploiting the geometric structure of adversarial space through path optimization, MoCo-EA provides an efficient and reliable method. Our work challenges the traditional view of adversarial examples as isolated points and opens new directions for both attack generation and defense research.

paragraphs: Evolutionary adversarial attacks search for input perturbations using populations of candidates, without needing model gradients. A difficulty arises when crossover combines successful candidates: discrete mixing can destroy the properties that made the parent perturbations effective. MoCo-EA changes this operation to use the geometric relationships between successful attacks.

The method optimizes a continuous Bézier curve connecting two parent perturbations and searches along that curve. Its motivation is the observed connectivity of successful adversarial examples: intermediate perturbations on suitable paths can preserve, and sometimes improve, attack effectiveness. This turns crossover into path optimization instead of assuming that discrete combinations of parent components will remain useful.

The paper reports that successful perturbations exhibit mode connectivity, that intermediate points on optimized paths transfer better than the endpoints, and that Bézier crossover outperforms discrete genetic operations while reducing convergence time and model queries. These findings support using connected regions of adversarial space to organize search. They also challenge a view of successful attacks as isolated discoveries by showing how relationships between candidates can contribute directly to attack generation.
summary.tldr: MoCo-EA improves gradient-free adversarial search by replacing discrete crossover with optimized continuous paths between successful perturbations.

title: MoCo-EA: Exploiting Adversarial Mode Connectivity for Efficient Evolutionary Attacks

abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have successfully employed search-based strategies to enhance code generation. However, existing methods typically rely on static, sparse public test cases for verification, leading to pseudo-correctness—where solutions overfit the visible public tests but fail to generalize to hidden test cases. We argue that optimizing against a fixed, weak environment inherently limits robustness. To address this, we propose AdverMCTS, a novel adversarial Monte Carlo Tree Search framework that combats pseudo-correctness by coupling code search with active vulnerability discovery. AdverMCTS formulates generation as a minimax-style game between a Solver agent, which synthesizes code candidates, and an Attacker agent, which evolves to generate targeted test cases that exploit logical divergences in the current solution pool. These discovered tests form a dynamic, progressively hostile filter that penalizes fragile reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AdverMCTS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, effectively reducing false positive rates and forcing the model to generalize beyond the initial constraints. The resources of this work are available at https://github.com/SIMONLQY/AdverMCTS.

paragraphs: Generated code can pass every visible test while still containing logical errors. When a search procedure repeatedly optimizes against a small, fixed test set, it may favor solutions tailored to those examples. The paper calls this pseudo-correctness and argues that improving code search also requires strengthening the environment used to judge candidates.

AdverMCTS couples Monte Carlo Tree Search with an evolving adversary. A Solver agent generates candidate programs, while an Attacker agent develops targeted tests that expose logical differences within the current candidate pool. The two agents form a minimax-style interaction: code candidates face increasingly challenging checks, and newly discovered weaknesses shape subsequent verification.

This makes testing part of the search process rather than a fixed checkpoint. The authors report that AdverMCTS significantly outperforms leading baselines, reduces false positives, and improves generalization beyond the initial tests. These findings support active vulnerability discovery as a way to distinguish robust solutions from programs that merely appear correct under sparse public examples.
summary.tldr: AdverMCTS improves generated code by making program search compete with an agent that continually invents targeted tests.

title: AdverMCTS: Combating Pseudo-Correctness in Code Generation via Adversarial Monte Carlo Tree Search

abstract: By incorporating test-time compute scaling, large reasoning models (LRMs) can solve complex problems through explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning processes. However, they often suffer from overthinking, resulting in redundant token outputs and degraded accuracy. Current methods to mitigate this issue remain limited: training-based approaches require substantial computational resources, while training-free methods rely on well-crafted prompts or unreliable confidence signals. In this work, we investigate early stopping from the perspective of attention distributions and propose a simple method, ASAG, which infers the model’s reasoning state and adaptively adjusts the generation strategy. The proposed framework is training-free and plug-and-play, enabling seamless integration into existing LRMs. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements across mainstream LRMs with varying parameter scales, including the DeepSeek-R1-Distill and Qwen3 series. Specifically, ASAG improves average accuracy by 3.2% while reducing the number of generated tokens by nearly 40% across all reasoning tasks on Qwen3-8B.

paragraphs: Longer reasoning does not always improve a language model’s answer. The paper focuses on overthinking, where extra generated reasoning becomes redundant and can reduce accuracy. Existing remedies either require substantial additional training or depend on carefully designed prompts and confidence signals that may be unreliable.

Attention-State Adaptive Generation, or ASAG, uses attention distributions to infer the model’s reasoning state. It then adjusts the generation strategy adaptively, including the decision to stop reasoning early. The framework requires no training and is designed to plug into existing reasoning models, making internal attention behavior a practical signal for controlling inference.

Experiments across nine benchmarks show consistent improvements in mainstream reasoning models of different sizes, including the DeepSeek-R1-Distill and Qwen3 families. On Qwen3-8B, the authors report a 3.2% improvement in average accuracy alongside nearly 40% fewer generated tokens across the reasoning tasks. The combined result matters because reduced output length accompanies improved correctness: in these evaluations, additional reasoning was sometimes an avoidable cost rather than a useful investment.
summary.tldr: ASAG uses attention distributions to adaptively stop reasoning, improving reported accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens without additional training.

title: Stop When Further Reasoning Won’t Help: Attention-State Adaptive Generation in Reasoning Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in mathematical reasoning, yet persistently suffer from hallucinations and erroneous logic. While formal theorem proving (FTP) shows promise in process-level reliability, it is limited to verification (checking known propositions). This leaves constructive problem-solving (finding unknown terms that satisfy specific conditions) underexplored and disconnected from process-level verifiability. To bridge this gap, we introduce FPS (Formal Problem-Solving), a principled framework to encompass the end-to-end problem-solving process in Lean 4. In FPS, the answer is an unknown metavariable coupled with a proof obligation, forcing it to be mathematically derived and verified. We further present D-FPS (Deductive FPS), which structures solving into forward derivation and backward verification, aligning more closely with human reasoning steps. Three benchmarks of over 1,000 problems are constructed for evaluation: FormalMath500, MiniF2F-Solving, and PutnamBench-Solving. We further propose RPE (Restricted Propositional Equivalence), a symbolic metric that evaluates semantic correctness beyond brittle string matching. Extensive experiments with state-of-the-art provers reveal that solving is significantly harder than proving, highlighting the “alignment tax” required to transition from loose validity checking to constructive, human-aligned reasoning. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Purewhite2019/formal_problem_solving_main.

Experiments with leading provers find that constructing solutions is substantially harder than proving propositions. This result identifies an additional burden in moving toward formally verified problem-solving: systems must discover appropriate mathematical objects while satisfying the logical constraints that certify them.
summary.tldr: FPS connects answer construction with Lean verification and shows that formal problem-solving remains substantially harder than theorem proving.

title: Beyond Theorem Proving: Formulation, Framework and Benchmark for Formal Problem-Solving

abstract: Neural scaling laws describe predictable power-law relationships between model size, dataset size, compute, and performance. While these laws guide the development of modern foundation models, the mechanisms underpinning them remain poorly understood, in part due to the absence of scalable analysis tools. To close this gap, we introduce spectral position: a scalable measure of which eigenvalues of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK) currently drive loss reduction. Applying this measure to scaling experiments, we find that spectral position decreases throughout training: learning shifts from dominant eigenmodes into the spectral tail. Larger models reach further into the tail than smaller models, revealing a size-dependent capacity we call spectral reach. This suggests why larger models achieve lower losses: they sustain learning on weak spectral signals inaccessible to smaller models. We further identify feature learning as a key enabler of spectral reach. It adaptively amplifies gradient magnitudes as learning advances, sustaining progress where frozen representations stall. This points to concrete interventions through architecture and optimizer design.

paragraphs: Scaling laws describe how performance changes with model size, data, and computation, but explaining the mechanism requires tools for observing learning itself. This paper introduces spectral position, a scalable measure of which eigenvalues of the empirical neural tangent kernel are currently associated with loss reduction.

In scaling experiments, spectral position falls during training: learning moves from dominant eigenmodes toward the spectral tail. Larger models reach farther into that tail than smaller models. The authors call this size-dependent ability spectral reach and suggest that it helps explain lower losses in larger models, which sustain learning on weaker spectral signals.

The study identifies feature learning as a key contributor. As training progresses, changing representations adaptively amplify gradient magnitudes, allowing progress where frozen representations stall. This connects model capacity to the continued development of useful features, rather than treating scale only as a parameter count. The findings point toward architecture and optimizer interventions that might improve spectral reach, while the proposed explanation of scaling is grounded in the reported experimental observations.
summary.tldr: Spectral reach tracks how larger models continue learning from weaker spectral signals, with feature learning helping sustain that progress.

title: Spectral Reach: Understanding Neural Scaling as Progress into the Spectral Tail

abstract: General audio source separation is a key capability for multimodal AI systems that can perceive and reason about sound. Despite substantial progress in recent years, existing separation models are either domain-specific, designed for fixed categories such as speech or music, or limited in controllability, supporting only a single prompting modality such as text. In this work, we present SAM AUDIO, a foundation model for general audio separation that unifies text, visual, and temporal span prompting within a single framework. Built on a diffusion transformer architecture, SAM AUDIO is trained with flow matching on large-scale audio data spanning speech, music, and general sounds, and can flexibly separate target sources described by language, visual masks, or temporal spans. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance across a diverse suite of benchmarks, including general sound, speech, music, and musical instrument separation in both in-the-wild and professionally produced audios, substantially outperforming prior general-purpose and specialized systems. Furthermore, we introduce a new real-world separation benchmark with human-labeled multimodal prompts and a reference-free evaluation model that correlates strongly with human judgment.
