paragraphs: Audio separation extracts a desired sound source from a mixture. Existing systems often specialize in a domain such as speech or music, or accept only one way of specifying the target. SAM Audio brings text descriptions, visual masks, and temporal spans into one model, allowing the desired source to be indicated through different kinds of evidence.

The model uses a diffusion transformer trained with flow matching on large-scale data covering speech, music, and general sounds. Its unified design connects broad sound coverage with flexible prompting. This matters because the same separation framework can respond to a language description, a visual selection, or a specified time interval.

The authors report state-of-the-art results across benchmarks for general sounds, speech, music, and individual instruments, covering both naturally recorded and professionally produced audio. They also introduce a real-world benchmark with human-labeled multimodal prompts and a reference-free evaluation model. That evaluator correlates strongly with human judgment, extending the contribution from source separation to assessing separation quality.
summary.tldr: SAM Audio separates diverse sound sources using text, visual, or temporal prompts within one model.

title: SAM Audio: Segment Anything in Audio

abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient inference, yet on static vision benchmarks, they often trail matched ANNs under short simulation horizons. Under a matched-backbone and matched-budget protocol without extra tricks, we find that this ANN-SNN accuracy gap is consistently smaller on representative continuous 1D temporal signal classification benchmarks than on image benchmarks. We attribute this to a mechanism-level mismatch: leaky integration naturally implements causal evidence accumulation over time for native temporal signals, while static images typically require amplitude-to-spike encoding, whose finite-window estimation error becomes non-negligible at short horizons. Guided by this view, we propose a plug-and-play framework that combines Multi-Scale Temporal Encoding (MTE) and Sparsity-Regularized Transform Encoding (STE). MTE replaces naive repetition with multi-scale streams and allocates scale-aligned multi-bit integer spikes to increase per-step information density, and STE replaces a controllable fraction of LIF units with a transform-encoding neuron trained using auxiliary reconstruction and sparsity regularization, with a synthesis branch used only during training. Across diverse 1D datasets and backbone families, MTE$\times$STE consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off over standard SNN baselines and matches or occasionally surpasses ANN counterparts.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks promise efficient inference, but short simulations often leave them less accurate than conventional neural networks on images. Under matched architectures and budgets, this paper finds a consistently smaller accuracy gap on representative continuous one-dimensional signal benchmarks. The authors attribute the difference to how naturally spiking neurons accumulate evidence arriving over time.

Static images typically require conversion from amplitudes to spikes, which introduces estimation error over short windows. Guided by this explanation, the authors combine two encoding methods. Multi-Scale Temporal Encoding supplies streams at different temporal scales and uses scale-aligned, multi-bit integer spikes to carry more information per step. The transform neurons use auxiliary reconstruction and sparsity objectives, with their synthesis branch needed only during training. Across varied one-dimensional datasets and backbone families, the combined framework improves the accuracy-efficiency balance over standard spiking baselines. It matches or sometimes exceeds conventional counterparts, supporting temporal signals as a favorable setting for these designs.
summary.tldr: Multi-scale and sparsity-regularized encoding improve spiking networks’ accuracy-efficiency trade-off for continuous temporal signals, sometimes surpassing conventional counterparts.

title: Narrowing the ANN–SNN Gap for Continuous 1D Temporal Signal Classification with Multi-Scale Temporal Encoding and Sparsity-Regularized Transform Encoding

abstract: Symbolic expressions can effectively characterize and predict circuit behavior, but deriving them directly from circuit schematics is challenging. This process requires accurate visual-to-symbolic construction of circuit structure from images and correct multi-step symbolic derivation, both of which impose strict correctness requirements. This work proposes AutoVSR, an automated framework for visual-to-symbolic generation of circuit expressions using Vision Language Models (VLMs). By reconstructing circuit diagrams into an executable intermediate representation (Executable IR) and leveraging a symbolic solver for reasoning, AutoVSR significantly improves the accuracy of symbolic expression generation. AutoVSR introduces two key innovations: an IR construction method guided by component rule retrieval and verification-based feedback, and a symbolic solver implemented as a planning agent equipped with a symbolic tool library for reliable multi-step derivation. Compared with end-to-end VLM approaches and specialized methods on the main symbolic expression generation task, AutoVSR achieves accuracy improvements of 30.01–59.45% and 41.96–51.84%, respectively. Moreover, AutoVSR surpasses closed-source state-of-the-art VLMs in inference cost and computational efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/LongfeiLi1/AutoVSR.

paragraphs: AutoVSR turns circuit schematic images into mathematical expressions describing circuit behavior. This requires two kinds of correctness: interpreting the components and connections in a picture, and carrying out a valid sequence of symbolic derivations. An error in the reconstructed circuit can undermine the reasoning that follows, even if the algebra itself is sound.

The framework connects visual interpretation to symbolic reasoning through an executable intermediate representation. A vision-language model constructs this representation with help from retrieved component rules and verification feedback. A separate planning agent then performs derivations using a library of symbolic tools. This gives the reasoning process a structured circuit description and explicit tools for its successive steps.

On the main expression-generation task, the paper reports accuracy improvements of 30.01–59.45% over end-to-end vision-language approaches and 41.96–51.84% over specialized methods. It also reports better inference cost and computational efficiency than closed-source state-of-the-art vision-language models. The results support combining verified visual reconstruction with tool-supported symbolic derivation for this demanding image-to-expression task.
summary.tldr: AutoVSR improves circuit-expression generation by combining verified visual reconstruction with a planning agent that uses symbolic tools.

title: AutoVSR: Automatic Visual-to-Symbolic Reasoning for Symbolic Expression Generation from Circuit Schematic

abstract: We propose a new “bi-metric” framework for designing nearest neighbor data structures. Our framework assumes two dissimilarity functions: a ground-truth metric that is accurate but expensive to compute, and a proxy metric that is cheaper but less accurate. In both theory and practice, we show how to construct data structures using only the proxy metric such that the query procedure achieves the accuracy of the expensive metric, while only using a limited number of calls to both metrics. Our theoretical results instantiate this framework for two popular nearest neighbor search algorithms: DiskANN and Cover Tree. In both cases we show that, as long as the proxy metric used to construct the data structure approximates the ground-truth metric up to a bounded factor, our data structure achieves arbitrarily good approximation guarantees with respect to the ground-truth metric. On the empirical side, we apply the framework to the text retrieval problem with two dissimilarity functions evaluated by ML models with vastly different computational costs. We observe that for almost all the large data sets in the BEIR benchmark, our approach achieves a considerably better accuracy-efficiency tradeoff than the alternatives, such as retrieve-then-rerank.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor search becomes expensive when the most accurate way to compare two items requires substantial computation. This paper studies a setting with two distance measures: an expensive measure that defines the desired answers and a cheaper, less accurate proxy. Its goal is to obtain accurate search results while limiting evaluations of both measures.

The framework builds its search data structures using only the cheaper proxy. At query time, it uses the two measures to approach the accuracy defined by the expensive one. The theoretical analysis covers DiskANN and Cover Tree. If the proxy approximates the expensive metric within a bounded factor, the resulting structures can provide arbitrarily good approximation guarantees relative to the expensive metric.

Experiments apply the framework to text retrieval, where different machine-learning models supply comparisons at very different computational costs. On almost all large BEIR datasets examined, the method achieves a better accuracy–efficiency balance than alternatives including retrieve-then-rerank. The contribution connects a conditional search guarantee with a practical way to spend expensive comparisons more effectively.
summary.tldr: A two-metric search framework builds indexes with cheap comparisons while selectively using expensive comparisons to improve retrieval accuracy.

title: A Bi-metric Framework for Efficient Nearest Neighbor Search

abstract: Diffusion-based image synthesis has made AI-generated images (AIGI) increasingly photorealistic, raising urgent concerns about authenticity in applications such as misinformation detection, digital forensics, and content moderation. Despite the substantial advances in AIGI detection, how to correct detected AI-generated images with visible artifacts and restore realistic appearance remains largely underexplored. Moreover, few existing work has established the connection between AIGI detection and artifact correction. To fill this gap, we propose GenShield, a unified autoregressive framework that jointly performs explainable AIGI detection and controllable artifact correction in a closed loop from diagnosis to restoration, revealing a mutually reinforcing relationship between these two tasks. We further introduce a Visual Chain-of-Thought based curriculum learning strategy that enables self-explained, multi-step "diagnose-then-repair" correction with an explicit stopping criterion. A high-quality dataset with large-scale "artifact-restored" pairs is also constructed alongside a unified evaluation pipeline. Extensive experiments on our correction benchmark and mainstream AIGI detection benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization of our method.

Despite the substantial advances in AIGI detection, how to correct detected AI-generated images with visible artifacts and restore realistic appearance remains largely underexplored. Moreover, few existing work has established the connection between AIGI detection and artifact correction. To fill this gap, we propose GenShield, a unified autoregressive framework that jointly performs explainable AIGI detection and controllable artifact correction in a closed loop from diagnosis to restoration, revealing a mutually reinforcing relationship between these two tasks. We further introduce a Visual Chain-of-Thought based curriculum learning strategy that enables self-explained, multi-step "diagnose-then-repair" correction with an explicit stopping criterion. A high-quality dataset with large-scale "artifact-restored" pairs is also constructed alongside a unified evaluation pipeline. Extensive experiments on our correction benchmark and mainstream AIGI detection benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization of our method.

paragraphs: GenShield connects two tasks that are often studied separately: detecting AI-generated images and correcting visible defects in them. Detection identifies evidence of synthetic origin, while correction aims to restore a more realistic appearance. The authors develop a unified autoregressive framework in which diagnosis and restoration form a closed loop, allowing the tasks to reinforce one another.

A visual chain-of-thought curriculum teaches the model to explain its diagnosis and carry out repairs over multiple steps. An explicit stopping criterion determines when the correction process should end. This makes artifact correction a guided sequence of assessments and changes, with control over the repair process rather than an unexplained single output.

The work also contributes a large dataset pairing images containing artifacts with restored versions, together with a unified evaluation pipeline. Experiments on the new correction benchmark and established detection benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization. The findings support studying detection and restoration together, with explanations helping connect identified defects to the subsequent corrections.
summary.tldr: GenShield combines explainable detection of AI-generated images with iterative, controllable correction of their visible artifacts.

title: GenShield: Unified Detection and Artifact Correction for AI-Generated Images

abstract: Event sequences from complex systems, such as clinical workflows, are often sparse and incomplete. As a result, downstream models are trained on data that only partially captures the underlying dynamics. Synthetic sequence generation can augment real data by filling in missing structure and improving coverage of rare patterns, but generated trajectories must remain realistic, satisfy domain constraints, and allow control. We propose the Forward-Chaining Temporal Point Process (FC-TPP), a framework for constraint-aware and controllable sequence generation in continuous time. FC-TPP maintains an explicit latent symbolic state encoding high-level predicates, which evolves through a differentiable multi-hop forward-chaining operator. Logical rules update the latent state based on recent events, while a temporal point process decoder generates future event times and types conditioned on this evolving state. By tying the generative dynamics to multi-hop reasoning in latent space, FC-TPP incorporates symbolic structure throughout generation rather than relying directly on raw event histories. Experiments on synthetic data and four semi-synthetic/real-world benchmarks—LogiCity, MIMIC-IV, EPIC-100, and IKEA ASM—show that FC-TPP achieves higher generation quality under limited and incomplete data, with stronger constraint adherence and greater controllability than purely neural and prior neuro-symbolic baselines.

These findings support maintaining explicit symbolic structure as part of the generative dynamics.

title: Forward-Chaining Temporal Point Process

abstract: Matrix functions such as square root, inverse roots, and orthogonalization play a central role in preconditioned gradient methods for neural network training. This has motivated the development of iterative algorithms that avoid explicit eigendecompositions and rely primarily on matrix multiplications, making them well suited for modern GPU accelerators. We present PRISM (Polynomial-fitting and Randomized Iterative Sketching for Matrix functions computation), a general framework for accelerating iterative algorithms for computing matrix functions. PRISM combines adaptive polynomial approximation with randomized sketching: at each iteration, it fits a polynomial surrogate to the current spectrum via a sketched least-squares problem, adapting to the instance at hand with minimal overhead. We apply PRISM to accelerate Newton–Schulz-like iterations for matrix square roots and orthogonalization, which are core primitives in machine learning. Unlike prior methods, PRISM requires no explicit spectral bounds or singular value estimates; it adapts automatically to the evolving spectrum. Empirically, PRISM accelerates training when integrated into Shampoo and Muon optimizers.

paragraphs: Some neural-network optimizers depend on matrix operations such as square roots and orthogonalization. Computing these operations efficiently matters for overall training speed. PRISM accelerates iterative matrix-function algorithms that mainly use matrix multiplications, preserving an approach suited to modern GPUs without requiring explicit eigendecomposition.

At each iteration, PRISM adapts a polynomial approximation to the matrix’s current spectrum. It does this through a randomized sketch and a least-squares fitting problem, keeping the adaptation overhead small. The framework does not require explicit spectral bounds or singular-value estimates, so it can adjust to the instance as the spectrum evolves.

The authors apply PRISM to Newton–Schulz-like iterations for matrix square roots and orthogonalization. When incorporated into the Shampoo and Muon optimizers, it empirically accelerates neural-network training. The contribution therefore reaches beyond speeding up an isolated numerical operation: it demonstrates that adaptive approximation of the matrix functions used inside optimizers can translate into faster training in the evaluated integrations.
summary.tldr: PRISM adaptively fits polynomial matrix-function approximations using randomized sketches, accelerating training when integrated into Shampoo and Muon.

title: PRISM: Distribution-free Adaptive Computation of Matrix Functions for Accelerating Neural Network Training

abstract: This position paper argues that the dominant paradigm of AI evaluation (which focuses on superhuman autonomous performance and so implicitly targets the goal of replacing humans) is guiding AI development in the wrong direction. Instead, the AI community should pivot to evaluating the performance of human–AI teams. We specify roughly what this would mean and argue that this collaborative shift will foster AI systems that act as true complements to human capabilities and therefore lead to far better societal outcomes than will the current process.
originalAbstract: This position paper argues that the dominant paradigm of AI evaluation (which focuses on superhuman autonomous performance and so implicitly targets the goal of replacing humans) is guiding AI development in the wrong direction. Instead, the AI community should pivot to evaluating the performance of human–AI teams. We specify roughly what this would mean and argue that this collaborative shift will foster AI systems that act as true complements to human capabilities and therefore lead to far better societal outcomes than will the current process.

paragraphs: This position paper questions what AI evaluations encourage developers to build. The authors argue that emphasizing autonomous systems that outperform people implicitly makes human replacement the target. Their concern is therefore broader than whether a particular benchmark measures performance accurately: the choice of evaluation target also shapes the direction of AI development.

They propose shifting that target toward the performance of people working with AI. Under this view, the relevant unit of evaluation is the human–AI team. A system’s contribution would be understood through what the partnership achieves, making its ability to complement human capabilities central to how progress is assessed.

The paper outlines this collaborative direction and argues that adopting it would produce better societal outcomes than the prevailing approach. This is a position about research priorities and their consequences. Its central implication is that deciding who or what gets evaluated helps determine whether future systems are developed primarily as independent performers or as useful partners.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that evaluating human–AI teams would steer development toward systems that complement people and improve societal outcomes.

abstract: Basis functions derived from an undirected graph connecting nearby samples from a Markov decision process (MDP) have proven useful for approximating value functions. The success of this technique is attributed to the smoothness of the basis functions with respect to the state space geometry. This paper explores the properties of bases created from directed graphs which are a more natural fit for expressing state connectivity. Digraphs capture the effect of non-reversible MDPs whose value functions may not be smooth across adjacent states. We provide an analysis using the Dirichlet sum of the directed graph Laplacian to show how the smoothness of the basis functions is affected by the graph’s invariant distribution. Experiments in discrete and continuous MDPs with nonreversible actions demonstrate a significant improvement in the policies learned using directed graph bases.

This paper explores the properties of bases created from directed graphs which are a more natural fit for expressing state connectivity. Digraphs capture the effect of non-reversible MDPs whose value functions may not be smooth across adjacent states. paragraphs: Approximating a value function requires a representation that captures how useful different states are for decision making. Earlier graph-based approaches build basis functions from undirected connections between nearby sampled states. Their usefulness has been attributed to smoothness with respect to the geometry of the state space.

This paper investigates directed graphs, which can express the direction of state connectivity. That distinction matters for non-reversible Markov decision processes, where adjacent states may have substantially different values. The authors analyze the directed graph Laplacian through its Dirichlet sum, showing how the graph's invariant distribution affects the smoothness of the resulting basis functions.

The approach therefore connects approximation geometry with the directional structure of the decision process. It questions whether ordinary adjacency alone is the right guide for constructing smooth value representations. Experiments in both discrete and continuous problems with non-reversible actions report significant improvements in learned policies, supporting directed bases in the settings evaluated.
summary.tldr: Directed graph bases account for non-reversible state connectivity and significantly improve learned policies in the reported experiments.

title: Constructing basis functions from directed graphs for value function approximation

abstract: Distance metric learning and nonlinear dimensionality reduction are two interesting and active topics in recent years. However, the connection between them is not thoroughly studied yet. In this paper, a transductive framework of distance metric learning is proposed and its close connection with many nonlinear spectral dimensionality reduction methods is elaborated. Furthermore, we prove a representer theorem for our framework, linking it with function estimation in an RKHS, and making it possible for generalization to unseen test samples. In our framework, it suffices to solve a sparse eigenvalue problem, thus datasets with 105 samples can be handled. Finally, experiment results on synthetic data, several UCI databases and the MNIST handwritten digit database are shown.

However, the connection between them is not thoroughly studied yet. In this paper, a transductive framework of distance metric learning is proposed and its close connection with many nonlinear spectral dimensionality reduction methods is elaborated. Furthermore, we prove a representer theorem for our framework, linking it with function estimation in an RKHS, and making it possible for generalization to unseen test samples. In our framework, it suffices to solve a sparse eigenvalue problem, thus datasets with 105 samples can be handled. Finally, experiment results on synthetic data, several UCI databases and the MNIST handwritten digit database are shown.

paragraphs: The paper connects two problems: learning how to measure distances between examples and finding a lower-dimensional representation of data. It proposes a transductive framework for distance metric learning and explains its close relationship with several nonlinear spectral dimensionality reduction methods. This gives the two tasks a shared mathematical treatment.

The authors also prove a representer theorem that connects the framework to estimating functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. This connection matters because it makes generalization to previously unseen samples possible. The framework therefore has a route beyond representing only the samples used to construct its initial solution.

Computationally, the framework requires solving a sparse eigenvalue problem. The abstract reports that this permits handling datasets of around one hundred thousand samples. Experiments cover synthetic data, UCI datasets, and handwritten digits from MNIST. Together, the theoretical connection and computational formulation offer a way to study distance learning through established spectral methods.
summary.tldr: A spectral framework connects distance metric learning with nonlinear dimensionality reduction and provides a route to generalizing beyond the observed samples.

title: A transductive framework of distance metric learning by spectral dimensionality reduction

abstract: Shannon’s Noisy-Channel model, which describes how a corrupted message might be reconstructed, has been the corner stone for much work in statistical language and speech processing. The model factors into two components: a language model to characterize the original message and a channel model to describe the channel’s corruptive process. The standard approach for estimating the parameters of the channel model is unsupervised Maximum-Likelihood of the observation data, usually approximated using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. In this paper we show that it is better to maximize the joint likelihood of the data at both ends of the noisy-channel. We derive a corresponding bi-directional EM algorithm and show that it gives better performance than standard EM on two tasks: (1) translation using a probabilistic lexicon and (2) adaptation of a part-of-speech tagger between related languages.

The model factors into two components: a language model to characterize the original message and a channel model to describe the channel’s corruptive process. The standard approach for estimating the parameters of the channel model is unsupervised Maximum-Likelihood of the observation data, usually approximated using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. In this paper we show that it is better to maximize the joint likelihood of the data at both ends of the noisy-channel. paragraphs: A noisy-channel model describes how an original message becomes corrupted and how it might be reconstructed. It separates a language model of the original message from a channel model of the corruption process. The paper focuses on learning the channel parameters without supervision, a task commonly approached by maximizing the likelihood of observed data.

The standard estimation procedure usually uses expectation-maximization, or EM. The authors instead propose maximizing the joint likelihood of data at both ends of the channel and derive a corresponding bidirectional EM algorithm. This changes the estimation objective so that learning accounts for the two ends together.

The method is evaluated on translation with a probabilistic lexicon and on adapting a part-of-speech tagger between related languages. In both tasks, the bidirectional procedure performs better than standard EM. These findings support the proposed joint-likelihood objective for the evaluated applications and show that changing how a noisy-channel model is estimated can improve its usefulness in language-processing tasks.
summary.tldr: Bidirectional EM learns noisy-channel models using joint likelihood at both ends and improves on standard EM in two language-processing tasks.

title: Unsupervised estimation for noisy-channel models

abstract: We present an algorithm, HI-MAT (Hierarchy Induction via Models And Trajectories), that discovers MAXQ task hierarchies by applying dynamic Bayesian network models to a successful trajectory from a source reinforcement learning task. HI-MAT discovers subtasks by analyzing the causal and temporal relationships among the actions in the trajectory. Under appropriate assumptions, HI-MAT induces hierarchies that are consistent with the observed trajectory and have compact value-function tables employing safe state abstractions. We demonstrate empirically that HI-MAT constructs compact hierarchies that are comparable to manually-engineered hierarchies and facilitate significant speedup in learning when transferred to a target task.
originalAbstract: We present an algorithm, HI-MAT (Hierarchy Induction via Models And Trajectories), that discovers MAXQ task hierarchies by applying dynamic Bayesian network models to a successful trajectory from a source reinforcement learning task. HI-MAT discovers subtasks by analyzing the causal and temporal relationships among the actions in the trajectory. Under appropriate assumptions, HI-MAT induces hierarchies that are consistent with the observed trajectory and have compact value-function tables employing safe state abstractions. We demonstrate empirically that HI-MAT constructs compact hierarchies that are comparable to manually-engineered hierarchies and facilitate significant speedup in learning when transferred to a target task.

paragraphs: HI-MAT discovers a hierarchy of reinforcement learning subtasks from a successful trajectory in a source task. It uses dynamic Bayesian network models to analyze causal and temporal relationships among the actions in that trajectory. The goal is to derive a MAXQ task hierarchy automatically from this evidence.

The hierarchy is built by identifying subtasks through those action relationships. Under appropriate assumptions, the authors show that the resulting hierarchy is consistent with the observed trajectory and has compact value-function tables using safe state abstractions. The qualification matters: these structural properties are supported under the stated assumptions, rather than promised for every trajectory and model.

Empirical results show that HI-MAT produces compact hierarchies comparable to manually engineered ones. Transferring these hierarchies to a target task also yields significant learning speedups in the experiments. The contribution combines automatic task decomposition with transfer: the organization discovered from successful behavior in one task can provide useful structure for learning another.
summary.tldr: HI-MAT discovers compact MAXQ hierarchies from successful behavior and empirically accelerates learning when those hierarchies transfer to a target task.

title: Automatic discovery and transfer of MAXQ hierarchies

abstract: We present a variational Bayesian inference algorithm for the stick-breaking construction of the beta process. We derive an alternate representation of the beta process that is amenable to variational inference, and present a bound relating the truncated beta process to its infinite counterpart. We assess performance on two matrix factorization problems, using a non-negative factorization model and a linear-Gaussian model.
originalAbstract: We present a variational Bayesian inference algorithm for the stick-breaking construction of the beta process. We derive an alternate representation of the beta process that is amenable to variational inference, and present a bound relating the truncated beta process to its infinite counterpart. We assess performance on two matrix factorization problems, using a non-negative factorization model and a linear-Gaussian model.

paragraphs: This paper develops variational Bayesian inference for the stick-breaking construction of the beta process. The computational challenge is to work with a prior whose full construction is infinite. The authors derive an alternative representation of the process that is suitable for variational inference, making that representation the foundation of their algorithm.

A second contribution concerns truncation: replacing the infinite construction with a finite one that can be used in computation. The paper provides a bound relating the truncated beta process to its infinite counterpart. This gives a mathematical connection between the finite approximation used in practice and the original probabilistic object, rather than leaving their relationship uncharacterized.

The authors assess the method on two matrix-factorization problems, one using a nonnegative factorization model and the other a linear-Gaussian model. These applications exercise the inference procedure in different modeling settings. Together, the alternative representation, truncation bound, and evaluations establish a route for applying variational inference to this beta-process construction.
summary.tldr: An alternative beta-process representation enables variational inference, supported by a truncation bound and two matrix-factorization evaluations.

title: Variational Inference for Stick-Breaking Beta Process Priors

abstract: As the size of datasets continues to grow, machine learning applications are becoming increasingly limited by the amount of available computational power. Taking advantage of modern hardware requires using multiple parallel programming models targeted at different devices (e.g. CPUs and GPUs). However, programming these devices to run efficiently and correctly is difficult, error-prone, and results in software that is harder to read and maintain. We present OptiML, a domain-specific language (DSL) for machine learning. OptiML is an implicitly parallel, expressive and high performance alternative to MATLAB and C++. OptiML performs domain-specific analyses and optimizations and automatically generates CUDA code for GPUs. We show that OptiML outperforms explicitly parallelized MATLAB code in nearly all cases.
originalAbstract: As the size of datasets continues to grow, machine learning applications are becoming increasingly limited by the amount of available computational power. Taking advantage of modern hardware requires using multiple parallel programming models targeted at different devices (e.g. CPUs and GPUs). However, programming these devices to run efficiently and correctly is difficult, error-prone, and results in software that is harder to read and maintain. We present OptiML, a domain-specific language (DSL) for machine learning. OptiML is an implicitly parallel, expressive and high performance alternative to MATLAB and C++. OptiML performs domain-specific analyses and optimizations and automatically generates CUDA code for GPUs. We show that OptiML outperforms explicitly parallelized MATLAB code in nearly all cases.

paragraphs: Growing datasets increase the computational demands of machine learning. Modern hardware offers parallel execution, but using CPUs and GPUs efficiently can require different programming models. The paper identifies this programming burden as a source of errors and as a reason code becomes harder to read and maintain.

OptiML is a domain-specific language designed for machine learning with implicit parallelism. It is presented as an expressive, high-performance alternative to MATLAB and C++. The system performs analyses and optimizations tailored to the machine-learning domain and automatically generates CUDA code for GPUs. Knowledge of the application domain therefore becomes part of how the system prepares efficient execution.

The reported comparison shows OptiML outperforming explicitly parallelized MATLAB code in nearly all tested cases. This supports the practical value of expressing machine-learning computations in a language whose implementation handles parallel execution. The result is qualified by the evaluated cases and is specifically a performance comparison with parallel MATLAB; the abstract also positions C++ as an alternative programming environment.
summary.tldr: OptiML uses machine-learning-specific analysis and automatic GPU code generation to deliver implicit parallelism and strong performance against parallel MATLAB.

title: OptiML: An Implicitly Parallel Domain-Specific Language for Machine Learning

abstract: In recent years, the crucial importance of metrics in machine learning algorithms has led to an increasing interest for optimizing distance and similarity functions. Most of the state of the art focus on learning Mahalanobis distances (requiring to fulfill a constraint of positive semi-definiteness) for use in a local k-NN algorithm. However, no theoretical link is established between the learned metrics and their performance in classification. In this paper, we make use of the formal framework of good similarities introduced by Balcan et al. to propose an algorithm for learning a non PSD linear similarity optimized in a nonlinear feature space, tailored to a use in a global linear classifier. We show that our approach has the property of stability, allowing us to derive a generalization bound on the classification error. Experiments performed on various datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach compared to state-of-the-art methods and provide evidence that (i) it is fast, (ii) robust to overfitting and (iii) produces very sparse models.

However, no theoretical link is established between the learned metrics and their performance in classification. In this paper, we make use of the formal framework of good similarities introduced by Balcan et al. to propose an algorithm for learning a non PSD linear similarity optimized in a nonlinear feature space, tailored to a use in a global linear classifier. We show that our approach has the property of stability, allowing us to derive a generalization bound on the classification error. Experiments performed on various datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach compared to state-of-the-art methods and provide evidence that (i) it is fast, (ii) robust to overfitting and (iii) produces very sparse models.

paragraphs: Learning a distance or similarity function can strongly affect classification. The paper contrasts its approach with methods that learn positive-semidefinite Mahalanobis distances for local nearest-neighbor classification, where a theoretical connection between the learned metric and classification performance is absent in the account given. Its goal is to build that connection into similarity learning.

Using a formal framework of good similarities, the authors learn a linear similarity without requiring positive semidefiniteness. The similarity is optimized in a nonlinear feature space and designed for a global linear classifier. This aligns the learned similarity with its intended classification use, while allowing a broader form than the constrained distance functions discussed.

The authors prove stability and use it to derive a generalization bound on classification error. Experiments across several datasets support effectiveness relative to contemporary methods and provide evidence of speed, resistance to overfitting, and very sparse models. The theoretical contribution links learning to classification accuracy, while the empirical results address whether that link comes with useful practical behavior.
summary.tldr: A similarity-learning method targets sparse global linear classification and provides a stability-based generalization bound.

title: Similarity Learning for Provably Accurate Sparse Linear Classification

abstract: Hyperplane hashing aims at rapidly searching nearest points to a hyperplane, and has shown practical impact in scaling up active learning with SVMs. Unfortunately, the existing randomized methods need long hash codes and a number of hash tables to achieve reasonable search accuracy. Thus, they suffer from reduced search speed and large memory overhead. To this end, this paper proposes a novel hyperplane hashing technique which yields compact hash codes. The key idea is the bilinear form of the proposed hash functions, which leads to higher collision probability than the existing hyperplane hash functions when using random projections. To further increase the performance, we propose a learning based framework in which bilinear functions are directly learned from the data. This yields compact yet discriminative codes, and also increases the search performance over the random projection based solutions. Large-scale active learning experiments carried out on two datasets with up to one million samples demonstrate the overall superiority of the proposed approach.

Thus, they suffer from reduced search speed and large memory overhead. To this end, this paper proposes a novel hyperplane hashing technique which yields compact hash codes. The key idea is the bilinear form of the proposed hash functions, which leads to higher collision probability than the existing hyperplane hash functions when using random projections. To further increase the performance, we propose a learning based framework in which bilinear functions are directly learned from the data. This yields compact yet discriminative codes, and also increases the search performance over the random projection based solutions. paragraphs: Hyperplane hashing searches quickly for data points near a hyperplane, a task useful for scaling active learning with support vector machines. Existing randomized approaches can require long codes and many hash tables to obtain reasonable accuracy. Those requirements increase memory use and reduce the speed advantage that hashing is intended to provide.

The paper proposes hash functions with a bilinear form to produce more compact codes. With random projections, these functions have higher collision probability than the existing hyperplane hash functions considered. The authors then introduce a framework that learns the bilinear functions directly from data, seeking codes that are both short and able to distinguish useful candidates.

Learning the functions improves search performance over the random-projection solutions reported in the paper. Large-scale active-learning experiments on two datasets, containing up to one million samples, demonstrate overall superiority of the proposed approach. The work links a change in hash-function design to practical improvements in the speed, storage, and search-quality trade-off.
summary.tldr: Bilinear hyperplane hashing produces compact codes, with learned functions further improving search performance in large-scale active-learning experiments.

title: Compact Hyperplane Hashing with Bilinear Functions

abstract: MAP inference for general energy functions remains a challenging problem. While most efforts are channeled towards improving the linear programming (LP) based relaxation, this work is motivated by the quadratic programming (QP) relaxation. We propose a novel MAP relaxation that penalizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the LP pairwise auxiliary variables, and QP equivalent terms given by the product of the unaries. We develop two efficient algorithms based on variants of this relaxation. The algorithms minimize the non-convex objective using belief propagation and dual decomposition as building blocks. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the solutions returned by our algorithms substantially improve over the LP relaxation.
originalAbstract: MAP inference for general energy functions remains a challenging problem. While most efforts are channeled towards improving the linear programming (LP) based relaxation, this work is motivated by the quadratic programming (QP) relaxation. We propose a novel MAP relaxation that penalizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the LP pairwise auxiliary variables, and QP equivalent terms given by the product of the unaries. We develop two efficient algorithms based on variants of this relaxation. The algorithms minimize the non-convex objective using belief propagation and dual decomposition as building blocks. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the solutions returned by our algorithms substantially improve over the LP relaxation.

paragraphs: MAP inference seeks the best joint assignment under a model's energy function, and general instances remain difficult. Linear programming relaxations provide one route to approximate solutions. This paper draws on a quadratic programming relaxation to modify how the relaxed problem represents relationships between variables.

The proposed objective penalizes a Kullback-Leibler divergence between pairwise auxiliary quantities in the linear relaxation and products of unary quantities associated with the quadratic formulation. In effect, it discourages disagreement between these two representations of pairwise behavior. The result links information from the LP and QP viewpoints within a new MAP relaxation.

The authors develop two efficient algorithms for variants of this formulation, using belief propagation and dual decomposition as components. Their objective is nonconvex, so the reported contribution is not an exact global solution guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show substantial improvements over the LP relaxation, demonstrating that the additional consistency penalty can improve the solutions obtained in the studied problems.
summary.tldr: A KL-divergence penalty connects LP and QP representations for MAP inference and substantially improves solutions over the LP relaxation in experiments.

title: LPQP for MAP: Putting LP Solvers to Better Use
